◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

SQL is the universal language of data. Every analyst job description lists it. Every database — Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift — speaks a dialect of SQL. The DataCamp SQL Associate exam and Data Analyst cert both test foundational SQL fluency. Master the basics and you can extract any answer from any structured data.

What SQL is — the simple definition

SQL = STRUCTURED QUERY LANGUAGE
A language for asking questions of relational databases.

You DESCRIBE what you want (declarative), not HOW to get it (imperative).

The database engine figures out the most efficient way to deliver the answer. 
-- Example: Get all customers in California
SELECT name, email
FROM customers
WHERE state = 'CA';

-- You said: "give me name + email of CA customers"
-- The engine handled: which index to use, how to scan, what order, how to filter

RDBMS — the engine under SQL

TermWhat it means
RDBMSRelational Database Management System — software that stores data in tables and lets you query with SQL
TableA 2D structure with rows (records) and columns (fields)
Row / RecordA single entity — one customer, one order, one event
Column / FieldA single attribute — name, price, date
Primary KeyColumn(s) that uniquely identify each row
Foreign KeyColumn that references a primary key in another table — links the two
SchemaThe structure of the database — which tables, which columns, which types, which relationships
DatabaseA collection of related tables (and views, indexes, etc.)

The major SQL dialects

EngineCommon useQuirks to know
PostgreSQLModern web apps, analytics, open-source workloadsStrictest SQL standard. Great window function support.
MySQL / MariaDBWeb apps, WordPress, classic LAMP stackPermissive about some syntax. LIMIT instead of FETCH.
SQL ServerMicrosoft enterprise, .NET stackUses TOP instead of LIMIT. T-SQL extensions.
SQLiteMobile apps, prototypes, single-file databasesWeakly typed. No real schema enforcement.
SnowflakeCloud data warehouseColumnar. Pays per query/storage. Very SQL-standard.
BigQueryGoogle cloud warehouse, massive datasetsStandard SQL with extensions. Backtick-quoted columns.
★ DIALECT TIP

90% of SQL is the same across all engines. The 10% that differs (LIMIT vs TOP, date functions, string concat) is what gets tested on exams. Pick one (PostgreSQL is the most "standard") and learn it well — the rest is small adjustments.

The DataCamp SQL Associate exam uses PostgreSQL syntax. The Tableau exam doesn't focus on dialects.

Declarative vs Imperative — the mental shift

# Imperative (Python — HOW to get the answer)
results = []
for customer in customers:
 if customer.state == 'CA':
 results.append((customer.name, customer.email))
results.sort(key=lambda r: r[0])

-- Declarative (SQL — WHAT you want)
SELECT name, email
FROM customers
WHERE state = 'CA'
ORDER BY name;

You don't tell the database to "loop through each row, check the state, add to a result set." You describe the result you want. The query optimizer figures out the actual execution.

The query lifecycle

▸ WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU SUBMIT A QUERY
  1. Parse — engine reads your SQL and checks syntax
  2. Validate — checks tables/columns exist, you have permissions
  3. Plan — query planner builds an execution plan (which indexes, join order, etc.)
  4. Optimize — picks the cheapest plan based on table statistics
  5. Execute — runs the plan, returns rows

Use EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in Postgres) to see the plan and find slow operations. Covered in ch5/s3.

SQL keywords are case-insensitive — convention is UPPERCASE

-- All three are equivalent
SELECT name FROM customers;
select name from customers;
SeLeCt name FrOm customers;

-- Convention: UPPERCASE keywords, lowercase identifiers
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name
FROM customers
WHERE active = TRUE;

Statement terminators

-- Every SQL statement ends with a semicolon
SELECT * FROM customers;

-- You can run multiple statements separated by ;
SELECT * FROM customers; SELECT * FROM orders;

-- The semicolon is technically optional if you're running one statement,
-- but always include it — required when running scripts or multiple statements

Comments

-- Single-line comment (two dashes)
SELECT name FROM customers; -- Comment at end of line

/* Multi-line
 block comment
 works in most dialects */
SELECT name FROM customers;

KeywordPurposeCovered in

SQL clause execution order — important and counterintuitive

SQL EVALUATES IN THIS ORDER (not the order you write!)
1. FROM — pick the source table(s)
2. WHERE — filter rows
3. GROUP BY — group filtered rows
4. HAVING — filter groups
5. SELECT — pick columns / compute expressions
6. DISTINCT — remove duplicate rows
7. ORDER BY — sort the result
8. LIMIT — restrict number of rows
⚠ EXAM TRAP

You write SELECT first, but it runs AFTER WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING. This is why:

-- This WORKS in some dialects, FAILS in others
SELECT salary * 1.1 AS new_salary
FROM employees
WHERE new_salary > 50000; -- ERROR: new_salary not yet defined when WHERE runs

-- You have to repeat the expression
SELECT salary * 1.1 AS new_salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary * 1.1 > 50000;
-- or use a CTE / subquery

SELECT aliases are NOT available in WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING (with rare dialect exceptions). They ARE available in ORDER BY.

Whitespace and formatting

-- All three are equivalent — SQL ignores whitespace
SELECT name,email FROM customers WHERE state='CA';

SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE state = 'CA';

SELECT
 name,
 email
FROM
 customers
WHERE
 state = 'CA';

-- Common convention: one clause per line, indented
-- Helps readability on complex queries

Your first query — a worked example

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
-- Imagine a customers table:
-- | id | first_name | last_name | email | state | signup_date |
-- |----|-----------|-----------|----------------|-------|-------------|
-- | 1 | Alice | Smith | alice@x.com | CA | 2024-01-15 |
-- | 2 | Bob | Jones | bob@y.com | NY | 2024-02-10 |
-- | 3 | Carol | Davis | carol@z.com | CA | 2024-03-22 |

-- Question: Who signed up in California in 2024?
SELECT first_name, last_name, signup_date
FROM customers
WHERE state = 'CA'
 AND signup_date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND signup_date < '2025-01-01'
ORDER BY signup_date;

-- Result:
-- | first_name | last_name | signup_date |
-- | Alice | Smith | 2024-01-15 |
-- | Carol | Davis | 2024-03-22 |

NULL — the third boolean value

-- NULL is NOT zero. NULL is NOT empty string. NULL means "no value / unknown".
-- It has special comparison behavior:

SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = NULL; -- WRONG! Always 0 rows
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email IS NULL; -- CORRECT

SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email != NULL; -- WRONG! Always 0 rows
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL; -- CORRECT
⚠ THE #1 SQL BUG

Beginners use = NULL and get zero rows back. Always use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

NULL also makes aggregates and comparisons behave oddly:

  • NULL = NULL → NULL (not TRUE!)
  • NULL + 5 → NULL
  • COUNT(*) includes NULLs; COUNT(column) excludes NULLs
  • AVG(column) ignores NULLs (denominator excludes them)
★ ON THE EXAM

"What is SQL?" → Structured Query Language; declarative; queries relational databases.

"Test for NULL?" → IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never = NULL.

"SQL execution order?" → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

"Can I use a SELECT alias in WHERE?" → No (with rare exceptions). Yes in ORDER BY.

"Primary key vs foreign key?" → PK uniquely identifies rows in this table; FK references PK of another table.

"NULL = NULL?" → NULL (not TRUE).

"COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)?" → COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) excludes NULL.

"PostgreSQL vs MySQL LIMIT?" → Both use LIMIT. SQL Server uses TOP.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • SQL is declarative — you describe the result, the engine plans the execution
  • An RDBMS organizes data in tables with rows and columns; primary keys identify rows; foreign keys link tables
  • Major dialects (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, etc.) share 90% syntax — focus on Postgres for DataCamp
  • Keywords are case-insensitive; UPPERCASE convention helps readability
  • SQL statements end with semicolons; comments use -- or /* ... */
  • Execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
  • NULL means "unknown" — use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never = NULL
  • COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) excludes NULLs
  • Whitespace is ignored — format for readability

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

SELECT, FROM, and WHERE are 80% of SQL. Every analytics question starts here. Once you can read and filter a table, you can answer any single-table question. The DataCamp SQL Associate exam tests these in every section, and they're the foundation for everything in the next 20 sections.

The basic shape of a query

CORE PATTERN
SELECT columns FROM table WHERE conditions;

Read aloud: "select these columns from this table where these conditions are true"

Optional: ORDER BY, LIMIT, GROUP BY, HAVING — covered in later sections. 
-- Simplest query — get all rows, all columns
SELECT * FROM customers;

-- Specific columns
SELECT first_name, last_name, email
FROM customers;

-- With filter
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM customers
WHERE state = 'CA';

SELECT: choosing what to return

-- All columns (avoid in production — fragile when schema changes)
SELECT * FROM customers;

-- Specific columns (preferred)
SELECT id, first_name, last_name
FROM customers;

-- Computed columns (expressions)
SELECT
 first_name,
 last_name,
 price * quantity AS revenue, -- multiply two columns
 UPPER(first_name) AS upper_name, -- function call
 'Hello ' || first_name AS greeting -- string concatenation (Postgres ||)
FROM orders;

-- Literals (constants)
SELECT
 'New York' AS city,
 100 AS bonus,
 first_name
FROM customers;

Column aliases — AS

-- Rename columns in the output (no impact on underlying table)
SELECT
 first_name AS fname,
 last_name AS lname,
 salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees;

-- AS is optional in most dialects
SELECT first_name fname FROM employees; -- works in Postgres/MySQL

-- Aliases with spaces or special characters — use double quotes
SELECT
 first_name AS "First Name",
 salary * 12 AS "Annual Salary"
FROM employees;
★ QUOTES MATTER

Single quotes 'CA' = string LITERAL (a value)

Double quotes "First Name" = column/table IDENTIFIER (a name)

Backticks `first_name` = column identifier in MySQL/BigQuery (not in Postgres)

Mixing these up is one of the most common SQL errors.

FROM: where the data lives

-- Simplest — one table
SELECT * FROM customers;

-- With schema prefix
SELECT * FROM public.customers; -- "public" is the default schema in Postgres
SELECT * FROM sales.orders; -- a different schema

-- With alias (saves typing on long queries with joins)
SELECT c.first_name, c.email
FROM customers c;

-- Or with AS
SELECT c.first_name
FROM customers AS c;

WHERE: filtering rows

-- Comparison operators
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE state = 'CA'; -- equals
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE age > 18; -- greater than
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE state != 'NY'; -- not equal (also: <>)
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE signup_date >= '2024-01-01';

-- Multiple conditions with AND
SELECT *
FROM customers
WHERE state = 'CA'
 AND age >= 18;

-- OR for either condition
SELECT *
FROM customers
WHERE state = 'CA'
 OR state = 'NY';

-- NOT to invert
SELECT *
FROM customers
WHERE NOT state = 'CA';
-- Equivalent to:
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE state != 'CA';

-- Combining — use parentheses to make grouping explicit
SELECT *
FROM customers
WHERE (state = 'CA' OR state = 'NY')
 AND age >= 18;
⚠ PRECEDENCE TRAP

AND binds tighter than OR. Without parens, this:

WHERE state = 'CA' OR state = 'NY' AND age >= 18

means CA OR (NY AND 18+) — NOT what you wanted. Always parenthesize mixed AND/OR.

WHERE: string comparisons

-- Exact match (case-sensitive in most dialects)
WHERE first_name = 'Alice';

-- Postgres is case-sensitive by default
WHERE first_name = 'alice'; -- 0 rows if data has 'Alice'

-- Case-insensitive comparison
WHERE LOWER(first_name) = 'alice';
WHERE first_name ILIKE 'alice'; -- Postgres only

-- Pattern matching with LIKE
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com'; -- ends with @gmail.com
WHERE first_name LIKE 'A%'; -- starts with A
WHERE first_name LIKE '_lice'; -- _ = exactly one character (Alice, Blice, etc.)
WHERE phone LIKE '555-____'; -- exactly 4 chars after 555-

-- % = any number of characters (zero or more)
-- _ = exactly one character
-- ILIKE = case-insensitive LIKE (Postgres)
-- For MySQL/others, use LOWER() comparisons

WHERE: NULL handling

-- WRONG — always returns 0 rows
WHERE email = NULL;
WHERE email != NULL;

-- CORRECT
WHERE email IS NULL;
WHERE email IS NOT NULL;

-- Common pattern: filter out NULLs before working with the value
SELECT first_name, email
FROM customers
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
 AND email LIKE '%@%';

-- Use COALESCE to substitute a default when NULL
SELECT first_name, COALESCE(email, 'no-email@example.com') AS email
FROM customers;

WHERE: numeric and date ranges

-- Numeric ranges
WHERE age >= 18 AND age <= 65;
WHERE age BETWEEN 18 AND 65; -- inclusive both ends
WHERE age NOT BETWEEN 18 AND 65;

-- Dates — use ISO format 'YYYY-MM-DD' (works in all dialects)
WHERE signup_date >= '2024-01-01';
WHERE signup_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31';

-- Watch out: BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31' MISSES anything on 2024-12-31 with a time component
-- e.g. '2024-12-31 14:00:00' > '2024-12-31 00:00:00'
-- Safer: use >= and < with the start of the next period
WHERE signup_date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND signup_date < '2025-01-01';

WHERE: set membership with IN

-- Awkward with OR
WHERE state = 'CA' OR state = 'NY' OR state = 'TX' OR state = 'FL';

-- Cleaner with IN
WHERE state IN ('CA', 'NY', 'TX', 'FL');

-- NOT IN to exclude
WHERE state NOT IN ('CA', 'NY');

-- IN with a subquery (covered in ch4)
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM premium_customers);
⚠ NOT IN + NULL TRAP

If any value in the IN list is NULL, NOT IN returns NO ROWS — even if it would otherwise match. This is because x NOT IN (...) compares against each value, and a NULL comparison is unknown, so the whole condition is unknown (false).

-- Surprising result: returns 0 rows even though many customers don't have NULL state
WHERE state NOT IN ('CA', 'NY', NULL);

-- Fix: filter NULLs in the subquery or list
WHERE state NOT IN ('CA', 'NY')
 AND state IS NOT NULL;

WHERE: filtering by computed expression

-- You can compute on the fly in WHERE
WHERE price * quantity > 100;
WHERE LOWER(email) LIKE '%@gmail.com';
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM signup_date) = 2024;
WHERE first_name || ' ' || last_name = 'Alice Smith';
★ PERFORMANCE TIP

Functions on indexed columns kill index usage. If you have an index on signup_date:

-- SLOW (can't use index)
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM signup_date) = 2024;

-- FAST (can use index)
WHERE signup_date >= '2024-01-01' AND signup_date < '2025-01-01';

Worked example — building from a question

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Translating a question to SQL

Question: "Show me all premium customers in California or New York who signed up in the last year, with their name and email."

Decompose:

  • Source: customers table
  • Columns needed: name, email
  • Filters: tier=premium AND state in (CA, NY) AND signup_date >= one year ago
SELECT
 first_name,
 last_name,
 email
FROM customers
WHERE tier = 'premium'
 AND state IN ('CA', 'NY')
 AND signup_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year';

Notice:

  • Each filter on its own line — easy to add/remove conditions
  • Indented WHERE clauses align visually
  • Used IN instead of state='CA' OR state='NY'
  • Used CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year' instead of hardcoded date — query stays current

Common SELECT/WHERE mistakes

⚠ TOP 5 BEGINNER MISTAKES
  1. WHERE col = NULL instead of IS NULL
  2. Mixing AND/OR without parens
  3. Using single quotes around column names ('name' instead of name)
  4. Using double quotes around string literals ("CA" instead of 'CA')
  5. SELECT * in production code — fragile when schema changes
★ ON THE EXAM

"Filter rows where col is empty?" → WHERE col IS NULL (NOT = NULL).

"Filter multiple values?" → WHERE state IN ('CA', 'NY', 'TX').

"Filter date range?" → WHERE date >= 'start' AND date < 'next_period_start' (safer than BETWEEN with timestamps).

"Pattern match for emails?" → WHERE email LIKE '%@domain.com'.

"Case-insensitive search in Postgres?" → ILIKE or LOWER() comparison.

"NOT IN (val1, val2, NULL)?" → returns 0 rows (NULL pollutes NOT IN).

"AND vs OR precedence?" → AND binds tighter than OR. Use parens.

"Aliases — quotes or no?" → No quotes unless the alias has spaces, then use double quotes.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • The core query: SELECT cols FROM table WHERE conditions
  • Avoid SELECT * in production — explicit columns are safer
  • Use aliases (AS) to rename columns; double quotes only for spaces/special chars
  • Single quotes = string literals; double quotes = identifiers; backticks = MySQL identifiers
  • Comparison: = != < > <= >= (also <> for not-equal)
  • Combine conditions with AND, OR, NOT — parenthesize when mixed
  • NULL: use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL; NOT IN with NULL returns no rows
  • Sets: WHERE col IN (...); ranges: BETWEEN (inclusive) or >= AND <
  • Patterns: LIKE with % (any chars) and _ (one char); ILIKE in Postgres for case-insensitive
  • Functions on indexed columns can prevent index use — restructure when possible

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

ORDER BY, LIMIT, and DISTINCT are the three keywords you reach for once you can get the right rows. They shape how results are presented and let you preview big tables without crashing your IDE. The DataCamp SQL Associate exam tests these heavily, especially in combination — "top 5 customers by revenue" is ORDER BY + LIMIT + JOIN, the most common pattern in real analytics work.

ORDER BY — sorting results

-- Sort ascending (default — A→Z, 0→9, oldest→newest)
SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY last_name;
SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY last_name ASC; -- explicit ASC

-- Sort descending (Z→A, 9→0, newest→oldest)
SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY last_name DESC;

-- Sort by multiple columns (primary, then tiebreaker)
SELECT * FROM customers
ORDER BY state ASC, last_name ASC;
-- All California rows first, alphabetical by last_name within CA
-- Then all New York rows alphabetical, etc.

-- Mix directions per column
SELECT * FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date DESC, total ASC;
-- Most recent dates first; within same date, smallest totals first

ORDER BY by column position

-- You CAN sort by position number (1-indexed, refers to SELECT list)
SELECT first_name, last_name, signup_date
FROM customers
ORDER BY 3 DESC; -- sort by signup_date (3rd column)

-- Equivalent to:
ORDER BY signup_date DESC

-- ⚠ Avoid in production — fragile if SELECT list changes
-- Useful for ad-hoc queries with complex computed columns

ORDER BY with aliases

-- Aliases ARE allowed in ORDER BY (unlike WHERE/HAVING)
SELECT
 first_name,
 last_name,
 salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY annual_salary DESC; -- works because SELECT runs before ORDER BY

-- You can also re-express the calculation
ORDER BY salary * 12 DESC; -- also works

ORDER BY with NULLs

⚠ DIALECT DIFFERENCE

NULL sort behavior differs by engine:

  • PostgreSQL: NULLs sort LAST in ASC, FIRST in DESC
  • MySQL/SQL Server: NULLs sort FIRST in ASC, LAST in DESC
  • Oracle: NULLs sort LAST by default

To control explicitly (Postgres/Oracle):

ORDER BY signup_date NULLS LAST;
ORDER BY signup_date DESC NULLS FIRST;

Workaround for engines without NULLS FIRST/LAST (MySQL):

ORDER BY CASE WHEN signup_date IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, signup_date;

Sort with CASE for custom order

-- Default alphabetical sort doesn't match business priority
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY status;
-- Result: cancelled, completed, processing, shipped, etc. (alphabetical)

-- Custom order — what you actually want
SELECT * FROM orders
ORDER BY CASE status
 WHEN 'processing' THEN 1
 WHEN 'shipped' THEN 2
 WHEN 'delivered' THEN 3
 WHEN 'cancelled' THEN 4
 ELSE 5
END;
-- Result in workflow order: processing first, cancelled last

LIMIT — restricting how many rows

-- Postgres, MySQL, SQLite — LIMIT
SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY signup_date DESC LIMIT 5;
-- Returns 5 most recent customers

-- SQL Server — TOP (placed in SELECT clause)
SELECT TOP 5 * FROM customers ORDER BY signup_date DESC;

-- Oracle — FETCH (standard SQL, also works in newer Postgres)
SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY signup_date DESC FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;

LIMIT for previewing big tables

-- ALWAYS add LIMIT when exploring an unfamiliar table
SELECT * FROM events LIMIT 10;
-- Returns first 10 rows — fast even if events has 100M rows

-- Without LIMIT, this could lock up your IDE for minutes (or hours)
SELECT * FROM events;
★ FIRST 10 IS NOT NECESSARILY THE FIRST 10

Without ORDER BY, LIMIT 10 returns ANY 10 rows — typically whatever's physically stored first, but not guaranteed. Add ORDER BY to get a deterministic preview:

SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY id LIMIT 10; -- first 10 by ID
SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10; -- 10 most recent

LIMIT with OFFSET — pagination

-- Skip the first N, return the next M
SELECT * FROM customers
ORDER BY signup_date DESC
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;
-- Skip 20, take 10 — i.e., rows 21-30

-- Page 1: OFFSET 0, LIMIT 10 → rows 1-10
-- Page 2: OFFSET 10, LIMIT 10 → rows 11-20
-- Page 3: OFFSET 20, LIMIT 10 → rows 21-30

-- Shorter syntax in MySQL/Postgres: LIMIT offset, count
SELECT * FROM customers LIMIT 20, 10; -- MySQL: skip 20, take 10
⚠ OFFSET IS SLOW ON BIG TABLES

To return OFFSET 1000000, the database has to find AND read AND discard the first million rows. For deep pagination, use keyset/cursor pagination instead:

-- Slow on large tables
SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 1000000;

-- Fast — uses index to skip directly
SELECT * FROM events WHERE id > 1000000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 10;

DISTINCT — removing duplicates

-- Get unique values of a column
SELECT DISTINCT state FROM customers;
-- Returns each state ONCE, even if 1000 customers share it

-- DISTINCT applies to ALL selected columns combined
SELECT DISTINCT state, city FROM customers;
-- Returns each unique (state, city) PAIR

-- Common patterns:
SELECT DISTINCT product_category FROM products
ORDER BY product_category;
-- "What categories exist?"

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders;
-- "How many unique customers placed orders?"

DISTINCT vs GROUP BY

-- These two are equivalent for "show unique X":
SELECT DISTINCT state FROM customers;
SELECT state FROM customers GROUP BY state;

-- Use DISTINCT when you only need unique values
-- Use GROUP BY when you also need to AGGREGATE per group
SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers
GROUP BY state;
-- DISTINCT cannot do this — you need GROUP BY for the count
★ DISTINCT WITH ORDER BY

The ORDER BY must reference columns that ARE in the DISTINCT list (or are constants):

-- VALID
SELECT DISTINCT state FROM customers ORDER BY state;

-- INVALID in standard SQL — signup_date is not in DISTINCT
SELECT DISTINCT state FROM customers ORDER BY signup_date;
-- Error: "ORDER BY expressions must appear in select list"

DISTINCT in aggregates

-- COUNT — total rows vs unique values
SELECT
 COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
 COUNT(customer_id) AS orders_with_customer,
 COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers
FROM orders;

-- Sample result:
-- total_orders: 10000
-- orders_with_customer: 9950 (50 orders have NULL customer)
-- unique_customers: 3200 (3200 distinct customers)

-- Works in other aggregates too
SELECT SUM(DISTINCT amount) FROM payments; -- rare; sums the unique values
SELECT AVG(DISTINCT score) FROM tests; -- rare

Combining all three: ORDER BY + LIMIT + DISTINCT

-- Common pattern: "top 10 states by customer count"
SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS num_customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY num_customers DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- "5 most recent unique signup dates"
SELECT DISTINCT signup_date
FROM customers
ORDER BY signup_date DESC
LIMIT 5;

-- "10 customers who signed up most recently"
SELECT first_name, last_name, signup_date
FROM customers
ORDER BY signup_date DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- "Top 5 unique product categories alphabetically"
SELECT DISTINCT category
FROM products
ORDER BY category
LIMIT 5;

Worked example — building a "latest activity" view

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Show the 10 most recent customers, sorted newest first. Then show me what unique states they're from."

-- Step 1: 10 most recent customers
SELECT first_name, last_name, state, signup_date
FROM customers
ORDER BY signup_date DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Result (10 rows):
-- Alice | Smith | CA | 2025-01-22
-- Bob | Jones | NY | 2025-01-21
-- Carol | Davis | CA | 2025-01-21
-- ...

-- Step 2: Unique states among those 10
-- (use a subquery — covered in ch4, but here's a preview)
SELECT DISTINCT state
FROM (
 SELECT state FROM customers
 ORDER BY signup_date DESC
 LIMIT 10
) AS recent_customers;

-- Result: ['CA', 'NY', 'TX']

Common mistakes

⚠ TOP BUGS WITH ORDER BY / LIMIT / DISTINCT
  1. LIMIT without ORDER BY on big tables — non-deterministic results, you might get different rows each query
  2. DISTINCT applied per-column when you wanted unique combos — DISTINCT is always across all selected columns
  3. ORDER BY position reference (1, 2, 3) that breaks when SELECT list changes
  4. OFFSET for deep pagination on big tables — slow; use keyset pagination
  5. DISTINCT when you should use GROUP BY (or vice versa) — DISTINCT is for unique values only, GROUP BY also aggregates
  6. Forgetting NULLS behavior in sort — varies by dialect
★ ON THE EXAM

"Sort descending?" → ORDER BY col DESC.

"Sort by multiple columns?" → ORDER BY col1, col2 DESC. Comma-separated, direction applies per column.

"Top 5 rows?" → LIMIT 5 (with ORDER BY for determinism).

"Top 5 in SQL Server?" → SELECT TOP 5 ... (no LIMIT in T-SQL).

"Pagination?" → LIMIT N OFFSET M (skip M, take N).

"Unique values?" → SELECT DISTINCT col.

"Unique combinations?" → SELECT DISTINCT col1, col2 (applies to all columns together).

"Count unique?" → COUNT(DISTINCT col).

"DISTINCT vs GROUP BY?" → DISTINCT is for uniqueness only; GROUP BY also aggregates per group.

"NULLS LAST in MySQL?" → not directly supported; use ORDER BY CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, col.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • ORDER BY sorts results — default ASC, use DESC for reverse
  • Multiple sort keys are comma-separated; each can have its own direction
  • Aliases ARE allowed in ORDER BY (unlike WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING)
  • NULL sort behavior varies by dialect — use NULLS FIRST/LAST in Postgres/Oracle
  • Use CASE in ORDER BY for custom (non-alphabetical) ordering
  • LIMIT restricts row count — Postgres/MySQL/SQLite use LIMIT, SQL Server uses TOP, Oracle uses FETCH
  • Always pair LIMIT with ORDER BY for deterministic results
  • OFFSET is slow on large tables — use keyset pagination (WHERE id > last_seen_id) for deep pages
  • DISTINCT removes duplicates — applies to ALL selected columns combined
  • COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-null values; useful for "how many unique customers"
  • DISTINCT vs GROUP BY: both deduplicate, but GROUP BY also enables aggregation

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

You can't filter data effectively without understanding SQL's operators and the strange behavior of NULL. The DataCamp SQL Associate exam tests NULL handling in almost every section because it's the #1 source of subtle bugs. Once you understand three-valued logic (TRUE / FALSE / NULL), most "why isn't this query working?" mysteries disappear.

Comparison operators

OperatorMeaningExample
=Equal toWHERE state = 'CA'
!= or <>Not equal to (both work; <> is standard)WHERE state <> 'NY'
< >Less than / greater thanWHERE age > 18
<= >=Less/greater than or equalWHERE score >= 70
BETWEENBetween two values (inclusive)WHERE age BETWEEN 18 AND 65
INEquals any value in a setWHERE state IN ('CA','NY')
LIKEPattern match (% any chars, _ one char)WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com'
IS NULLTests for NULL (NEVER use = NULL)WHERE phone IS NULL
EXISTSTrue if subquery returns any rowsWHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ...)

Mathematical operators

SELECT
 price + tax AS total, -- addition
 price - discount AS net, -- subtraction
 quantity * price AS subtotal, -- multiplication
 total / count AS avg_per_item, -- division
 price % 100 AS remainder -- modulo (most dialects)
FROM orders;

-- Integer division behavior varies:
-- Postgres: 10 / 3 = 3 (integer), 10.0 / 3 = 3.333 (float)
-- MySQL: 10 / 3 = 3.3333 always (uses DIV for integer)
-- SQL Server: 10 / 3 = 3 (integer), 10.0 / 3 = 3.333
⚠ INTEGER DIVISION TRAP

In Postgres and SQL Server, dividing two integers gives an integer (truncated). This can silently produce wrong percentages:

-- WRONG: gives 0 because both sides are int
SELECT 50 / 100 AS pct; -- 0

-- RIGHT: cast to numeric/decimal
SELECT 50.0 / 100 AS pct; -- 0.50
SELECT CAST(50 AS NUMERIC) / 100; -- 0.50
SELECT 50::numeric / 100; -- Postgres shorthand
SELECT 50 * 1.0 / 100; -- common trick

-- For "percent of total":
SELECT 100.0 * SUM(passed) / COUNT(*) AS pass_pct
FROM tests;

Logical operators: AND, OR, NOT

-- AND — all conditions must be true
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE state = 'CA' AND age >= 18;

-- OR — any condition true
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE state = 'CA' OR state = 'NY';

-- NOT — invert a condition
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE NOT state = 'CA';
-- Equivalent to: WHERE state <> 'CA'

-- Chain freely
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE total > 100
 AND status = 'completed'
 AND order_date >= '2024-01-01';

Operator precedence — AND binds tighter than OR

⚠ THE PARENTHESES TRAP

Mixed AND/OR without parens evaluates AND first. This:

WHERE state = 'CA' OR state = 'NY' AND age >= 18

...actually means:

WHERE state = 'CA' OR (state = 'NY' AND age >= 18)

So you get ALL Californians (regardless of age) plus only adult New Yorkers.

Always parenthesize mixed AND/OR:

WHERE (state = 'CA' OR state = 'NY') AND age >= 18

Precedence ranking (high to low)

RankOperators
1 (highest)NOT
2Comparisons: = < > etc.; IS IN LIKE BETWEEN
3AND
4 (lowest)OR

The NULL behavior — three-valued logic

SQL HAS THREE TRUTH VALUES, NOT TWO
Every comparison can return: TRUE, FALSE, or NULL (unknown).

WHERE only passes rows where the condition is TRUE.
Rows where the condition is NULL are DROPPED — same as FALSE for filtering.

This single fact explains 90% of NULL-related bugs.

NULL comparison truth table

-- Comparisons with NULL ALWAYS return NULL
NULL = NULL → NULL (NOT TRUE!)
NULL = 5 → NULL
NULL <> 5 → NULL
NULL < 5 → NULL
NULL + 5 → NULL
NULL || 'text' → NULL (string concat)

-- This means:
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE phone = NULL; -- 0 rows (NULL is not TRUE)
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE phone <> NULL; -- 0 rows
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE phone IS NULL; -- ✓ CORRECT
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE phone IS NOT NULL;

Three-valued logic for AND / OR / NOT

ABA AND BA OR B
TRUETRUETRUETRUE
TRUEFALSEFALSETRUE
TRUENULLNULLTRUE
FALSEFALSEFALSEFALSE
FALSENULLFALSENULL
NULLNULLNULLNULL

Key insight: TRUE OR NULL = TRUE (short-circuits). FALSE AND NULL = FALSE (short-circuits). All others stay NULL.

NULL pitfall: NOT IN with NULL values

-- Imagine a column suppliers.is_blocked that has values: TRUE, FALSE, NULL
-- And you want suppliers NOT in the blocked set:

SELECT * FROM all_suppliers
WHERE supplier_id NOT IN (
 SELECT supplier_id FROM suppliers WHERE is_blocked
);
-- If the subquery returns ANY NULL supplier_id, this query returns ZERO ROWS!
-- Why? "x NOT IN (a, b, NULL)" expands to:
-- x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL
-- The last comparison is NULL, so the whole condition is NULL → row dropped.

-- FIX: filter out NULLs in the subquery
SELECT * FROM all_suppliers
WHERE supplier_id NOT IN (
 SELECT supplier_id FROM suppliers
 WHERE is_blocked AND supplier_id IS NOT NULL
);

-- OR use NOT EXISTS (which handles NULLs correctly):
SELECT * FROM all_suppliers a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM suppliers s
 WHERE s.supplier_id = a.supplier_id AND s.is_blocked
);

NULL handling functions

-- COALESCE — returns first non-NULL argument
SELECT
 COALESCE(phone, mobile, 'no contact') AS contact
FROM customers;
-- If phone exists, use it; else mobile; else 'no contact'

-- NULLIF — returns NULL if two values are equal (useful for div-by-zero)
SELECT
 revenue / NULLIF(orders, 0) AS revenue_per_order
FROM stores;
-- Without NULLIF, divide-by-zero raises an error
-- With NULLIF, dividing by 0 gives NULL instead

-- IFNULL (MySQL) / ISNULL (SQL Server) — 2-arg shortcut
SELECT IFNULL(phone, 'none') FROM customers; -- MySQL
SELECT ISNULL(phone, 'none') FROM customers; -- SQL Server
-- COALESCE is the portable equivalent and supports more args

-- CASE for complex NULL logic
SELECT
 CASE
 WHEN phone IS NULL AND mobile IS NULL THEN 'no contact'
 WHEN phone IS NULL THEN mobile
 ELSE phone
 END AS contact
FROM customers;

NULL in aggregates

-- Aggregates IGNORE NULLs (except COUNT(*))
-- Sample data: scores = [80, 90, NULL, 100]

SELECT
 COUNT(*), -- 4 (counts all rows)
 COUNT(score), -- 3 (excludes NULL)
 SUM(score), -- 270 (treats NULL as 0 by ignoring)
 AVG(score), -- 90.0 (270/3 — NULL excluded from BOTH numerator and denominator)
 MIN(score), -- 80
 MAX(score) -- 100
FROM tests;

-- WATCH OUT: AVG can surprise you
-- "Average score including unscored students treated as 0":
SELECT AVG(COALESCE(score, 0)) FROM tests; -- 67.5 (270/4)
★ THE NULL MENTAL MODEL

Think of NULL as "we don't know the value." Then:

  • "Is unknown = 5?" → We don't know → NULL
  • "Is unknown = unknown?" → We don't know → NULL
  • "Is unknown TRUE?" → We don't know → NULL → row dropped from WHERE
  • "Is the average score?" → average of what we know → ignore unknowns

This logic is consistent. Memorize it once and NULL stops being surprising.

Boolean columns and short-circuits

-- Postgres has a real BOOLEAN type
SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_active; -- equivalent to is_active = TRUE
SELECT * FROM users WHERE NOT is_active;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_active IS TRUE;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_active IS NOT FALSE; -- handles NULL too

-- MySQL stores booleans as TINYINT (0/1)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_active = 1;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_active; -- also works in MySQL

-- SQL Server uses BIT (0/1)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_active = 1;

Worked example — applying NULL logic

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Find all employees NOT in the engineering department. Note: some employees have NULL department (consultants)."

-- WRONG — drops the NULL-department rows
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department <> 'Engineering';
-- Returns only employees with explicit non-Engineering departments
-- Consultants (NULL dept) are dropped because NULL <> 'Engineering' is NULL

-- Decide: are consultants "not in engineering"?
-- If yes — include them:
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE department <> 'Engineering' OR department IS NULL;

-- If no — exclude both engineers AND consultants:
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE department <> 'Engineering' AND department IS NOT NULL;

The right answer depends on the business question. SQL forces you to be explicit about how NULL should behave.

Common NULL bugs to watch for

⚠ NULL BUG CHECKLIST
  1. Used = NULL or != NULL instead of IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
  2. Used NOT IN on a list/subquery that contains NULL
  3. Compared two nullable columns and got unexpected zero rows
  4. Used SUM, AVG, or COUNT(col) without realizing NULLs are excluded
  5. Concatenated strings and got NULL because one piece was NULL — use COALESCE
  6. Divided by a column that could be 0 — use NULLIF
  7. Joined on a NULL column expecting matches — NULL never joins to NULL
★ ON THE EXAM

"Test for NULL?" → IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

"NULL = NULL?" → NULL (not TRUE).

"Replace NULL with default?" → COALESCE(col, default).

"Avoid divide-by-zero?" → x / NULLIF(y, 0).

"Three-valued logic — FALSE OR NULL?" → NULL.

"TRUE OR NULL?" → TRUE (short-circuits).

"NOT IN (NULL)?" → returns zero rows; filter out NULL or use NOT EXISTS.

"AVG on column with NULLs?" → ignores NULLs in both numerator and denominator.

"COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)?" → COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) excludes NULLs.

"Operator precedence AND vs OR?" → AND binds tighter. Always parenthesize.

"Integer division 50/100?" → 0 in Postgres/SQL Server (truncates). Cast or use 50.0.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Comparison operators: =, <> / !=, <, >, <=, >=
  • SQL has THREE truth values: TRUE, FALSE, NULL — comparisons with NULL always return NULL
  • WHERE only passes rows where condition is TRUE (NULL gets dropped like FALSE)
  • Always use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL — never = NULL
  • Logical operators: AND binds tighter than OR — parenthesize mixed expressions
  • NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns zero rows; use NOT EXISTS as safer alternative
  • Aggregates ignore NULL (except COUNT(*)); AVG divides by count of non-NULLs
  • COALESCE(col, fallback) returns first non-NULL — the universal NULL-replacer
  • NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a = b — great for avoiding divide-by-zero
  • Integer division truncates in Postgres/SQL Server — cast to numeric or use a decimal in the expression

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The basic WHERE clause handles single-value filters, but real questions need more — "any of these states", "between these dates", "emails ending in @gmail.com". The DataCamp SQL Associate exam tests IN/BETWEEN/LIKE in nearly every section. Combined with the NULL traps from ch1/s4, these are the most common bug-producers in real analytics queries.

IN — matching any value in a set

-- Awkward with OR
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE state = 'CA' OR state = 'NY' OR state = 'TX' OR state = 'FL';

-- Clean with IN
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE state IN ('CA', 'NY', 'TX', 'FL');

-- NOT IN to exclude
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE state NOT IN ('CA', 'NY');

-- Works with numbers too
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE status_id IN (1, 3, 5, 7);

-- Works with dates
SELECT * FROM events
WHERE event_date IN ('2024-12-25', '2024-01-01', '2024-07-04');

IN with a subquery

-- IN can take a subquery that returns a list of values
SELECT *
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
 SELECT customer_id
 FROM orders
 WHERE total > 1000
);
-- Customers who have placed at least one order over $1000

-- The subquery can have its own WHERE, GROUP BY, etc.
SELECT *
FROM products
WHERE category_id IN (
 SELECT category_id
 FROM categories
 WHERE is_active = TRUE
);

The NOT IN + NULL trap (revisited)

⚠ THE NUMBER 1 ANALYTICS BUG
-- If the subquery returns ANY NULL, NOT IN returns ZERO rows
SELECT *
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (
 SELECT customer_id FROM blocked_users
);
-- If blocked_users has even one row with NULL customer_id → result is empty

Why? Because x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) means x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL. The last comparison is NULL, the AND short-circuits to NULL, and the row gets dropped.

Two fixes:

-- Fix 1: filter NULL in subquery
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (
 SELECT customer_id FROM blocked_users
 WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
)

-- Fix 2: use NOT EXISTS (handles NULL correctly)
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM blocked_users b
 WHERE b.customer_id = customers.customer_id
)

NOT EXISTS is the bulletproof pattern — recommend always using it instead of NOT IN with subqueries.

BETWEEN — range matching (inclusive)

-- Equivalent to: x >= low AND x <= high
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 100;
-- Includes both endpoints

-- Same as:
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price >= 10 AND price <= 100;

-- Reversed bounds fail silently (always zero rows)
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 100 AND 10; -- ⚠ 0 rows!

-- NOT BETWEEN
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price NOT BETWEEN 10 AND 100;
-- price < 10 OR price > 100

BETWEEN with dates — the timestamp trap

⚠ THE BETWEEN-WITH-TIMESTAMPS TRAP

If your column has a time component, BETWEEN can silently exclude data:

-- Imagine order_date is TIMESTAMP: '2024-12-31 14:30:00' for example
-- You want all December 2024 orders:

-- BAD — misses anything after midnight on Dec 31
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-12-01' AND '2024-12-31'
-- Translates to: order_date BETWEEN '2024-12-01 00:00:00' AND '2024-12-31 00:00:00'
-- So an order at '2024-12-31 14:30:00' is EXCLUDED

-- BETTER — use half-open range with the start of the next period
WHERE order_date >= '2024-12-01'
 AND order_date < '2025-01-01'
-- This catches everything in December correctly

The "half-open" pattern >= start AND < next_start is the safest way to filter date ranges.

BETWEEN with text — lexicographic

-- BETWEEN works on strings too — sorts alphabetically
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE last_name BETWEEN 'A' AND 'M';
-- Names starting with A through L (inclusive)
-- 'M' is included if exactly 'M'; 'Mc' would NOT be included since 'Mc' > 'M'

-- Watch out: case-sensitive in Postgres
WHERE last_name BETWEEN 'a' AND 'm';
-- Won't match 'Anderson' or 'Brown' because uppercase letters sort before lowercase

LIKE — pattern matching

TWO WILDCARDS
% matches ZERO OR MORE of any character
_ matches EXACTLY ONE character

LIKE is case-sensitive in most dialects. Use ILIKE in PostgreSQL for case-insensitive. 
-- Starts with 'A'
WHERE first_name LIKE 'A%';
-- Matches: 'Alice', 'Anderson', 'A', 'Abe'
-- Does NOT match: 'alice' (case-sensitive in Postgres), 'Bob'

-- Ends with '@gmail.com'
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com';
-- Matches: 'alice@gmail.com', 'bob.jones@gmail.com'

-- Contains 'sale' anywhere
WHERE product_name LIKE '%sale%';
-- Matches: 'sale item', 'flash sale', 'wholesale account'

-- Starts with 'A' AND ends with 'son'
WHERE last_name LIKE 'A%son';
-- Matches: 'Anderson', 'Atkinson'

-- Exact length matching with _
WHERE phone LIKE '555-____';
-- 555- followed by exactly 4 of any character

-- Combinations
WHERE phone LIKE '5__-____';
-- Starts with 5, then 2 chars, dash, then 4 chars

Case-insensitive matching

-- PostgreSQL: ILIKE
WHERE email ILIKE '%@GMAIL.com';
-- Matches '@gmail.com', '@Gmail.COM', etc.

-- Universal alternative: LOWER() comparison
WHERE LOWER(email) LIKE '%@gmail.com';

-- ⚠ Functions on indexed columns prevent index use
-- A functional index on LOWER(email) would help
-- ILIKE in Postgres uses available indexes if you have a citext column type

Escaping wildcards

-- What if you need a literal % or _ in your search?
-- Default escape character is backslash in some dialects, undefined in others

-- Use ESCAPE clause for clarity
WHERE description LIKE '%50\%%' ESCAPE '';
-- Find descriptions containing "50%" (literal percent sign)

-- Or pick your own escape character
WHERE filename LIKE '%report#_2024%' ESCAPE '#';
-- Find filenames containing "report_2024" (literal underscore)

LIKE vs regex

-- LIKE is limited — only % and _ wildcards
-- For more complex patterns, use regex (varies by dialect)

-- PostgreSQL ~ (case-sensitive) and ~* (case-insensitive)
WHERE phone ~ '^\d{3}-\d{4}$'; -- exactly NNN-NNNN format
WHERE email ~* '^.+@.+\..+$'; -- basic email shape (case-insensitive)

-- SQL Server: PATINDEX, LIKE with [character classes]
WHERE name LIKE '[A-C]%'; -- starts with A, B, or C

-- MySQL: REGEXP
WHERE phone REGEXP '^[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}$';
★ PERFORMANCE NOTE

LIKE patterns that start with a wildcard can't use an index:

WHERE email LIKE 'alice%' -- FAST (can use index on email)
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com' -- SLOW (full table scan)
WHERE email LIKE '%alice%' -- SLOW

-- For "ends with" or "contains" searches at scale, consider:
-- • Reversed column + index (for "ends with")
-- • Full-text search (for "contains")
-- • Trigram indexes (Postgres pg_trgm)

Combining filters for real questions

-- "Premium customers in major markets who signed up in last 6 months and have a personal Gmail"
SELECT first_name, last_name, email, signup_date
FROM customers
WHERE tier = 'premium'
 AND state IN ('CA', 'NY', 'TX', 'FL', 'IL')
 AND signup_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '6 months'
 AND email ILIKE '%@gmail.com'
 AND age BETWEEN 25 AND 55
ORDER BY signup_date DESC;

Worked example — finding suspicious accounts

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Flag accounts that look suspicious: free-email-domain users who registered with prepaid card BINs and are based outside our supported regions."

SELECT
 user_id,
 email,
 country,
 card_bin,
 signup_date
FROM accounts
WHERE
 -- Free email domains
 (email ILIKE '%@gmail.com'
 OR email ILIKE '%@yahoo.com'
 OR email ILIKE '%@hotmail.com'
 OR email ILIKE '%@outlook.com'
 OR email ILIKE '%@protonmail.com')

 -- Prepaid card BINs (first 6 digits of card number)
 AND card_bin IN ('411111', '424242', '555555', '378282')

 -- Not in supported regions
 AND country NOT IN ('US', 'CA', 'GB', 'AU', 'DE', 'FR')

 -- Recently signed up
 AND signup_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'

ORDER BY signup_date DESC;

Notice:

  • Group of OR conditions wrapped in parentheses — combined with AND outside
  • ILIKE for case-insensitive email matching
  • IN for the BIN list and NOT IN for excluded countries
  • Each filter on its own line, indented for readability
  • If the country column has any NULL values, the NOT IN trap applies — add AND country IS NOT NULL if needed

Common bugs with these operators

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES
  1. BETWEEN 100 AND 10 — reversed bounds, returns zero rows silently
  2. BETWEEN start_date AND end_date on TIMESTAMP — misses late-day data on end_date
  3. NOT IN (subquery) when subquery has NULLs — returns zero rows
  4. LIKE case sensitivity assumed wrong direction (depends on dialect)
  5. LIKE '%text%' on big indexed tables — index can't be used, very slow
  6. IN ('1', '2', '3') when column is numeric — implicit cast can hide errors
  7. Confusing _ wildcard (one char) with regex's . (one char)
★ ON THE EXAM

"Multiple values in WHERE?" → WHERE col IN (val1, val2, val3).

"Range filter inclusive?" → WHERE col BETWEEN low AND high (or use >= AND <=).

"Pattern match?" → WHERE col LIKE 'pattern%' (% = any, _ = one).

"Case-insensitive LIKE in Postgres?" → ILIKE. Elsewhere: LOWER(col) LIKE LOWER(pattern).

"NOT IN with NULL in subquery?" → returns zero rows. Use NOT EXISTS instead.

"Date range with timestamps?" → date_col >= '2024-01-01' AND date_col < '2025-01-01'.

"Search for literal % character?" → use ESCAPE clause: LIKE '%50\%%' ESCAPE ''.

"BETWEEN reversed (100 AND 10)?" → zero rows, no error. Verify your bounds.

"Find customers with NULL in a column?" → WHERE col IS NULL (not = NULL).

"LIKE starting with %?" → can't use index, slow on big tables.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • IN (val1, val2, ...) replaces multiple OR'd equality conditions
  • NOT IN with NULL values returns no rows — use NOT EXISTS as the safer alternative
  • BETWEEN low AND high is inclusive on BOTH ends; reversed bounds (high THEN low) silently returns no rows
  • For date ranges with timestamps, use half-open range >= start AND < next_period_start
  • LIKE wildcards: % matches any sequence, _ matches exactly one character
  • LIKE is case-sensitive in Postgres; use ILIKE for case-insensitive matching
  • LIKE patterns starting with % can't use indexes — full scans
  • For complex patterns (regex), use ~ / ~* in Postgres, REGEXP in MySQL, LIKE with character classes in SQL Server
  • Escape literal % or _ with the ESCAPE clause
  • Always parenthesize OR groups when mixing with AND for clarity

Exercise form: range filter — SELECT * FROM employees WHERE age BETWEEN 25 AND 35 — BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

GROUP BY turns row-level data into business answers: total sales by region, customer count by tier, average rating by product. Almost every business question involves grouping. The DataCamp SQL Associate exam tests GROUP BY heavily, especially the "every SELECT column must be aggregated or grouped" rule — the single most-failed concept on the exam.

Aggregate functions — collapsing rows to a value

FunctionReturnsNULL behavior
COUNT(*)Number of rows in the groupCounts all rows including NULLs
COUNT(col)Number of non-NULL valuesSkips NULLs
COUNT(DISTINCT col)Number of unique non-NULL valuesSkips NULLs and dupes
SUM(col)Total of numeric valuesSkips NULLs (returns NULL if all NULL)
AVG(col)Mean — SUM / COUNT(col)Skips NULLs in both numerator AND denominator
MIN(col)Smallest valueSkips NULLs
MAX(col)Largest valueSkips NULLs
STRING_AGG(col, sep)Concatenate strings (Postgres)Skips NULLs

Aggregates without GROUP BY — single result row

-- Aggregate over the entire table
SELECT
 COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
 SUM(total) AS total_revenue,
 AVG(total) AS avg_order,
 MIN(total) AS smallest,
 MAX(total) AS largest
FROM orders;

-- Result is a single row:
-- total_orders | total_revenue | avg_order | smallest | largest
-- 10000 | 850000 | 85.0 | 5.99 | 4999.99

-- Combine with WHERE to aggregate over a filtered subset
SELECT
 AVG(total) AS avg_order_2024
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND order_date < '2025-01-01';

GROUP BY — aggregating per group

GROUP BY MENTAL MODEL
GROUP BY collapses rows that share the same value(s) in the grouped column(s) into ONE row each.

Every selected column must either be:
  1. In the GROUP BY clause (a grouping key), OR
  2. Inside an aggregate function

This is the #1 GROUP BY rule. Break it → error in standard SQL. 
-- Without GROUP BY: one row across all of orders
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders; -- 10000

-- With GROUP BY: one row per group
SELECT
 state,
 COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY state;
-- Result:
-- state | order_count
-- CA | 3500
-- NY | 2200
-- TX | 1800
-- ...

-- Multiple grouping keys — one row per UNIQUE combination
SELECT
 state,
 EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS year,
 COUNT(*) AS order_count,
 SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY state, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date);
-- Result:
-- state | year | order_count | revenue
-- CA | 2023 | 1500 | 120000
-- CA | 2024 | 2000 | 175000
-- NY | 2023 | 1000 | 85000
-- ...

The "must be grouped or aggregated" rule

-- WRONG — first_name is not grouped or aggregated
SELECT state, first_name, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY state;
-- ERROR: column "first_name" must appear in GROUP BY or be used in aggregate function

-- Why? Each "state" group might have many first_names — which one would SQL pick?
-- Standard SQL refuses to guess.

-- RIGHT — add first_name to GROUP BY
SELECT state, first_name, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY state, first_name;
-- Now you get one row per (state, first_name) pair

-- OR aggregate first_name somehow
SELECT
 state,
 MIN(first_name) AS first_alphabetically,
 COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY state;
⚠ MYSQL EXCEPTION

Older MySQL versions silently allow non-grouped, non-aggregated columns and return an arbitrary value. This is "feature" called ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY being off. The result is silently wrong data. Modern MySQL (5.7.5+) defaults to strict mode and matches standard SQL. The DataCamp exam uses PostgreSQL — strict from day one.

GROUP BY with expressions

-- Group by a computed expression
SELECT
 EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS year,
 EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS month,
 SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date),
 EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)
ORDER BY year, month;

-- More portable: DATE_TRUNC
SELECT
 DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
 SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
ORDER BY month;

-- GROUP BY column position (1-indexed, refers to SELECT list)
SELECT state, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY 1; -- equivalent to GROUP BY state

-- Useful for grouping by complex expressions — but fragile
SELECT
 SUBSTRING(email FROM POSITION('@' IN email) + 1) AS domain,
 COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY 1; -- avoids repeating the messy expression

GROUP BY with CASE — bucketing

-- Bucket continuous data into categories
SELECT
 CASE
 WHEN age < 18 THEN 'minor'
 WHEN age < 65 THEN 'adult'
 ELSE 'senior'
 END AS age_group,
 COUNT(*) AS num_customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY CASE
 WHEN age < 18 THEN 'minor'
 WHEN age < 65 THEN 'adult'
 ELSE 'senior'
END;
-- Result:
-- age_group | num_customers
-- minor | 50
-- adult | 4200
-- senior | 1750

-- Cleaner alternative with column position
SELECT
 CASE
 WHEN age < 18 THEN 'minor'
 WHEN age < 65 THEN 'adult'
 ELSE 'senior'
 END AS age_group,
 COUNT(*) AS num_customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY 1;

-- Or use a subquery / CTE (cleaner — see ch4/s2)
WITH labeled AS (
 SELECT *,
 CASE
 WHEN age < 18 THEN 'minor'
 WHEN age < 65 THEN 'adult'
 ELSE 'senior'
 END AS age_group
 FROM customers
)
SELECT age_group, COUNT(*)
FROM labeled
GROUP BY age_group;

Combining filters with GROUP BY

-- WHERE filters BEFORE grouping; HAVING filters AFTER (ch2/s3)

-- "Total 2024 revenue per state, only including states with completed orders"
SELECT
 state,
 SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND order_date < '2025-01-01'
 AND status = 'completed'
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

Aggregate functions you'll use less often

-- VARIANCE and standard deviation
SELECT VARIANCE(price), STDDEV(price) FROM products;

-- Median (Postgres — note odd syntax)
SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY price)
FROM products;

-- ARRAY_AGG / STRING_AGG — collect grouped values
SELECT
 state,
 STRING_AGG(first_name, ', ' ORDER BY first_name) AS customer_list
FROM customers
GROUP BY state;
-- state | customer_list
-- CA | Alice, Bob, Carol
-- NY | Dan, Eve

-- ARRAY_AGG produces an array (Postgres):
SELECT
 state,
 ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT city) AS cities
FROM customers
GROUP BY state;

The SELECT-with-aggregate trap

⚠ MIXING AGGREGATES AND NON-AGGREGATES
-- WRONG — mixing scalar value with aggregate
SELECT first_name, COUNT(*) FROM customers;
-- ERROR: first_name not grouped/aggregated

-- WRONG — implicit row picking
SELECT first_name, MAX(salary) FROM employees;
-- Error in standard SQL. Even if it worked, which row's first_name?

Two valid fixes:

-- Option 1: GROUP BY
SELECT first_name, MAX(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY first_name;

-- Option 2: Window function (covered in ch4/s3)
SELECT first_name, salary,
 MAX(salary) OVER () AS highest_overall
FROM employees;

Worked example — building an analytics report

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "For Q4 2024, show me revenue, order count, average order value, and unique customers per state. Sort by revenue descending."

SELECT
 state,
 COUNT(*) AS order_count,
 COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers,
 SUM(total) AS revenue,
 AVG(total) AS avg_order_value,
 MIN(order_date) AS first_order,
 MAX(order_date) AS last_order
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-10-01'
 AND order_date < '2025-01-01'
 AND status = 'completed'
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

-- Sample output:
-- state | order_count | unique_customers | revenue | avg_order_value | first_order | last_order
-- CA | 2500 | 1800 | 220000 | 88.00 | 2024-10-01 | 2024-12-31
-- NY | 1800 | 1200 | 160000 | 88.89 | 2024-10-02 | 2024-12-31
-- ...

Notice:

  • WHERE filters BEFORE grouping (date and status)
  • Only one column (state) is in GROUP BY — every other SELECT column is an aggregate
  • COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) counts unique customers
  • ORDER BY uses an alias from SELECT (allowed in ORDER BY)

GROUP BY ROLLUP / CUBE — subtotals and grand totals

-- ROLLUP adds subtotal and grand total rows
SELECT
 state,
 EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS year,
 SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP(state, year)
ORDER BY state NULLS LAST, year NULLS LAST;
-- Result:
-- state | year | revenue
-- CA | 2023 | 100000
-- CA | 2024 | 120000
-- CA | NULL | 220000 ← subtotal for CA all years
-- NY | 2023 | 80000
-- NY | 2024 | 95000
-- NY | NULL | 175000 ← subtotal for NY all years
-- NULL | NULL | 395000 ← grand total

-- CUBE returns all possible groupings (more rows)
GROUP BY CUBE(state, year)
★ ON THE EXAM

"What does GROUP BY do?" → Collapses rows sharing the same group-key values into one row per group.

"Rule for SELECT with GROUP BY?" → Every column must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate function.

"COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)?" → COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values.

"How does AVG handle NULLs?" → Excludes them from BOTH numerator and denominator.

"Total revenue per category?" → SELECT category, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY category.

"Unique customers per state?" → SELECT state, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders GROUP BY state.

"Filter before grouping?" → WHERE. Filter after grouping? → HAVING (next section).

"Sort grouped results?" → ORDER BY runs AFTER GROUP BY; you can sort by aggregates or grouped columns.

"Group by computed expression?" → Repeat the expression in GROUP BY, or use column position (e.g., GROUP BY 1).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Aggregate functions collapse multiple rows to one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
  • Without GROUP BY, aggregates return ONE row across the entire (filtered) table
  • With GROUP BY, aggregates return ONE row per unique combination of group keys
  • Rule: every SELECT column must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate
  • Multiple group keys produce one row per UNIQUE combination of values
  • WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping; HAVING filters AFTER (ch2/s3)
  • COUNT(*) includes NULLs; COUNT(col) and COUNT(DISTINCT col) exclude NULLs
  • AVG ignores NULLs in both numerator and denominator
  • You can GROUP BY expressions or column positions
  • Use CASE inside GROUP BY for bucketing continuous values
  • ROLLUP and CUBE add subtotal/grand-total rows for hierarchical reporting

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

WHERE and HAVING both filter — but at different stages of the query. Mixing them up produces wrong results or errors. The DataCamp SQL Associate exam tests "WHERE vs HAVING" placement in every aggregation question. Get this right once and the rest of grouped queries becomes mechanical.

The fundamental difference

WHERE vs HAVING
WHERE filters individual ROWS — runs BEFORE grouping.
  Can reference: any column from the source table(s).
  CANNOT reference: aggregate functions (they don't exist yet).

HAVING filters GROUPS — runs AFTER grouping.
  Can reference: grouping columns, and aggregate expressions.
  CANNOT reference: ungrouped row-level columns.

Both can appear in the same query. 
-- Question: "States with more than 100 customers"
-- "State" is the group; "more than 100" is per-group, so HAVING

SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers
GROUP BY state
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100;

-- Result:
-- state | customer_count
-- CA | 350
-- NY | 180
-- TX | 142

-- WHERE would not work here — at the WHERE stage, COUNT(*) doesn't exist yet
SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers
WHERE COUNT(*) > 100 -- ERROR: aggregate not allowed in WHERE
GROUP BY state;

SQL clause execution order — the key to understanding

CLAUSE EXECUTION ORDER
1. FROM — source tables
2. WHERE — filter ROWS
3. GROUP BY — collapse to groups
4. HAVING — filter GROUPS
5. SELECT — pick columns / compute
6. DISTINCT — dedup
7. ORDER BY — sort
8. LIMIT — restrict count

WHERE can't see aggregates because aggregates don't exist until GROUP BY runs.
HAVING can use aggregates because it runs AFTER GROUP BY.

Using both WHERE and HAVING

-- Question: "States with more than 100 ADULT customers"
-- Filter to adults (row-level) → group by state → keep groups with >100

SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS adult_customer_count
FROM customers
WHERE age >= 18 -- row-level filter
GROUP BY state
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100; -- group-level filter

-- The flow:
-- 1. Pull all customer rows
-- 2. Drop rows where age < 18 (WHERE)
-- 3. Group remaining rows by state
-- 4. Drop groups with count <= 100 (HAVING)
-- 5. Output state and count

Same condition — choose WHERE when possible

-- These two return the SAME result:

-- Option A: filter in WHERE (preferred — faster)
SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'US' -- row-level condition, push to WHERE
GROUP BY state;

-- Option B: filter in HAVING (works but slower)
SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers
GROUP BY state, country
HAVING country = 'US'; -- group-level condition

-- Why prefer WHERE? It filters BEFORE grouping, so GROUP BY processes fewer rows.
★ RULE OF THUMB

If a filter doesn't involve an aggregate, put it in WHERE.

If a filter does involve an aggregate, it MUST go in HAVING.

The query optimizer can sometimes move filters between WHERE and HAVING — but don't rely on this. Write the right one yourself.

HAVING with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX

-- Categories with more than 50 products
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 50;

-- Categories where average price > $100
SELECT category, AVG(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING AVG(price) > 100;

-- Products with at least one $1000+ order
SELECT product_id, MAX(amount) AS max_order
FROM orders
GROUP BY product_id
HAVING MAX(amount) >= 1000;

-- Customers who spent more than $5000 total
SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS lifetime_value
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(total) > 5000
ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC;

HAVING with multiple conditions

-- Combine HAVING conditions with AND / OR — same as WHERE
SELECT
 state,
 COUNT(*) AS customer_count,
 AVG(lifetime_value) AS avg_ltv
FROM customers
GROUP BY state
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100
 AND AVG(lifetime_value) > 500;
-- States with both: more than 100 customers AND average LTV over $500

-- OR works too
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1000 OR AVG(lifetime_value) > 1000;

HAVING without GROUP BY

-- Technically valid — treats the whole table as one big group
SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(total)
FROM orders
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1000;

-- Either returns 1 row (if condition is met) or 0 rows.
-- Rare; usually you'd just check COUNT(*) > 1000 in your app code.

Can HAVING use aliases from SELECT?

-- Dialect-dependent:
-- PostgreSQL — NO (must repeat the expression)
SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM customers
GROUP BY state
HAVING cnt > 100; -- ERROR in Postgres
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100; -- ✓ works

-- MySQL — YES (alias usable in HAVING)
HAVING cnt > 100; -- works in MySQL

-- For portability, always repeat the expression in HAVING.
-- ORDER BY is the only clause that universally allows SELECT aliases.

Putting it all together — a complete query lifecycle

▸ FULL LIFECYCLE WALKTHROUGH

Question: "Find states where ADULT customers placed more than $50,000 in COMPLETED orders during 2024, sorted by revenue."

SELECT
 c.state,
 COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count,
 SUM(o.total) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.age >= 18
 AND o.status = 'completed'
 AND o.order_date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND o.order_date < '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY c.state
HAVING SUM(o.total) > 50000
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

Execution order:

  1. FROM + JOIN — combine orders with customers
  2. WHERE — drop rows that aren't adult + completed + 2024
  3. GROUP BY — group remaining rows by state
  4. HAVING — keep only groups where SUM(total) > 50000
  5. SELECT — output state, order count, revenue
  6. ORDER BY — sort by revenue descending

Every WHERE condition is row-level (age, status, date). Every HAVING condition is aggregate-level. This is the canonical shape of an analytics query.

The most common HAVING mistake

⚠ #1 BUG: USING WHERE WITH AGGREGATES
-- WRONG — can't use COUNT(*) in WHERE
SELECT state, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
WHERE COUNT(*) > 100
GROUP BY state;
-- Error: "aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE"

Fix: move the aggregate condition to HAVING.

SELECT state, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY state
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100;

#2 mistake: putting row-level filters in HAVING

⚠ WRONG STAGE
-- Works but inefficient
SELECT state, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY state, country
HAVING country = 'US';

-- Better — push the filter down to WHERE
SELECT state, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'US'
GROUP BY state;

Pushing filters to WHERE means GROUP BY processes fewer rows — significant speedup on big tables.

HAVING with subqueries

-- "Categories whose average price exceeds the overall product average"
SELECT category, AVG(price) AS cat_avg
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING AVG(price) > (
 SELECT AVG(price) FROM products
);

-- The subquery returns a single number — the overall average
-- HAVING compares each category's avg to that constant
★ ON THE EXAM

"Filter by an aggregate?" → HAVING.

"Filter by a row column?" → WHERE.

"Both?" → WHERE filters first, then GROUP BY, then HAVING.

"COUNT(*) > 5 in WHERE?" → ERROR. Move to HAVING.

"Same condition — which to use?" → WHERE if possible (filters earlier = faster).

"SELECT alias usable in HAVING?" → MySQL yes, Postgres no. Repeat the expression for portability.

"HAVING without GROUP BY?" → valid; treats the table as one group. Usually rare.

"Why WHERE before HAVING?" → SQL execution order: WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping; HAVING filters groups AFTER.

"States with more than 100 customers?" → GROUP BY state HAVING COUNT(*) > 100.

"Adult customers per state?" → WHERE age >= 18 GROUP BY state (no HAVING needed unless filtering aggregates).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping; HAVING filters groups AFTER
  • WHERE cannot reference aggregate functions; HAVING can
  • Filters that don't involve aggregates should go in WHERE (faster)
  • Filters that involve aggregates MUST go in HAVING
  • Both clauses can appear in the same query — WHERE first, HAVING second
  • HAVING uses the same comparison operators as WHERE: =, <, >, BETWEEN, IN, etc.
  • HAVING with multiple conditions: combine with AND / OR (parens for clarity)
  • SELECT aliases work in HAVING in MySQL but NOT in PostgreSQL — repeat the expression for portability
  • HAVING without GROUP BY treats the entire table as one group (rare use case)
  • HAVING can use subqueries — e.g., compare to overall average
  • Common bug: using an aggregate in WHERE — always move to HAVING

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

CASE is SQL's IF/ELSE — letting you transform, bucket, label, and compute conditionally inline. It's the single most-used "real-world" SQL feature on the DataCamp exam after SELECT/WHERE/JOIN. Master CASE and you'll never need a temp table or scripting language just to relabel data.

The two CASE forms

SEARCHED CASE (the flexible one)
CASE
 WHEN condition1 THEN value1
 WHEN condition2 THEN value2
 ...
 ELSE default_value
END
Each WHEN can have ANY boolean condition. Evaluates top-to-bottom; first match wins.

SIMPLE CASE (the shortcut) 
CASE column
 WHEN value1 THEN result1
 WHEN value2 THEN result2
 ...
 ELSE default_value
END
Only tests equality against the column. Less flexible. 
-- Searched CASE — most common
SELECT
 first_name,
 age,
 CASE
 WHEN age < 18 THEN 'minor'
 WHEN age < 65 THEN 'adult'
 ELSE 'senior'
 END AS age_group
FROM customers;

-- Simple CASE — for single-column equality only
SELECT
 order_id,
 CASE status
 WHEN 'pending' THEN 'Awaiting payment'
 WHEN 'paid' THEN 'Processing'
 WHEN 'shipped' THEN 'In transit'
 WHEN 'delivered' THEN 'Complete'
 ELSE 'Unknown'
 END AS status_label
FROM orders;

The ELSE clause — what happens with no match

-- WITHOUT ELSE: returns NULL when nothing matches
SELECT
 age,
 CASE
 WHEN age < 18 THEN 'minor'
 WHEN age >= 65 THEN 'senior'
 END AS age_group
FROM customers;
-- Adults aged 18-64 get NULL — probably not what you want

-- WITH ELSE: explicit default
SELECT
 age,
 CASE
 WHEN age < 18 THEN 'minor'
 WHEN age >= 65 THEN 'senior'
 ELSE 'adult'
 END AS age_group
FROM customers;
-- Now everyone gets a label

-- ALWAYS include ELSE unless you specifically want NULL for unmatched rows

Order of conditions matters

-- WRONG ORDER — adult catches everything before more specific conditions
SELECT
 age,
 CASE
 WHEN age >= 0 THEN 'adult' -- TOO BROAD!
 WHEN age < 18 THEN 'minor' -- never reached
 WHEN age >= 65 THEN 'senior' -- never reached
 END AS age_group
FROM customers;
-- Every row gets 'adult' because the first WHEN matches all

-- RIGHT — most specific first, broadest last
SELECT
 age,
 CASE
 WHEN age < 18 THEN 'minor'
 WHEN age >= 65 THEN 'senior'
 ELSE 'adult'
 END AS age_group
FROM customers;
★ FIRST MATCH WINS

CASE evaluates WHEN clauses top-to-bottom. As soon as one returns TRUE, that THEN value is used and no further conditions are checked. Always put the most specific/narrow conditions first, broader ones last.

CASE in SELECT — labeling and transforming

-- Computed label
SELECT
 order_id,
 total,
 CASE
 WHEN total >= 1000 THEN 'High'
 WHEN total >= 100 THEN 'Medium'
 ELSE 'Low'
 END AS order_size
FROM orders;

-- Computed numeric value (multiplier)
SELECT
 product_id,
 price,
 CASE
 WHEN category = 'Premium' THEN price * 1.20 -- 20% markup
 WHEN category = 'Sale' THEN price * 0.80 -- 20% discount
 ELSE price
 END AS adjusted_price
FROM products;

-- Computed boolean
SELECT
 customer_id,
 CASE
 WHEN total_purchases > 10 AND total_spent > 1000 THEN TRUE
 ELSE FALSE
 END AS is_vip
FROM customers;

-- Combine multiple CASE expressions
SELECT
 customer_id,
 CASE WHEN total_spent > 1000 THEN 'big spender' ELSE 'normal' END AS spend_tier,
 CASE WHEN signup_date < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year' THEN 'veteran' ELSE 'new' END AS tenure
FROM customers;

CASE in WHERE — conditional filtering

-- Use CASE inside WHERE to apply different logic per row
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE
 CASE
 WHEN category = 'Electronics' THEN price > 500
 WHEN category = 'Books' THEN price > 50
 ELSE price > 100
 END;
-- Different price threshold per category

-- More readable alternative — OR conditions
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE (category = 'Electronics' AND price > 500)
 OR (category = 'Books' AND price > 50)
 OR (category NOT IN ('Electronics', 'Books') AND price > 100);

CASE in ORDER BY — custom sort orders

-- Alphabetical sort doesn't match business priority
SELECT * FROM orders
ORDER BY status;
-- Returns: cancelled, completed, pending, processing, shipped — alphabetical

-- Custom workflow order
SELECT * FROM orders
ORDER BY
 CASE status
 WHEN 'pending' THEN 1
 WHEN 'processing' THEN 2
 WHEN 'shipped' THEN 3
 WHEN 'delivered' THEN 4
 WHEN 'cancelled' THEN 5
 END,
 order_date DESC;
-- Now status appears in workflow order, with newest order_date within each status

-- Push NULLs to the end (works in any dialect)
ORDER BY
 CASE WHEN priority IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END,
 priority;
-- Same result as Postgres's "NULLS LAST"

CASE inside aggregates — conditional counting and summing

THE MOST POWERFUL PATTERN
SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = conditional count
SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN col ELSE 0 END) = conditional sum
AVG(CASE WHEN ... THEN col ELSE NULL END) = conditional average

Lets you slice and dice in a single GROUP BY without multiple queries or subqueries. 
-- Count of orders by status, AS COLUMNS (pivot-style)
SELECT
 state,
 COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
 SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_count,
 SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_count,
 SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'pending' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY state;
-- Result:
-- state | total | completed | cancelled | pending
-- CA | 1500 | 1200 | 100 | 200
-- NY | 1000 | 850 | 50 | 100

-- Revenue split by category
SELECT
 DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
 SUM(total) AS total_revenue,
 SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'electronics' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS electronics_rev,
 SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'clothing' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS clothing_rev,
 SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'books' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS books_rev
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date);

-- Percentages
SELECT
 state,
 COUNT(*) AS total,
 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS pct_completed
FROM orders
GROUP BY state;
★ POSTGRES SHORTCUT — FILTER
-- The FILTER clause (Postgres, standard SQL) is cleaner than CASE
SELECT
 state,
 COUNT(*) AS total,
 COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'completed') AS completed_count,
 COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY state;

-- Equivalent to SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) but more readable.
-- Not available in MySQL — use CASE there.

NULLIF and COALESCE — CASE shortcuts

-- NULLIF(a, b) → NULL if a = b, else a
-- Equivalent to: CASE WHEN a = b THEN NULL ELSE a END
SELECT
 NULLIF(price, 0) AS price_or_null
FROM products;
-- Use case: avoid divide-by-zero
SELECT revenue / NULLIF(orders, 0) AS revenue_per_order FROM stores;

-- COALESCE(a, b, c) → first non-NULL value
-- Equivalent to: CASE WHEN a IS NOT NULL THEN a WHEN b IS NOT NULL THEN b ELSE c END
SELECT
 COALESCE(phone, mobile, email, 'no contact') AS contact_method
FROM customers;

Worked example — building a sales dashboard query

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Pivoted sales dashboard

Question: "For each state, show: total orders, total revenue, percentage of orders that were premium-tier, and a 'performance' label (HIGH if revenue > $100k, MEDIUM if > $50k, LOW otherwise)."

SELECT
 state,
 COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
 SUM(total) AS revenue,

 -- Premium percentage
 ROUND(
 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN tier = 'premium' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*),
 2
 ) AS premium_pct,

 -- Performance label
 CASE
 WHEN SUM(total) > 100000 THEN 'HIGH'
 WHEN SUM(total) > 50000 THEN 'MEDIUM'
 ELSE 'LOW'
 END AS performance,

 -- Per-tier revenue split
 SUM(CASE WHEN tier = 'premium' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS premium_revenue,
 SUM(CASE WHEN tier = 'standard' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS standard_revenue

FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

-- Sample output:
-- state | total_orders | revenue | premium_pct | performance | premium_revenue | standard_revenue
-- CA | 2500 | 220000 | 35.40 | HIGH | 110000 | 110000
-- NY | 1800 | 160000 | 28.20 | HIGH | 65000 | 95000
-- TX | 1200 | 78000 | 22.10 | MEDIUM | 25000 | 53000
-- WA | 400 | 32000 | 18.50 | LOW | 7000 | 25000

One query produces a full analytics dashboard with three CASE patterns: percentage with SUM/CASE, label with CASE, and pivoted columns with SUM/CASE.

CASE in GROUP BY — bucketing for aggregation

-- Bucket customers by spend, then count per bucket
SELECT
 CASE
 WHEN lifetime_value > 5000 THEN 'whale'
 WHEN lifetime_value > 1000 THEN 'big spender'
 WHEN lifetime_value > 100 THEN 'regular'
 ELSE 'browser'
 END AS spend_segment,
 COUNT(*) AS num_customers,
 AVG(lifetime_value) AS avg_ltv_in_segment
FROM customers
GROUP BY
 CASE
 WHEN lifetime_value > 5000 THEN 'whale'
 WHEN lifetime_value > 1000 THEN 'big spender'
 WHEN lifetime_value > 100 THEN 'regular'
 ELSE 'browser'
 END
ORDER BY avg_ltv_in_segment DESC;

-- ⚠ NOTE: must repeat the CASE expression in GROUP BY (Postgres)
-- Some dialects let you reference column 1, but it's fragile

Nested CASE

-- CASE inside CASE for multi-dimensional logic
SELECT
 customer_id,
 CASE
 WHEN country = 'US' THEN
 CASE
 WHEN state IN ('CA', 'NY', 'TX') THEN 'major US market'
 ELSE 'other US'
 END
 WHEN country IN ('CA', 'GB', 'AU') THEN 'tier 1 international'
 ELSE 'tier 2 international'
 END AS market_segment
FROM customers;

-- For complex logic, consider a CTE or lookup table instead — more readable

Common CASE bugs

⚠ TYPICAL CASE MISTAKES
  1. Wrong condition order — broad WHEN at top catches everything
  2. Forgot ELSE — unmatched rows get NULL silently
  3. Mixed return types — CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 'unknown' END errors because of type mismatch (int vs text)
  4. Used = with NULL inside CASE — WHEN col = NULL never matches. Use WHEN col IS NULL
  5. Forgot END — every CASE needs a matching END
  6. CASE in WHERE overkill — direct OR conditions usually clearer
  7. Not repeating the CASE expression in GROUP BY — error in Postgres
★ ON THE EXAM

"How to label rows by condition?" → CASE WHEN x THEN 'a' ELSE 'b' END.

"Count rows matching a condition (within GROUP BY)?" → SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).

"Pivot data into columns?" → multiple SUM(CASE WHEN ...) in SELECT with GROUP BY.

"Custom sort order?" → ORDER BY CASE col WHEN 'a' THEN 1 WHEN 'b' THEN 2 END.

"Avoid divide-by-zero?" → NULLIF(divisor, 0).

"First non-NULL value?" → COALESCE(a, b, c, ...).

"CASE WHEN col = NULL?" → never matches. Use WHEN col IS NULL.

"Postgres FILTER clause?" → cleaner alternative to SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).

"Order of WHENs?" → top-to-bottom; first match wins. Specific conditions first.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END is SQL's if/else expression
  • Searched CASE (with WHEN cond) is more flexible than Simple CASE (with WHEN value)
  • Evaluates top-to-bottom; first matching WHEN wins; ELSE provides default
  • Without ELSE, unmatched rows get NULL
  • Use CASE in SELECT to compute labels, transform values, build flags
  • Use CASE in ORDER BY for custom (non-alphabetical) sort orders
  • Most powerful pattern: SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) for conditional counts
  • Use this pattern to pivot rows into columns (one column per category)
  • Postgres FILTER clause is a cleaner alternative: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE cond)
  • NULLIF and COALESCE are convenient CASE shortcuts for NULL handling
  • Postgres requires you to REPEAT the CASE expression in GROUP BY (no aliasing)
  • For multi-level logic, nested CASE works but a CTE may be clearer
