Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real databases split data across many tables — customers in one, orders in another, products in a third. JOINs are how you reassemble the pieces to answer business questions. INNER JOIN is the default: "give me rows where the link exists in both tables." The DataCamp SQL Associate exam tests JOINs in nearly every question after the basics, and INNER JOIN is the foundation everything else builds on.

Why we split data into multiple tables

NORMALIZATION — STORE EACH FACT ONCE
Instead of storing customer name and email on every order row...

• One customers table: id, name, email, address...
• One orders table: id, customer_id, total, date...

Each order references the customer by ID. Update name once, all orders see it.
This is RELATIONAL design. JOINs let you re-combine the tables when you need them together. 
-- customers table
-- | id | first_name | email |
-- |----|-----------|----------------|
-- | 1 | Alice | alice@x.com |
-- | 2 | Bob | bob@y.com |
-- | 3 | Carol | carol@z.com |

-- orders table
-- | id | customer_id | total | order_date |
-- |----|------------|--------|-------------|
-- | 100| 1 | 50.00 | 2024-12-01 |
-- | 101| 1 | 75.00 | 2024-12-15 |
-- | 102| 2 | 30.00 | 2024-12-20 |

-- "Show each order with the customer's name and email"
-- Need data from BOTH tables — JOIN them.

INNER JOIN — the default JOIN

INNER JOIN SYNTAX
SELECT cols
FROM table_a a
INNER JOIN table_b b
 ON a.key = b.key
Returns ONLY rows where the ON condition matches in BOTH tables.
Unmatched rows from EITHER table are dropped.
The INNER keyword is optional — JOIN alone defaults to INNER. 
-- Join orders to customers, get name + order info
SELECT
 o.id AS order_id,
 o.order_date,
 o.total,
 c.first_name,
 c.email
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;

-- Result (only orders with matching customers):
-- order_id | order_date | total | first_name | email
-- 100 | 2024-12-01 | 50.00 | Alice | alice@x.com
-- 101 | 2024-12-15 | 75.00 | Alice | alice@x.com
-- 102 | 2024-12-20 | 30.00 | Bob | bob@y.com

-- Carol has no orders → she's dropped from result
-- If an order had customer_id pointing to a deleted customer → that order is dropped too

Table aliases — saves typing on every column reference

-- Without aliases — verbose
SELECT customers.first_name, orders.total
FROM customers
INNER JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id;

-- With aliases — clean
SELECT c.first_name, o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;

-- Common convention: use the first letter or a short abbreviation
FROM products p
INNER JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id

-- AS is optional in FROM but allowed
FROM customers AS c
INNER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id;
★ ALWAYS QUALIFY COLUMNS IN JOINS

When tables share column names (very common: id, name, created_at), the engine doesn't know which one you mean:

-- AMBIGUOUS — both tables have "id"
SELECT id FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;
-- ERROR: column reference "id" is ambiguous

-- FIX: prefix with table alias
SELECT c.id AS customer_id, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;

Even when not strictly required, prefixing every column with its table alias makes queries much easier to read and maintain.

The ON clause — your join condition

-- Simple equality (most common)
ON c.id = o.customer_id

-- Compound condition (composite key — both columns must match)
ON oi.order_id = o.id AND oi.line_number = al.line_number

-- Conditional join (less common but valid)
ON c.country = o.shipping_country AND o.status != 'cancelled'

-- Range join (very rare; usually a sign you should reconsider the schema)
ON e.salary BETWEEN s.min_salary AND s.max_salary

JOIN order doesn't matter for INNER JOIN

-- These two are logically equivalent
SELECT * FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
SELECT * FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;

-- Convention: lead with the "fact" table (orders) and JOIN the "dimensions" (customers, products)
-- The query optimizer decides the actual execution order regardless

-- IMPORTANT: this is NOT true for LEFT/RIGHT JOIN (covered in ch3/s2)

JOIN + WHERE — combining tables and filtering

-- Get California customers' completed orders
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 o.order_date,
 o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.state = 'CA'
 AND o.status = 'completed';

-- The flow:
-- 1. Combine customer + order rows (FROM + JOIN)
-- 2. Filter to CA + completed (WHERE)
-- 3. Project final columns (SELECT)
★ FILTER IN ON vs FILTER IN WHERE

For INNER JOIN, putting a filter in ON or WHERE gives the SAME result — because both happen before output. The optimizer can move filters between them.

-- Both return the same rows for INNER JOIN
-- Version A: filter in ON
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'completed'

-- Version B: filter in WHERE
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'

For LEFT/RIGHT JOIN, this is NOT true and the difference matters — covered in next section. Convention: keep join conditions in ON, filters in WHERE.

Multiple joins — chaining tables

-- Three-table query: order item details
SELECT
 o.id AS order_id,
 c.first_name AS customer,
 p.name AS product,
 oi.quantity,
 oi.unit_price,
 oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS line_total
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
INNER JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
INNER JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY o.id, oi.line_number;

-- Each JOIN connects one more table.
-- The order of joins is just syntactic — optimizer chooses real execution order.

USING — shortcut for same-named columns

-- If both tables have a column with the EXACT same name:
SELECT * FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c USING (customer_id);
-- Equivalent to ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id

-- The joined column appears ONCE in SELECT * (no duplicate)
-- Common pattern in clean schemas where foreign key = primary key by name

-- ⚠ Note: requires the column name to match exactly in both tables
-- Postgres, MySQL, SQLite support USING; SQL Server does NOT

NATURAL JOIN — automatic JOIN on same-named columns

-- Automatically joins on ALL columns with matching names
SELECT * FROM orders NATURAL JOIN customers;
-- Joins on customer_id IF that's the only shared column name
-- IF tables share id AND created_at, it joins on BOTH (often a bug!)

-- ⚠ Avoid in production — fragile when schemas change
-- If you add a new same-named column to one table, the join silently changes meaning
-- DataCamp may show NATURAL JOIN but most teams forbid it

JOINs with aggregation

-- "Total revenue per state"
SELECT
 c.state,
 COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS order_count,
 SUM(o.total) AS revenue
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.state
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

-- "Top 5 customers by lifetime value"
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 c.last_name,
 SUM(o.total) AS lifetime_value
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.id, c.first_name, c.last_name
ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC
LIMIT 5;

The hidden duplication trap

⚠ JOIN MULTIPLIES ROWS

If a customer has 5 orders, joining customers to orders gives 5 rows for that customer:

-- Surprise! Customer "Alice" appears 5 times
SELECT c.first_name, o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;

-- Sample result:
-- Alice | 50
-- Alice | 75
-- Alice | 100
-- Alice | 25
-- Alice | 200

-- Sum gives correct revenue
SELECT c.first_name, SUM(o.total)
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.first_name;

-- But COUNT(c.id) would OVER-COUNT customers
-- Use COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) when counting customers via a joined orders table

The most common SQL bug: COUNT after a JOIN over-counts because the JOIN multiplies rows.

The four-step JOIN mental model

★ HOW JOINS ACTUALLY WORK
  1. Take rows from table A
  2. For each row in A, look for matching rows in B (the ON condition)
  3. Output combined rows where match exists (INNER JOIN keeps only matches)
  4. Apply WHERE, GROUP BY, etc. to the combined result

So if A has 100 rows and each matches 3 rows in B, the combined result has 300 rows. Then WHERE filters, GROUP BY collapses, etc.

Worked example — analytics by category

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Show me the top 5 product categories by completed-order revenue in 2024, plus the order count for each."

Tables involved: orders, order_items, products. We need products' category, joined through order_items, restricted to 2024 completed orders.

SELECT
 p.category,
 COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS order_count,
 SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
INNER JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
 AND o.order_date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND o.order_date < '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5;

-- Result:
-- category | order_count | revenue
-- electronics | 8500 | 1250000
-- clothing | 12000 | 850000
-- books | 9200 | 425000
-- home | 5400 | 380000
-- toys | 3200 | 215000

Notice:

  • COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) not COUNT(*) — because joining order_items multiplies rows per order
  • Three tables chained with INNER JOIN
  • WHERE clause restricts at the JOIN-result level
  • GROUP BY at the highest level (category), then sort, then LIMIT

Common INNER JOIN bugs

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES
  1. Forgotten ON clause → produces a cartesian product (every row of A paired with every row of B). With 1000 × 1000 rows, that's 1 million result rows.
  2. Wrong JOIN condition (e.g., o.customer_id = c.first_name) — type mismatch or all rows fail to match, returning empty result
  3. Joining on a NULLable column — NULL never matches NULL, so rows with NULL keys are silently dropped (this is intentional but often surprising)
  4. COUNT after JOIN over-counts because JOIN multiplies rows — use COUNT(DISTINCT col)
  5. Ambiguous column reference — both tables have the same column name and you didn't prefix
  6. Forgetting that INNER JOIN drops unmatched rows from BOTH tables — customers with no orders disappear
★ ON THE EXAM

"Default JOIN type?" → INNER. JOIN alone = INNER JOIN.

"What does INNER JOIN return?" → Only rows where the ON condition matches in BOTH tables.

"Customers with their orders?" → customers INNER JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id.

"Unmatched rows?" → DROPPED by INNER JOIN. Use LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER to keep them (next section).

"What if I forget ON?" → Cartesian product — every A row paired with every B row.

"Count after JOIN?" → Use COUNT(DISTINCT col) to avoid over-counting.

"USING vs ON?" → USING is shortcut when column name matches exactly in both tables.

"NATURAL JOIN?" → Auto-joins on ALL same-named columns. Avoid in production (fragile).

"NULL in join key?" → NULL never matches NULL; rows silently dropped.

"Ambiguous column?" → Always prefix with table alias.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • JOIN combines rows from multiple tables based on a matching condition
  • INNER JOIN (or just JOIN) returns only rows that match in BOTH tables
  • Syntax: FROM a INNER JOIN b ON a.key = b.key
  • Use table aliases (FROM customers c) to shorten column references
  • Always qualify columns with table aliases when names could be ambiguous
  • JOIN order doesn't matter for INNER JOIN (matters for OUTER joins — next section)
  • You can JOIN any number of tables by chaining INNER JOIN ... ON ...
  • For INNER JOIN, filters in ON or WHERE are equivalent (not so for OUTER joins)
  • JOIN can multiply rows — use COUNT(DISTINCT col) to avoid double-counting
  • Forgetting ON produces a cartesian product — every A row × every B row
  • USING(col) is a shortcut when both tables have the same column name
  • NATURAL JOIN auto-joins on all same-named columns but is fragile; avoid

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

INNER JOIN drops unmatched rows. That's wrong when the question is "show me all customers, INCLUDING those with no orders." LEFT JOIN (and the lesser-used RIGHT, FULL) preserves unmatched rows on one or both sides. This is THE most-tested SQL concept on every exam after basic SELECT — and the most-misused one in real analytics queries.

The three OUTER JOIN types

OUTER JOIN VARIANTS
LEFT [OUTER] JOIN — Keep ALL rows from LEFT table, match where possible, fill NULL where no match
RIGHT [OUTER] JOIN — Keep ALL rows from RIGHT table, match where possible, fill NULL where no match
FULL [OUTER] JOIN — Keep ALL rows from BOTH tables, fill NULL on either side where no match

The OUTER keyword is optional in all three. LEFT JOIN = LEFT OUTER JOIN.

LEFT JOIN — the workhorse

-- customers: 1=Alice, 2=Bob, 3=Carol
-- orders: 100→customer 1, 101→customer 1, 102→customer 2
-- Carol has no orders.

-- INNER JOIN drops Carol
SELECT c.first_name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;
-- Result:
-- Alice | 100
-- Alice | 101
-- Bob | 102
-- (no Carol)

-- LEFT JOIN keeps Carol with NULL order_id
SELECT c.first_name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;
-- Result:
-- Alice | 100
-- Alice | 101
-- Bob | 102
-- Carol | NULL ← preserved with NULL for unmatched right-side columns
★ MENTAL MODEL — LEFT JOIN

Read it as: "Give me ALL rows from the left table. For each one, attach matching rows from the right. If there's no match, attach NULLs."

The LEFT table is "the table you're reporting on." The RIGHT table is "extra context."

The most common LEFT JOIN pattern — "show all + their extras"

-- "All customers and their total spend (zero for non-shoppers)"
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS total_spend
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.id, c.first_name
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;

-- Without COALESCE, customers with no orders get NULL for SUM
-- With COALESCE, they show 0.00 which is usually what reports want

-- "All products and their order count"
SELECT
 p.name,
 COUNT(oi.id) AS times_ordered
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name;
-- ⚠ Important: COUNT(oi.id) not COUNT(*).
-- COUNT(*) counts the rows including the NULL-filled ones for never-ordered products → wrong!
-- COUNT(oi.id) skips NULLs → returns 0 for never-ordered products → correct!
⚠ COUNT(*) AFTER LEFT JOIN — THE TRAP
-- BUG: Products never ordered get count of 1 (the NULL-filled row)
SELECT p.name, COUNT(*) AS times_ordered
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.name;

-- FIX: count the joined column, not *
SELECT p.name, COUNT(oi.id) AS times_ordered
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.name;
-- COUNT(oi.id) is 0 for products without matching orders because COUNT ignores NULL

After LEFT JOIN, always count the JOINED side's PK to avoid this trap.

Finding what's MISSING — anti-join pattern

-- "Customers who have NEVER placed an order"
SELECT c.first_name, c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
-- The LEFT JOIN attaches orders; WHERE o.id IS NULL keeps only customers
-- whose join produced a NULL right side — i.e., they had no matching order

-- Alternative: NOT EXISTS (often clearer)
SELECT c.first_name, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);

-- "Products never sold"
SELECT p.name
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE oi.id IS NULL;
★ THE ANTI-JOIN IDIOM

"LEFT JOIN + WHERE right-side-col IS NULL" is the pattern for "find rows in A that have no match in B." Memorize this — it appears constantly in real analytics work and on exams.

RIGHT JOIN — mostly avoid

-- RIGHT JOIN is just LEFT JOIN with tables swapped
SELECT c.first_name, o.total
FROM orders o
RIGHT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
-- ALL customers; orders attached where they exist; Carol kept with NULL

-- Equivalent (and clearer):
SELECT c.first_name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;
★ CONVENTION: USE LEFT JOIN

Most teams discourage RIGHT JOIN because:

  • Harder to read — the "important" table is on the right
  • Every RIGHT JOIN can be rewritten as a LEFT JOIN by swapping tables
  • Chains of LEFT JOIN scan naturally top-to-bottom

RIGHT JOIN exists for completeness but rarely improves clarity. Convert to LEFT JOIN.

FULL OUTER JOIN — keep both sides

-- Imagine you have two sources for customer data:
-- crm_customers: customers with CRM IDs and contact info
-- billing_customers: customers with billing IDs and invoice info
-- Some customers in only one source, some in both.

SELECT
 COALESCE(c.email, b.email) AS email,
 c.crm_id,
 b.billing_id
FROM crm_customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN billing_customers b ON c.email = b.email;
-- Result:
-- email | crm_id | billing_id
-- alice@x.com | 1 | A100
-- bob@y.com | NULL | A101 ← in billing only
-- carol@z.com | 2 | NULL ← in crm only

-- Use COALESCE to pull the first non-NULL value across the joined columns

-- Find mismatches between sources
SELECT
 c.email AS crm_email,
 b.email AS billing_email
FROM crm_customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN billing_customers b ON c.email = b.email
WHERE c.email IS NULL OR b.email IS NULL;
-- Lists customers present in only one source
⚠ DIALECT SUPPORT

FULL OUTER JOIN is NOT supported in MySQL (until recent versions). Workaround: LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN:

SELECT ... FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON ...
UNION
SELECT ... FROM A RIGHT JOIN B ON ...;

Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle, SQLite all support FULL OUTER JOIN.

The most important rule — JOIN order matters for OUTER joins

⚠ LEFT JOIN ORDER MATTERS
-- These are DIFFERENT (not equivalent for LEFT JOIN!)

-- Version A: keep ALL customers
SELECT c.first_name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;
-- Carol appears with NULL order_id

-- Version B: keep ALL orders (every order has a customer_id by FK, so probably same as INNER JOIN here)
SELECT c.first_name, o.id
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
-- Carol does NOT appear (she has no order to anchor on)

For INNER JOIN, table order doesn't matter. For LEFT/RIGHT JOIN, it absolutely does.

Filter in ON vs WHERE — the critical distinction for OUTER joins

⚠ FILTER PLACEMENT MATTERS FOR LEFT JOIN
-- "Customers and their COMPLETED orders (zero for those without)"

-- Version A: filter in ON — keeps unmatched customers (correct intent)
SELECT c.first_name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
 ON c.id = o.customer_id
 AND o.status = 'completed';
-- All customers shown. Their orders attached IF status = 'completed', else NULL.
-- Carol (no orders) appears with NULL.

-- Version B: filter in WHERE — drops the unmatched customers (becomes INNER JOIN!)
SELECT c.first_name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed';
-- Customers with NO completed orders are dropped because o.status of NULL ≠ 'completed'.
-- Carol is dropped.

Rule: For LEFT JOIN, filters on the LEFT table go in WHERE; filters on the RIGHT table usually go in ON to preserve the LEFT JOIN behavior.

Multiple OUTER joins — chaining

-- "All customers, their orders, AND the items in those orders (when present)"
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 o.id AS order_id,
 p.name AS product_name,
 oi.quantity
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
ORDER BY c.first_name;

-- A customer with no orders → 1 row with NULLs for everything right of c
-- A customer with an empty order → 1 row with NULL for product_name and quantity
-- A customer with a fully-populated order → multiple rows, one per line

Worked example — customer ranking with missing data

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "For every customer, show their lifetime order count and revenue. Include customers who have zero orders. Show the 10 highest-revenue customers (zero-spenders at the bottom)."

SELECT
 c.id,
 c.first_name,
 c.last_name,
 COUNT(o.id) AS order_count,
 COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
 ON o.customer_id = c.id
 AND o.status = 'completed' -- filter on RIGHT table goes in ON
GROUP BY c.id, c.first_name, c.last_name
ORDER BY revenue DESC, order_count DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Why these choices:
-- COUNT(o.id) not COUNT(*) → so zero-order customers count as 0, not 1
-- COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) → so NULL revenue becomes 0.00 for display
-- Filter in ON → preserves customers with no completed orders
-- GROUP BY includes c.first_name + c.last_name → needed by Postgres strict mode

Visualizing the four JOIN types

★ VENN DIAGRAM RECAP
 A only A and B B only

INNER JOIN: [ ▓▓▓▓▓▓ ] only the overlap
LEFT JOIN: [ ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓ ] A side + overlap
RIGHT JOIN: [ ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓ ] overlap + B side
FULL OUTER: [ ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓ ] everything

Anti-join (LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.col IS NULL) = "A only" — neither A∩B nor B alone.

Common bugs with OUTER joins

⚠ TOP MISTAKES
  1. Filter on right table in WHERE after LEFT JOIN → silently becomes INNER JOIN
  2. COUNT(*) after LEFT JOIN → counts the NULL-filled rows. Use COUNT(joined_col)
  3. Forgetting COALESCE for SUM/aggregates → result shows NULL instead of 0
  4. Wrong join order for LEFT JOIN — the "preserved" side must be on the LEFT
  5. NULL-on-NULL match assumption — NULL never matches NULL even in OUTER joins
  6. FULL OUTER JOIN in MySQL — not supported in older versions; use UNION trick
★ ON THE EXAM

"Show all X even if they have no Y?" → LEFT JOIN.

"What does LEFT JOIN do?" → Keeps ALL left rows; right side NULL when no match.

"Customers with no orders?" → LEFT JOIN orders, WHERE orders.id IS NULL.

"COUNT after LEFT JOIN?" → Use COUNT(joined_col), not COUNT(*).

"Filter in ON or WHERE?" → Filters on RIGHT table → ON (preserves LEFT JOIN). Filters on LEFT table → WHERE.

"RIGHT JOIN vs LEFT JOIN?" → Equivalent if you swap the table order. Stick with LEFT JOIN.

"FULL OUTER JOIN purpose?" → Keep ALL rows from both tables — for reconciliation of two sources.

"SUM after LEFT JOIN gives NULL?" → Wrap with COALESCE(SUM(col), 0).

"Anti-join pattern?" → LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.col IS NULL = "left side only."

"NULL joins NULL?" → NEVER. Use IS NULL/IS NOT NULL or wrap with COALESCE if joining on nullable keys.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • LEFT JOIN keeps ALL rows from the LEFT table; fills NULL where no right match
  • RIGHT JOIN is the mirror — keeps RIGHT table rows. Conventional advice: rewrite as LEFT JOIN
  • FULL OUTER JOIN keeps ALL rows from BOTH tables — used for source-reconciliation
  • Anti-join idiom: LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.col IS NULL for "in A but not in B"
  • JOIN order matters for OUTER joins (unlike INNER) — preserved side goes on LEFT
  • Filter placement matters: filters on RIGHT table in ON preserves the JOIN; in WHERE turns it into INNER
  • COUNT(*) trap: after LEFT JOIN, COUNT(*) counts NULL-filled rows as 1. Use COUNT(joined_col)
  • Use COALESCE to convert NULL aggregates to defaults (usually 0)
  • NULL never matches NULL in JOIN — even in OUTER joins
  • FULL OUTER JOIN is NOT supported in older MySQL; workaround with LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Self joins let you compare rows within the same table — finding pairs of records, employees and their managers, comparing this month to last month. Cross joins generate every combination of two sets, useful for date scaffolds and Cartesian comparisons. Both appear less often than INNER/LEFT JOINs but solve problems no other SQL pattern can. DataCamp specifically tests recognizing when these are the right tool.

Self joins — joining a table to itself

SELF JOIN PATTERN
Join the same table TWICE using DIFFERENT aliases.

Each alias represents a different "copy" of the table.
The ON condition compares values across the two copies.

Common uses:
  • Hierarchies (employees → managers)
  • Comparing rows pairwise
  • Finding consecutive events

Classic example — employees and managers

-- Employees table — each row has a manager_id pointing to another employee
-- | id | name | manager_id |
-- |----|---------|------------|
-- | 1 | Alice | NULL | ← CEO
-- | 2 | Bob | 1 | ← reports to Alice
-- | 3 | Carol | 1 | ← reports to Alice
-- | 4 | Dan | 2 | ← reports to Bob

-- "Show each employee with their manager's name"
SELECT
 e.name AS employee,
 m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id;
-- Result:
-- Alice | NULL (CEO, no manager)
-- Bob | Alice
-- Carol | Alice
-- Dan | Bob

-- Why LEFT JOIN? So Alice (no manager) appears with NULL instead of being dropped.
-- e = "employee role" of the table; m = "manager role" of the SAME table.

Self join — comparing rows pairwise

-- "Find pairs of employees who share a manager"
SELECT
 a.name AS emp_a,
 b.name AS emp_b,
 a.manager_id
FROM employees a
INNER JOIN employees b
 ON a.manager_id = b.manager_id
 AND a.id < b.id -- avoid pairing (Bob,Bob) and (Carol,Bob)+(Bob,Carol) dupes
WHERE a.manager_id IS NOT NULL;
-- Result:
-- emp_a | emp_b | manager_id
-- Bob | Carol | 1

-- The "a.id < b.id" trick is a self-join idiom that:
-- • Removes self-pairs: prevents (Bob,Bob)
-- • Removes mirror pairs: keeps (Bob,Carol), drops (Carol,Bob)

Self join — comparing consecutive periods

-- monthly_revenue table:
-- | month | revenue |
-- |-------------|---------|
-- | 2024-01-01 | 10000 |
-- | 2024-02-01 | 12000 |
-- | 2024-03-01 | 11500 |

-- "Show each month's revenue alongside the previous month's"
SELECT
 cur.month,
 cur.revenue AS current_rev,
 prev.revenue AS prior_rev,
 cur.revenue - prev.revenue AS change
FROM monthly_revenue cur
LEFT JOIN monthly_revenue prev
 ON prev.month = cur.month - INTERVAL '1 month';

-- Result:
-- month | current_rev | prior_rev | change
-- 2024-01-01 | 10000 | NULL | NULL
-- 2024-02-01 | 12000 | 10000 | 2000
-- 2024-03-01 | 11500 | 12000 | -500

-- Note: window functions (ch4/s3) usually do this more elegantly with LAG()
-- But self-join is the universal approach that works in any dialect

Self join — hierarchical lookups (multiple levels)

-- "Show each employee with their manager AND their manager's manager (grand-boss)"
SELECT
 e.name AS employee,
 m.name AS manager,
 gm.name AS grand_boss
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
LEFT JOIN employees gm ON gm.id = m.manager_id;
-- Each LEFT JOIN climbs one level up the hierarchy.
-- For arbitrary-depth hierarchies, use a recursive CTE (covered in ch4/s2)

Cross joins — the cartesian product

CROSS JOIN
Returns every COMBINATION of rows from two tables.
No ON clause — every row of A is paired with every row of B.

If A has M rows and B has N rows, the result has M × N rows.
Useful when you specifically WANT every pairing.
Dangerous when accidental — produces enormous result sets. 
-- Three sizes × four colors → twelve combinations
-- sizes: S, M, L
-- colors: red, blue, green, black

SELECT s.size, c.color
FROM sizes s
CROSS JOIN colors c;

-- Result (12 rows):
-- S | red
-- S | blue
-- S | green
-- S | black
-- M | red
-- M | blue
-- ...etc

-- Same query using implicit comma syntax (older, still valid)
SELECT s.size, c.color
FROM sizes s, colors c;
-- ⚠ But this looks like a missing JOIN bug! Use CROSS JOIN keyword explicitly.

Real use case — generating date scaffolds

-- Problem: report by store × day, including stores with zero sales on some days
-- If you just GROUP BY (store, day), you miss days where no sales happened.

-- Solution: CROSS JOIN stores with all days, then LEFT JOIN to sales

SELECT
 s.id AS store_id,
 s.name AS store_name,
 d.day,
 COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS revenue
FROM stores s
CROSS JOIN generate_series(
 '2024-01-01'::date,
 '2024-01-31'::date,
 '1 day'::interval
) AS d(day)
LEFT JOIN orders o
 ON o.store_id = s.id
 AND o.order_date = d.day
GROUP BY s.id, s.name, d.day
ORDER BY s.id, d.day;
-- Result: every store gets a row for every day, with revenue = 0 if no sales
-- Without CROSS JOIN, days with no sales for a store would be missing

-- Postgres uses generate_series for date scaffolds.
-- MySQL: use a numbers/calendar table. SQL Server: use master..spt_values trick.

Cross join + filter ≈ inner join

-- Old-school SQL style — equivalent to INNER JOIN
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c, orders o
WHERE c.id = o.customer_id;

-- Modern equivalent (preferred — clearer JOIN intent)
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;
⚠ ACCIDENTAL CROSS JOIN — THE BIG ONE

Comma-syntax JOINs without a WHERE clause produce a cartesian product. With two 10,000-row tables, that's 100 million rows. Your query freezes or fills storage.

-- DANGER: a forgotten WHERE = 100M rows
SELECT * FROM customers c, orders o;

-- Same risk: explicit CROSS JOIN without ON (which there isn't one for CROSS)
SELECT * FROM customers CROSS JOIN orders;

Always use explicit INNER JOIN syntax. Comma syntax exists for compatibility but is footgun-prone.

Real cross join uses

  • Date scaffolds — generate every (store, day) combination so reports have zero-rows for inactive days
  • Cohort comparisons — pair every value of a small lookup with every record
  • Generating test data — combine sample customers × sample products to seed an orders table
  • Combination generation — every (size, color) for a product catalog
  • Threshold testing — compare every metric value against every threshold
-- "Test every (employee, threshold) combination to find which thresholds each passed"
SELECT
 e.name,
 t.threshold,
 CASE WHEN e.score >= t.threshold THEN 'pass' ELSE 'fail' END AS result
FROM employees e
CROSS JOIN (VALUES (60), (70), (80), (90)) AS t(threshold);

-- Every employee gets 4 rows, one per threshold

Self join + range — find duplicates and overlaps

-- "Find duplicate customer emails in the database"
SELECT a.id AS id_a, b.id AS id_b, a.email
FROM customers a
INNER JOIN customers b
 ON a.email = b.email
 AND a.id < b.id; -- ensures distinct pairs, no self-match
-- Pairs of customer IDs sharing an email

-- "Find overlapping bookings"
-- bookings: | id | room_id | start_time | end_time |
SELECT a.id AS booking_a, b.id AS booking_b
FROM bookings a
INNER JOIN bookings b
 ON a.room_id = b.room_id
 AND a.id < b.id
 AND a.start_time < b.end_time
 AND b.start_time < a.end_time;
-- Pairs of bookings in the same room with overlapping time ranges
-- This is the canonical interval-overlap pattern

Worked example — running monthly comparison

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Build a monthly report showing each month's revenue, the previous month's revenue, and the month-over-month percent change. Cover all months in 2024 even if there were zero sales (date scaffold)."

-- Use a CROSS JOIN to ensure all 12 months exist (date scaffold via generate_series),
-- a LEFT JOIN to attach revenue per month, and a SELF JOIN (via the scaffold) to
-- pull the prior month's value.

WITH months AS (
 SELECT generate_series(
 '2024-01-01'::date,
 '2024-12-01'::date,
 '1 month'::interval
 )::date AS month
),
monthly AS (
 SELECT
 m.month,
 COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS revenue
 FROM months m
 LEFT JOIN orders o
 ON DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) = m.month
 AND o.status = 'completed'
 GROUP BY m.month
)
SELECT
 cur.month,
 cur.revenue AS current_rev,
 prev.revenue AS prior_rev,
 CASE
 WHEN prev.revenue IS NULL OR prev.revenue = 0 THEN NULL
 ELSE ROUND(100.0 * (cur.revenue - prev.revenue) / prev.revenue, 2)
 END AS pct_change
FROM monthly cur
LEFT JOIN monthly prev
 ON prev.month = cur.month - INTERVAL '1 month'
ORDER BY cur.month;

This single query combines:

  • Date scaffold via generate_series (Postgres) and a CTE (months)
  • LEFT JOIN to orders so months with zero sales aren't dropped
  • Self join on the result (monthly) to pair each month with the previous month
  • CASE to avoid divide-by-zero in percent calculation
  • COALESCE so zero-sales months show 0 not NULL

Common bugs

⚠ TYPICAL MISTAKES
  1. Forgetting both aliases in a self join — column references become ambiguous
  2. Self-pairing: omitting a.id < b.id gives duplicate pairs and self-matches
  3. Accidental cross join from comma syntax with missing WHERE
  4. Cross join on big tables — exponential row growth crashes queries
  5. Self join with INNER instead of LEFT when you want to keep "roots" (CEO with no manager)
  6. Using cross join for what should be a calculation — e.g., generating thresholds inline when a CASE would do
★ ON THE EXAM

"Find managers of employees?" → SELF JOIN employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id.

"Avoid duplicate pairs in self join?" → Add a.id < b.id to the ON condition.

"Show CEO with no manager?" → LEFT JOIN (not INNER) on the self join.

"Cartesian product?" → CROSS JOIN (no ON clause).

"Comma-syntax JOIN?" → FROM a, b WHERE a.id = b.id — works but use explicit JOIN syntax.

"Date scaffold?" → CROSS JOIN with generate_series (Postgres) or a calendar table.

"Find pairs of overlapping intervals?" → Self join with a.start < b.end AND b.start < a.end.

"Compare row to previous row?" → Self join shifted by interval, or use LAG() window function.

"Two tables of M and N rows in cross join?" → M × N result rows.

"Find duplicates by email?" → Self join on email with a.id < b.id.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • SELF JOIN means joining a table to itself using two different aliases
  • Classic uses: employee-manager hierarchies, comparing pairs, consecutive-period comparisons
  • Use LEFT JOIN in self joins when you want to keep "root" rows (no parent)
  • The a.id < b.id trick eliminates self-pairs and mirror duplicates
  • CROSS JOIN returns every combination — M × N rows for tables of size M and N
  • Cross joins are powerful for date scaffolds, threshold tests, generating combinations
  • Accidental cross joins (comma-syntax with missing WHERE) can produce massive results
  • Cross join + WHERE on join condition = old-style INNER JOIN — use explicit JOIN keyword
  • Generate date scaffolds with generate_series (Postgres) or a calendar table (others)
  • Self join + range conditions is the canonical pattern for overlap detection
  • For pure "previous row" comparisons, window functions (LAG) are usually cleaner than self join

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real analytics queries rarely involve just two tables. A typical "show me revenue by region and category" query joins orders → customers → addresses → products → categories — five tables in one query. Joining many tables, handling NULLs across them, and ordering joins for performance is what separates beginner SQL from production-ready analyst SQL. DataCamp's harder questions almost always involve 3+ table joins.

Chaining JOINs — the canonical pattern

-- Five-table query: full order detail report
SELECT
 o.id AS order_id,
 c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer,
 a.city,
 a.state,
 p.name AS product,
 cat.name AS category,
 oi.quantity,
 oi.unit_price,
 oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS line_total
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
INNER JOIN addresses a ON a.id = o.shipping_address_id
INNER JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
INNER JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
INNER JOIN categories cat ON cat.id = p.category_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY o.id, oi.line_number;

-- Each JOIN adds one more table.
-- The result has one row per (order, line item) pair.
-- WHERE filters across all joined tables (you can reference any).

Reading a multi-table JOIN — the "spine" pattern

★ HOW TO STRUCTURE A MULTI-TABLE JOIN

Most analytics queries have a clear "spine" — one fact table at the center, with dimension tables attached. Convention:

  1. Start FROM with the fact table (orders, events, transactions)
  2. Add dimensions one at a time with JOIN
  3. Use short, predictable aliases (o, c, p, cat...)
  4. Indent each JOIN consistently — easy to scan
  5. Keep filters in WHERE at the bottom

This pattern matches how the data is organized and makes the query read like a story.

Mixing INNER and LEFT JOINs

-- Question: "All customers, their orders if any, and the product category if known"
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 o.id AS order_id,
 o.total,
 cat.name AS category
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
LEFT JOIN categories cat ON cat.id = p.category_id
ORDER BY c.first_name;
-- Customers with no orders: all right-side cols are NULL
-- Orders without categories: just cat columns are NULL

-- Once you go LEFT, you usually stay LEFT.
-- A single INNER JOIN downstream silently drops everything the LEFT chain preserved!
⚠ THE "INNER AFTER LEFT" TRAP
-- Customers without orders should be preserved, right?
SELECT c.first_name, o.id, cat.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
INNER JOIN categories cat ON cat.id = o.category_id;
-- ^^^^^ INNER JOIN here drops all customers with NULL o.category_id!
-- Customers with no orders had NULL for o.category_id → INNER JOIN drops them.
-- Result: silently became "customers WITH orders only" — your LEFT JOIN was wasted.

Rule: If you LEFT JOIN a table, all downstream JOINs that reference that table should also be LEFT JOIN (or use carefully designed ON conditions).

JOIN with conditions in the ON clause

-- Sometimes you want to attach a row only if multiple conditions hold

-- "Customers and their MOST RECENT order (if any)"
-- This pattern requires window functions or a subquery — covered in ch4

-- "Customers and any completed orders from 2024"
SELECT c.first_name, o.id, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
 ON o.customer_id = c.id
 AND o.status = 'completed'
 AND o.order_date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND o.order_date < '2025-01-01';
-- ON has multiple conditions joined by AND
-- For LEFT JOIN, filtering in ON is critical — same filter in WHERE would drop unmatched customers
-- (Covered in ch3/s2 — re-emphasizing because it's the #1 mistake)

-- For INNER JOIN, ON-filter vs WHERE-filter is equivalent — but conventionally:
-- ON: how tables connect
-- WHERE: which result rows to keep

Joining on multiple columns (composite keys)

-- Some relationships span two columns — e.g., a calendar joined by (year, month)
SELECT
 s.year,
 s.month,
 s.region,
 s.revenue,
 t.target
FROM sales s
INNER JOIN targets t
 ON t.year = s.year
 AND t.month = s.month
 AND t.region = s.region;
-- Three-column composite key match

-- USING shortcut (if columns share the same name in both tables)
SELECT ...
FROM sales s
INNER JOIN targets t USING (year, month, region);
-- Equivalent and more concise — but column names must match exactly

Joining on inequality / range

-- "Each employee's salary band" — table of salary ranges
-- salary_bands:
-- | grade | min_salary | max_salary |
-- |-------|-----------|-----------|
-- | E1 | 0 | 50000 |
-- | E2 | 50001 | 80000 |
-- | E3 | 80001 | 120000 |

SELECT
 e.name,
 e.salary,
 sb.grade
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN salary_bands sb
 ON e.salary BETWEEN sb.min_salary AND sb.max_salary;
-- Each employee matched to exactly one band based on their salary

-- "Find orders that fell within each promotion's date range"
SELECT
 o.id AS order_id,
 p.name AS promo_name
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN promotions p
 ON o.order_date >= p.start_date
 AND o.order_date <= p.end_date;
-- An order can match MULTIPLE promotions if dates overlap
⚠ RANGE JOINS ARE EXPENSIVE

Equality joins (a.id = b.id) can use hash or merge joins — O(N) or O(N log N).

Range joins (a.x BETWEEN b.low AND b.high) often force nested loops — O(N × M).

On big tables this can be hundreds of times slower. For production, consider:

  • Pre-computing the band/category and joining on equality
  • Bucketing into discrete keys first
  • Using window functions with partition keys

Order of joins — what the optimizer does

-- SQL is declarative. The query plan reorders joins to minimize work:
-- 1. Smallest tables joined first (smaller intermediate results)
-- 2. Most-restrictive filters applied early
-- 3. Indexes used to avoid full scans

-- You can see the actual plan with EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN SELECT ...; -- estimated plan
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...; -- actual runtime stats (Postgres)
EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT ...; -- Oracle
SHOW PLAN_ALL ON; ...; -- SQL Server

-- The optimizer is usually right. Hints (FORCE JOIN ORDER, etc.) are last resort.

When join order DOES matter for correctness — OUTER joins

-- This LEFT JOIN behaves as expected:
SELECT c.name, o.total, p.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id;
-- All customers preserved; right side nullable if no match downstream

-- Reordering can break the chain — these are NOT equivalent:
SELECT c.name, o.total, p.name
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
-- Now all PRODUCTS are preserved; customers may be NULL
-- Different question, different answer

JOINs and aggregation — the row-multiplication trap (revisited)

-- Goal: total spend per customer
-- Wrong attempt — joins multiply rows BEFORE SUM
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 SUM(o.total) AS spend
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
INNER JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.first_name;
-- BUG: each order with 3 line items is duplicated 3x by the order_items join
-- → SUM(o.total) over-counts by line count

-- FIX 1: aggregate before joining
WITH per_customer AS (
 SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spend
 FROM orders
 GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.first_name, COALESCE(pc.spend, 0) AS spend
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN per_customer pc ON pc.customer_id = c.id;

-- FIX 2: SUM DISTINCT (rarely the right answer — relies on order ID uniqueness)
SELECT c.first_name, SUM(DISTINCT o.total) FROM ...
-- Only works if you know totals are unique; rarely true. Avoid.
★ THE GENERAL RULE

If you're aggregating across tables that have one-to-many relationships, aggregate before joining. Use a CTE (next chapter) or subquery to pre-aggregate, then join the resulting one-row-per-key table.

Worked example — full order analytics report

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Show top 10 customers by 2024 revenue. Include their primary shipping city and the count of unique product categories they bought from. Include all customers even if they had only one category."

SELECT
 c.first_name,
 c.last_name,
 a.city,
 COUNT(DISTINCT cat.id) AS unique_categories,
 SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
INNER JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
INNER JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
INNER JOIN categories cat ON cat.id = p.category_id
LEFT JOIN addresses a ON a.id = c.primary_shipping_address_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
 AND o.order_date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND o.order_date < '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.first_name, c.last_name, a.city
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Notice:
-- INNER JOIN for the fact path (must have orders + items + products + category)
-- LEFT JOIN for addresses (some customers might lack a primary address)
-- COUNT(DISTINCT cat.id) prevents over-counting from row multiplication
-- GROUP BY includes c.id (the PK) so name/city are uniquely tied to one customer

Anti-join across multiple tables

-- "Customers who NEVER ordered a 'premium' product"
SELECT c.first_name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1
 FROM orders o
 JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
 JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
 WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
 AND p.tier = 'premium'
);

-- NOT EXISTS handles NULLs cleanly; NOT IN with a subquery is fragile
-- Equivalent with LEFT JOIN + IS NULL anti-join (harder for multi-step paths)

Joining tables with different grain — be careful

-- "Grain" = what each row represents.
-- customers: one row per customer
-- orders: one row per order (multiple per customer)
-- order_items: one row per line (multiple per order)
-- payments: one row per payment (multiple per order — partial payments)

-- Joining orders + order_items + payments without thinking:
SELECT o.id, oi.quantity, p.amount
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
INNER JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id;
-- An order with 3 items and 2 payments → 3 × 2 = 6 result rows!
-- Aggregates like SUM(p.amount) will be 3x too high

-- Always aggregate to consistent grain before joining
WITH order_totals AS (
 SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS total
 FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
),
payment_totals AS (
 SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid
 FROM payments GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT
 o.id,
 ot.total,
 pt.paid
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN order_totals ot ON ot.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN payment_totals pt ON pt.order_id = o.id;
-- Now each table is at order-grain before joining

Common multi-table JOIN bugs

⚠ TOP MISTAKES IN MULTI-TABLE JOINS
  1. INNER after LEFT — silently undoes the LEFT JOIN preservation
  2. Row multiplication from one-to-many — aggregates over-count
  3. Grain mismatch — joining tables at different grains without pre-aggregating
  4. Forgetting alias prefixes on columns shared by multiple tables
  5. Range/inequality joins on big tables — kills performance
  6. Mixing ON-filters and WHERE-filters incorrectly for OUTER joins
  7. Cycles in joins — joining A→B→C→A produces redundant paths
★ ON THE EXAM

"5-table report — order?" → Start with the fact table, JOIN dimensions one at a time, filter in WHERE.

"INNER JOIN after LEFT JOIN problem?" → Drops the rows the LEFT JOIN was preserving.

"Composite join key?" → Use ON a.k1 = b.k1 AND a.k2 = b.k2 or USING (k1, k2).

"Range/BETWEEN join?" → Possible but expensive; pre-bucket if performance matters.

"SUM going wrong after joins?" → Row multiplication from one-to-many; pre-aggregate to single grain.

"COUNT(DISTINCT col)?" → Necessary when joins multiply rows for the same key.

"Find rows in A with no related B?" → LEFT JOIN B + WHERE B.col IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS.

"Order of joins matters?" → Logically only for OUTER joins; physically the optimizer reorders.

"EXPLAIN?" → Shows the query plan — what indexes, what join algorithm, estimated rows.

"5 tables joined?" → Same pattern as 2 — just more JOIN lines. Use clear aliases.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Chain JOINs with one JOIN ... ON ... per table — read top-to-bottom as a "story"
  • Start FROM with the fact table; attach dimensions with JOIN
  • Once you LEFT JOIN, stay with LEFT — an INNER JOIN downstream silently filters
  • Multiple ON conditions with AND for composite keys or filtered joins
  • USING(col1, col2) is the shortcut when join columns share names
  • Range joins (BETWEEN, >=) are expensive — avoid on huge tables when possible
  • Logical join order matters for OUTER joins; physical order is up to the optimizer
  • Use EXPLAIN to see what the optimizer actually does
  • Row multiplication from one-to-many JOINs over-counts aggregates — pre-aggregate to consistent grain
  • Use NOT EXISTS for anti-joins across multi-step paths; cleaner than LEFT JOIN + IS NULL with chains
  • COUNT(DISTINCT col) protects against row multiplication when counting unique entities

Many-to-many pattern: students and courses connect through a JUNCTION table — enrollments(student_id, course_id) with two foreign keys; each row is one student-course pairing, and the pair is typically the primary key.

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Subqueries are queries inside queries. They let you compute a value or build a derived table on the fly, without persisting it. Most "find customers who spent more than the average" type questions involve subqueries. The DataCamp SQL Associate exam tests scalar, inline, and correlated subqueries — and the trickiest exam questions almost always hinge on understanding when a subquery is the right tool vs a JOIN or CTE.

Three flavors of subquery

TypeReturnsUsed in
ScalarA single value (one row, one column)SELECT, WHERE, HAVING — anywhere a value goes
Inline (derived table)A table of rows and columnsFROM clause
CorrelatedA value computed PER OUTER ROWWHERE, SELECT (less common)

Scalar subqueries — a value-on-demand

-- "Customers who spent more than the average customer"
-- Need: (1) the average lifetime spend (a single number)
-- (2) all customers, filter by spend > that number

SELECT first_name, last_name, lifetime_spend
FROM customers
WHERE lifetime_spend > (
 SELECT AVG(lifetime_spend) FROM customers
);
-- The subquery returns ONE NUMBER (e.g., 1247.50)
-- The outer query then compares each customer's spend against it

Scalar subqueries in SELECT

-- Add the company-wide average to every row for context
SELECT
 first_name,
 lifetime_spend,
 (SELECT AVG(lifetime_spend) FROM customers) AS company_avg,
 lifetime_spend - (SELECT AVG(lifetime_spend) FROM customers) AS diff_from_avg
FROM customers;

-- ⚠ The subquery runs every time? No — the optimizer typically runs it ONCE.
-- But it can still be slow if the subquery is complex; consider WITH (CTE)
⚠ SCALAR SUBQUERIES MUST RETURN ≤1 ROW
-- If the subquery returns >1 row, you get a runtime error
SELECT first_name
FROM customers
WHERE state = (SELECT state FROM customers WHERE first_name = 'Alice');
-- If 3 customers are named Alice with different states → ERROR
-- "more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression"

Fix: use IN (returns multiple values) or aggregate the subquery (LIMIT 1, MAX(), etc.).

WHERE state IN (SELECT state FROM customers WHERE first_name = 'Alice');

Subqueries with IN / NOT IN / ANY / ALL

-- "Customers who have placed at least one order over $1000"
SELECT first_name
FROM customers
WHERE id IN (
 SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 1000
);

-- "Customers who have NEVER placed an order"
SELECT first_name
FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (
 SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
);
-- ⚠ Always exclude NULL from NOT IN subqueries (the trap from ch1/s4)

-- ANY (alias: SOME) — true if ANY row matches the comparison
SELECT name FROM products
WHERE price > ANY (SELECT price FROM products WHERE category = 'budget');
-- "Products priced higher than at least one budget product"

-- ALL — true if ALL rows match
SELECT name FROM products
WHERE price > ALL (SELECT price FROM products WHERE category = 'budget');
-- "Products priced higher than EVERY budget product"
-- Equivalent: WHERE price > (SELECT MAX(price) FROM products WHERE category = 'budget')

EXISTS / NOT EXISTS — the cleaner anti-join

-- "Customers who have placed at least one order"
SELECT first_name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);
-- EXISTS returns TRUE the moment ANY matching row is found
-- The "SELECT 1" is convention — what you select doesn't matter, only the existence

-- "Customers who have NEVER placed an order"
SELECT first_name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);
-- NOT EXISTS handles NULLs cleanly — preferred over NOT IN with subqueries

-- Performance: EXISTS often beats IN on big tables because it short-circuits
-- (stops scanning the subquery once any row matches)
★ EXISTS vs IN — A SIMPLE RULE

Functionally these often produce the same result:

  • WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
  • WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = id)

For NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS they're NOT equivalent when NULLs are involved — NOT EXISTS is correct and NOT IN is fragile.

For performance, EXISTS short-circuits while IN materializes the full set first — EXISTS usually wins on big tables.

Inline subqueries (derived tables) — subqueries in FROM

-- Pattern: build a derived table inside FROM, then query against it
SELECT
 customer_segment,
 AVG(total_spend) AS avg_spend
FROM (
 SELECT
 customer_id,
 CASE
 WHEN SUM(total) > 1000 THEN 'high'
 WHEN SUM(total) > 100 THEN 'medium'
 ELSE 'low'
 END AS customer_segment,
 SUM(total) AS total_spend
 FROM orders
 GROUP BY customer_id
) AS segments
GROUP BY customer_segment;
-- Two-step query: bucket customers, then aggregate the buckets
-- Inner query produces a per-customer table; outer query groups it

-- ⚠ Most dialects REQUIRE an alias for the derived table
FROM (SELECT ...) AS segments -- ✓ required in Postgres/SQL Server
FROM (SELECT ...) segments -- AS optional in most

Inline subquery in JOIN

-- "Each customer with their order count and total spend"
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 stats.order_count,
 stats.total_spend
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (
 SELECT
 customer_id,
 COUNT(*) AS order_count,
 SUM(total) AS total_spend
 FROM orders
 WHERE status = 'completed'
 GROUP BY customer_id
) stats ON stats.customer_id = c.id;
-- Pre-aggregate orders → join one row per customer onto customers
-- Avoids row multiplication, lets you use one stats source in multiple SELECTs

Correlated subqueries — re-evaluated per outer row

CORRELATED SUBQUERY
A subquery that REFERENCES a column from the OUTER query.

It re-runs for EACH row of the outer query, parametrized by that row's value.

Powerful — but expensive on big tables. Often replaceable with JOIN or window function. 
-- "Each customer's MOST RECENT order date"
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 (
 SELECT MAX(o.order_date)
 FROM orders o
 WHERE o.customer_id = c.id ← references outer c.id
 ) AS last_order_date
FROM customers c;
-- The subquery runs once per customer, filtered to that customer's orders
-- Result: one row per customer with their max order date (NULL if no orders)

-- Equivalent with LEFT JOIN + aggregation
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 MAX(o.order_date) AS last_order_date
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.first_name;
-- For most cases, the JOIN+GROUP BY version is faster and more idiomatic

Correlated subqueries with EXISTS

-- This is almost ALWAYS a correlated subquery
SELECT first_name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);
-- The outer c.id is referenced inside the subquery — correlated.
-- The optimizer is smart about this pattern; usually fast.

When correlated subqueries are necessary

-- "Each product where the price is above the category average"
SELECT
 p1.name,
 p1.category,
 p1.price
FROM products p1
WHERE p1.price > (
 SELECT AVG(price)
 FROM products p2
 WHERE p2.category = p1.category ← correlation: per-category average
);

-- Hard to do without correlation: need a different average per row
-- Modern alternative: window functions (covered in ch4/s3)
SELECT name, category, price,
 AVG(price) OVER (PARTITION BY category) AS cat_avg
FROM products
WHERE price > AVG(price) OVER (PARTITION BY category);
-- Window functions are usually faster and clearer than correlated subqueries

Subqueries that return multiple rows AND columns

-- Multi-column IN — match composite keys
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE (customer_id, product_id) IN (
 SELECT customer_id, product_id
 FROM repeat_purchases
);
-- Postgres + a few others support row-value IN; SQL Server doesn't natively

-- Multi-row but single column — the standard IN pattern
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM premium_customers);

Subquery vs JOIN — when to use which

GoalBest tool
Filter by membership in another tableIN subquery or JOIN+DISTINCT
Find rows that exist in one table but not anotherNOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN + IS NULL
Show a derived single value as a columnScalar subquery in SELECT
Pre-aggregate then joinInline subquery in FROM, or CTE
"Above group average" per rowCorrelated subquery or window function
Reuse the same logic multiple timesCTE (covered in ch4/s2)

Worked example — products outperforming their category

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Find products whose 2024 revenue exceeded their category's average product revenue."

-- Step 1: per-product revenue (inline subquery in FROM)
-- Step 2: per-category average via correlated subquery

SELECT
 p.name,
 p.category,
 pr.revenue
FROM (
 SELECT
 product_id,
 SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS revenue
 FROM order_items oi
 JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
 WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND o.order_date < '2025-01-01'
 GROUP BY product_id
) pr
INNER JOIN products p ON p.id = pr.product_id
WHERE pr.revenue > (
 SELECT AVG(revenue)
 FROM (
 SELECT
 product_id,
 SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS revenue
 FROM order_items oi2
 JOIN orders o2 ON o2.id = oi2.order_id
 WHERE o2.order_date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND o2.order_date < '2025-01-01'
 GROUP BY product_id
 ) pr2
 JOIN products p2 ON p2.id = pr2.product_id
 WHERE p2.category = p.category
);
-- ⚠ This is unwieldy. CTEs (ch4/s2) and window functions (ch4/s3)
-- make this MUCH cleaner. Re-visit after those sections.

Common subquery mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL BUGS
  1. Scalar subquery returning multiple rows — runtime error. Add LIMIT 1 or aggregate
  2. NOT IN with NULL in subquery — returns zero rows. Use NOT EXISTS or filter NULL out
  3. Missing alias on derived table — most dialects require FROM (SELECT ...) AS x
  4. Correlated subquery on huge tables — re-runs for each outer row; can be 1000x slower than a JOIN
  5. Forgetting that scalar subquery can return NULL — e.g., MAX() on an empty subset
  6. Using subquery when CTE is clearer — for multi-step logic, CTE wins on readability
★ ON THE EXAM

"Subquery returning one value?" → scalar — usable in SELECT, WHERE, HAVING.

"Subquery in FROM?" → inline / derived table — must have an alias.

"Subquery referencing the outer query?" → correlated; re-runs per outer row.

"Find customers with NO orders?" → NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id).

"Above-average X?" → WHERE x > (SELECT AVG(x) FROM ...).

"NOT IN trap?" → NULLs in the subquery return zero rows; use NOT EXISTS instead.

"ANY vs ALL?" → ANY = at least one matches; ALL = every one matches.

"Scalar subquery returns 0 rows?" → returns NULL (not an error).

"Scalar subquery returns 2 rows?" → runtime error.

"EXISTS vs IN?" → similar for matches; for "NOT," EXISTS is bulletproof and IN is fragile.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Three subquery types: scalar (one value), inline/derived table (multi-row), correlated (per-outer-row)
  • Scalar subqueries must return ≤1 row — runtime error if more
  • Use IN / NOT IN with single-column subqueries; ANY / ALL for comparisons
  • EXISTS is more efficient than IN on big tables — short-circuits on first match
  • NOT EXISTS handles NULLs correctly; NOT IN is fragile when subquery may include NULL
  • Inline subqueries (in FROM) need an alias in most dialects — FROM (SELECT ...) AS x
  • Correlated subqueries reference outer rows — powerful but can be slow
  • Use scalar subqueries in SELECT to add a constant or per-context value to every row
  • Pre-aggregate via inline subquery to avoid row-multiplication when joining
  • For repeated subquery logic, CTEs (next section) are cleaner
  • For per-group calculations, window functions (ch4/s3) often beat correlated subqueries

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

CTEs (Common Table Expressions) let you name and chain temporary result sets within a single query. They turn 200-line nested-subquery monsters into readable top-to-bottom flow. Modern SQL exam questions almost always have a "cleaner with a CTE" answer. Once you're comfortable with CTEs, you stop writing nested subqueries.

CTE basics — the WITH clause

CTE SYNTAX
WITH cte_name AS (
 SELECT ...
)
SELECT ... FROM cte_name ...;
Defines a named, temporary result set used in the main query that follows.

Scoped to the query — disappears after execution.
Improves readability vs deeply nested subqueries.
Same performance as inline subqueries in most modern engines. 
-- Without CTE — nested subquery
SELECT segment, COUNT(*) AS num_customers
FROM (
 SELECT
 customer_id,
 CASE
 WHEN SUM(total) > 1000 THEN 'high'
 WHEN SUM(total) > 100 THEN 'medium'
 ELSE 'low'
 END AS segment
 FROM orders
 GROUP BY customer_id
) AS labeled
GROUP BY segment;

-- With CTE — same thing, top-to-bottom
WITH labeled AS (
 SELECT
 customer_id,
 CASE
 WHEN SUM(total) > 1000 THEN 'high'
 WHEN SUM(total) > 100 THEN 'medium'
 ELSE 'low'
 END AS segment
 FROM orders
 GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT segment, COUNT(*) AS num_customers
FROM labeled
GROUP BY segment;
-- The CTE reads top-to-bottom: "first, build labeled. Then, count by segment."

CTEs in any clause

-- CTE can be used in JOINs
WITH high_value_customers AS (
 SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS lifetime_spend
 FROM orders
 GROUP BY customer_id
 HAVING SUM(total) > 1000
)
SELECT c.first_name, hvc.lifetime_spend
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN high_value_customers hvc ON hvc.customer_id = c.id;

-- CTE used in WHERE via subquery
WITH state_avg AS (
 SELECT state, AVG(total) AS avg_spend
 FROM customers
 GROUP BY state
)
SELECT c.first_name, c.lifetime_spend
FROM customers c
WHERE c.lifetime_spend > (
 SELECT avg_spend FROM state_avg WHERE state = c.state
);

Chaining multiple CTEs

-- Multiple CTEs in one WITH — comma-separated
WITH
order_totals AS (
 SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spend
 FROM orders
 WHERE status = 'completed'
 GROUP BY customer_id
),
segments AS (
 SELECT
 customer_id,
 spend,
 CASE
 WHEN spend > 5000 THEN 'whale'
 WHEN spend > 1000 THEN 'high'
 WHEN spend > 100 THEN 'medium'
 ELSE 'low'
 END AS segment
 FROM order_totals
),
segment_summary AS (
 SELECT
 segment,
 COUNT(*) AS num_customers,
 AVG(spend) AS avg_spend
 FROM segments
 GROUP BY segment
)
SELECT * FROM segment_summary
ORDER BY avg_spend DESC;

-- Read top-to-bottom:
-- 1. Sum order totals per customer
-- 2. Bucket them into segments
-- 3. Aggregate per segment
-- 4. Show the result

-- Each CTE can reference earlier ones (segments uses order_totals)
★ STRUCTURE A COMPLEX QUERY WITH CTEs

For any multi-step analysis, break it into named CTEs:

  • One CTE per logical step
  • Name each CTE for what it represents (not what it computes)
  • Build each step against the result of the previous
  • The final SELECT is usually short — most of the work is in the CTEs

Test each CTE individually by changing the final SELECT to SELECT * FROM cte_name to inspect intermediate results.

CTE vs subquery — performance

-- Used to be: CTEs were "optimization fences" in Postgres — always materialized
-- Modern Postgres (12+): CTEs are usually INLINED — same plan as a subquery

-- Same result whether you use CTE or inline subquery:
WITH x AS (SELECT * FROM big_table WHERE id > 1000)
SELECT * FROM x WHERE name = 'Alice';

SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM big_table WHERE id > 1000) x
WHERE name = 'Alice';

-- To FORCE materialization (rare, usually for debugging):
WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM big_table WHERE id > 1000)
SELECT * FROM x WHERE name = 'Alice';

-- Use CTEs for READABILITY, not for performance hints

Recursive CTEs — the only way to do hierarchies of arbitrary depth

RECURSIVE CTE STRUCTURE
WITH RECURSIVE cte_name AS (
 -- BASE CASE: initial rows
 SELECT ...

 UNION ALL

 -- RECURSIVE STEP: rows derived from the previous iteration
 SELECT ... FROM cte_name JOIN ... WHERE ...
)
SELECT * FROM cte_name;
Used for: hierarchies (org charts, categories), graph traversal, generating sequences.

Postgres / SQL Server / Oracle support RECURSIVE. MySQL 8+. SQLite 3.8+. 
-- Employees with arbitrary-depth reporting chains
-- Goal: build a path from each employee to the CEO

WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
 -- Base case: top-level employees (no manager)
 SELECT
 id,
 name,
 manager_id,
 name AS path,
 1 AS depth
 FROM employees
 WHERE manager_id IS NULL

 UNION ALL

 -- Recursive step: find employees whose manager IS already in chain
 SELECT
 e.id,
 e.name,
 e.manager_id,
 c.path || ' > ' || e.name AS path,
 c.depth + 1 AS depth
 FROM employees e
 INNER JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth, path FROM chain
ORDER BY depth, name;
-- Result:
-- id | name | depth | path
-- 1 | Alice | 1 | Alice
-- 2 | Bob | 2 | Alice > Bob
-- 3 | Carol | 2 | Alice > Carol
-- 4 | Dan | 3 | Alice > Bob > Dan

-- This is impossible without recursive CTEs (or vendor-specific extensions)

Generating sequences with recursive CTEs

-- "Generate the integers 1 through 10"
WITH RECURSIVE numbers AS (
 SELECT 1 AS n
 UNION ALL
 SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 10
)
SELECT * FROM numbers;
-- Result: 1, 2, 3, ..., 10

-- "Generate every day in 2024" — date scaffold without generate_series
WITH RECURSIVE days AS (
 SELECT DATE '2024-01-01' AS day
 UNION ALL
 SELECT day + INTERVAL '1 day' FROM days WHERE day < DATE '2024-12-31'
)
SELECT * FROM days;
-- Works in MySQL 8+, SQL Server, etc. — useful when generate_series isn't available
⚠ INFINITE RECURSION

If the recursive step doesn't make progress toward termination, the CTE runs forever:

-- BAD: missing WHERE clause = infinite loop
WITH RECURSIVE bad AS (
 SELECT 1 AS n
 UNION ALL
 SELECT n + 1 FROM bad -- runs until memory exhausted
)
SELECT * FROM bad;

Most engines have a default recursion depth limit (Postgres: unlimited by default but configurable; SQL Server: 100). Always include a WHERE clause that limits depth.

Worked example — multi-step customer analysis

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Identify customers whose 2024 spend was BOTH higher than their personal 2023 spend AND higher than their state's 2024 average."

-- Break into named steps, each a CTE

WITH spend_2023 AS (
 SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spend
 FROM orders
 WHERE order_date >= '2023-01-01' AND order_date < '2024-01-01'
 AND status = 'completed'
 GROUP BY customer_id
),
spend_2024 AS (
 SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spend
 FROM orders
 WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01'
 AND status = 'completed'
 GROUP BY customer_id
),
state_avg_2024 AS (
 SELECT c.state, AVG(s24.spend) AS avg_spend
 FROM spend_2024 s24
 INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = s24.customer_id
 GROUP BY c.state
)
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 c.last_name,
 c.state,
 s23.spend AS spend_2023,
 s24.spend AS spend_2024,
 sa.avg_spend AS state_avg_2024
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN spend_2024 s24 ON s24.customer_id = c.id
INNER JOIN spend_2023 s23 ON s23.customer_id = c.id
INNER JOIN state_avg_2024 sa ON sa.state = c.state
WHERE s24.spend > s23.spend
 AND s24.spend > sa.avg_spend
ORDER BY s24.spend DESC;

-- Reads top-to-bottom:
-- spend_2023 → spend_2024 → state_avg_2024 → final filter
-- Each CTE is testable independently — change the final SELECT to inspect

Re-using a CTE multiple times

-- A CTE can be referenced multiple times in the same query
WITH order_totals AS (
 SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spend
 FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'
 GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT
 'Top 5' AS section, c.first_name, ot.spend
FROM order_totals ot
INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = ot.customer_id
ORDER BY ot.spend DESC LIMIT 5

UNION ALL

SELECT
 'Bottom 5' AS section, c.first_name, ot.spend
FROM order_totals ot -- ← reused!
INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = ot.customer_id
ORDER BY ot.spend ASC LIMIT 5;
-- Two queries combined via UNION, both using the same CTE

CTE vs subquery vs temp table

PatternScopeReusable?Use when
Inline subquerySingle use in queryNoSimple, one-off transform
CTEWhole queryYes (in same query)Multi-step logic, readability
ViewPersistentAcross queriesReusable across sessions, naming abstractions
Temp tableSessionYes (in session)Reuse a heavy result across queries in a session
★ DEFAULT TO CTEs

When in doubt, write a CTE. They're:

  • More readable than nested subqueries
  • Self-documenting (each CTE has a name)
  • Testable in isolation
  • Same performance as the equivalent subquery in modern engines
  • Required for recursion (hierarchies)

Common CTE bugs

⚠ TYPICAL ISSUES
  1. Forgetting commas between multiple CTEs in WITH
  2. Putting WITH after another clause — WITH must be at the start
  3. Referencing a later CTE from an earlier one — CTEs are evaluated in order, top to bottom
  4. Forgetting RECURSIVE keyword in Postgres for recursive CTEs (some dialects allow without)
  5. Infinite recursion from missing termination condition
  6. Using CTE for performance hints — modern optimizers inline anyway
  7. Returning more columns than needed — only the final SELECT columns reach the user
★ ON THE EXAM

"CTE keyword?" → WITH.

"Multiple CTEs?" → comma-separated: WITH a AS (...), b AS (...) SELECT ...

"Reference earlier CTE?" → Yes, in later CTEs and the main query.

"Reference later CTE from earlier?" → No, order matters.

"Recursive CTE?" → WITH RECURSIVE name AS (base UNION ALL recursive_step).

"Hierarchies in SQL?" → Recursive CTE — only way without vendor extensions.

"CTE vs subquery performance?" → Same in modern engines (Postgres 12+, SQL Server, etc.).

"Reuse a CTE in same query?" → Yes, by referencing its name multiple times.

"CTE scope?" → Single query; disappears after.

"Infinite loop in recursive CTE?" → Add a termination condition (e.g., depth limit).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • CTEs (WITH clause) are named, temporary result sets scoped to one query
  • Improve readability vs nested subqueries — read top-to-bottom
  • Same performance as equivalent inline subquery in modern engines (Postgres 12+, SQL Server, etc.)
  • Multiple CTEs in one WITH are comma-separated; each can reference earlier ones
  • CTEs are referenceable anywhere in the main query — SELECT, JOIN, WHERE, etc.
  • Default to CTEs for any multi-step logic; reach for subqueries only for trivial inline cases
  • Recursive CTEs use WITH RECURSIVE — needed for hierarchies and graph traversal
  • Structure: base case → UNION ALL → recursive step (referencing the CTE)
  • Always include a termination condition to avoid infinite recursion
  • Use recursive CTEs to generate sequences (numbers, dates) when generate_series unavailable
  • A CTE can be referenced multiple times in the same query — useful for UNION patterns
  • Test individual CTEs by changing the final SELECT to SELECT * FROM cte_name
