◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Window functions let you do per-row calculations that look at OTHER rows — running totals, ranks, comparing to previous/next row, percentiles within a group. They solve problems that used to require self-joins, correlated subqueries, or scripts. The DataCamp SQL Associate exam has at least 2-3 window function questions, and they're heavily tested because they separate intermediate from advanced SQL.

What a window function does

WINDOW FUNCTION CORE IDEA
A regular aggregate (SUM, COUNT) collapses many rows into ONE row.
A window function computes an aggregate for each row, BUT KEEPS THE ROW.

SELECT
 col,
 AGGREGATE_FN(...) OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY sort_col)
FROM table;
The OVER (...) clause defines the "window" — which rows the function sees for the current row. 
-- Regular aggregate: collapses to one row per group
SELECT state, AVG(spend) FROM customers GROUP BY state;
-- state | avg_spend
-- CA | 1200
-- NY | 950

-- Window function: keeps every row, attaches the state average
SELECT
 first_name,
 state,
 spend,
 AVG(spend) OVER (PARTITION BY state) AS state_avg
FROM customers;
-- first_name | state | spend | state_avg
-- Alice | CA | 1500 | 1200 ← CA's avg attached
-- Bob | CA | 900 | 1200 ← same
-- Carol | NY | 1100 | 950 ← NY's avg
-- Dan | NY | 800 | 950

The OVER clause — defining the window

ComponentPurpose
PARTITION BY colGroup rows for the window (like GROUP BY but doesn't collapse). Optional — no partition = entire result set.
ORDER BY colOrder rows within the partition. Required for ranking/cumulative functions.
ROWS BETWEEN ... AND ...The frame — which rows from the partition the function looks at. Advanced.
 
-- Different windows give different results
SELECT
 name,
 state,
 spend,
 AVG(spend) OVER () AS overall_avg,
 AVG(spend) OVER (PARTITION BY state) AS state_avg,
 AVG(spend) OVER (PARTITION BY state, tier) AS state_tier_avg
FROM customers;
-- Three different averages computed for each row

Ranking functions — ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK

FunctionTie behaviorOutput for [100, 90, 90, 80]
ROW_NUMBER()Always 1, 2, 3 — ties broken arbitrarily1, 2, 3, 4
RANK()Same value gets same rank; skips next1, 2, 2, 4
DENSE_RANK()Same value gets same rank; no skip1, 2, 2, 3
 
-- "Rank customers within each state by spend"
SELECT
 first_name,
 state,
 spend,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY spend DESC) AS rownum,
 RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY spend DESC) AS rank,
 DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY spend DESC) AS dense
FROM customers;

-- Result:
-- first_name | state | spend | rownum | rank | dense
-- Alice | CA | 1500 | 1 | 1 | 1
-- Bob | CA | 1500 | 2 | 1 | 1 ← tie at top
-- Carol | CA | 900 | 3 | 3 | 2 ← RANK skipped 2; DENSE didn't
-- Dan | CA | 600 | 4 | 4 | 3
-- Eve | NY | 1100 | 1 | 1 | 1 ← partition reset for NY
-- Frank | NY | 800 | 2 | 2 | 2

Top-N per group — the classic ROW_NUMBER pattern

-- "Top 3 customers by spend in each state"
WITH ranked AS (
 SELECT
 first_name,
 state,
 spend,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY spend DESC) AS rn
 FROM customers
)
SELECT first_name, state, spend
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;
-- Only the top 3 per state

-- This pattern is impossible (or very ugly) with regular SQL.
-- It's one of the most-tested SQL exam patterns.

NTILE — bucketing into N equal groups

-- Split customers into 4 quartiles by spend
SELECT
 first_name,
 spend,
 NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY spend) AS quartile
FROM customers;
-- quartile 1 = bottom 25%
-- quartile 2 = 25-50%
-- quartile 3 = 50-75%
-- quartile 4 = top 25%

-- With partition: quartiles WITHIN each state
SELECT
 first_name, state, spend,
 NTILE(4) OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY spend) AS state_quartile
FROM customers;

LAG and LEAD — accessing other rows

LAG / LEAD
LAG(col, offset, default) OVER (ORDER BY ...) = value from N rows EARLIER
LEAD(col, offset, default) OVER (ORDER BY ...) = value from N rows LATER

Most common: previous row (offset=1) for month-over-month, day-over-day comparisons. 
-- Monthly revenue with previous month for comparison
SELECT
 month,
 revenue,
 LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month_rev,
 revenue - LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS month_over_month_change
FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY month;

-- Result:
-- month | revenue | prev_month_rev | month_over_month_change
-- 2024-01-01 | 10000 | NULL | NULL
-- 2024-02-01 | 12000 | 10000 | 2000
-- 2024-03-01 | 11500 | 12000 | -500

-- LAG with default — replace NULL with 0
LAG(revenue, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY month)

-- Partitioned LAG — previous month WITHIN EACH STATE
LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY month)

-- LEAD — value from NEXT row (useful for "what's coming")
LEAD(end_date, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY start_date)
-- "When did this user's session end?" — peek at the start of the NEXT session

FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE — bookends

-- First and last value within each partition
SELECT
 customer_id,
 order_date,
 total,
 FIRST_VALUE(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS first_order,
 LAST_VALUE(total) OVER (
 PARTITION BY customer_id
 ORDER BY order_date
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
 ) AS last_order
FROM orders;

-- ⚠ LAST_VALUE has a frame trap:
-- By default the window frame is "UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW"
-- So LAST_VALUE = the CURRENT row, not the actual last
-- Always add: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
-- OR use FIRST_VALUE with reversed ORDER BY

Running totals and cumulative aggregates

-- Running total of revenue over time
SELECT
 order_date,
 daily_revenue,
 SUM(daily_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS cumulative
FROM daily_revenue;
-- Result:
-- order_date | daily_revenue | cumulative
-- 2024-01-01 | 100 | 100
-- 2024-01-02 | 150 | 250
-- 2024-01-03 | 80 | 330

-- When ORDER BY is present and no frame specified, default frame is:
-- "RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW"
-- = all rows from start to current → cumulative sum

-- Running average — "average so far"
AVG(daily_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)

-- Running count, max, min — all work the same
COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)
MAX(daily_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)

-- Cumulative WITHIN each state
SUM(daily_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY order_date)
-- Each state has its own running total, resets per partition

Moving averages — fixed-size window frame

-- 7-day moving average of daily revenue
SELECT
 order_date,
 daily_revenue,
 AVG(daily_revenue) OVER (
 ORDER BY order_date
 ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
 ) AS ma7
FROM daily_revenue;
-- For each day, average over today + 6 prior days = 7 days total

-- Centered 7-day moving average (3 before + current + 3 after)
AVG(daily_revenue) OVER (
 ORDER BY order_date
 ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 3 FOLLOWING
)

-- "All rows from start of partition to current" (cumulative)
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

-- "Just this row and the next 2"
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND 2 FOLLOWING

-- "Everything in the partition"
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING

Percent of total and percentile — analytic patterns

-- Each customer's spend as percent of their state's total
SELECT
 first_name,
 state,
 spend,
 100.0 * spend / SUM(spend) OVER (PARTITION BY state) AS pct_of_state
FROM customers;

-- Each customer's percentile within state
SELECT
 first_name,
 state,
 spend,
 PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY spend) AS pct_rank
FROM customers;
-- PERCENT_RANK returns 0..1 (0 for lowest, 1 for highest)

-- CUME_DIST — cumulative distribution (rank/N)
CUME_DIST() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY spend)

Window functions can't go in WHERE — fix with subquery/CTE

-- ERROR: WHERE evaluates BEFORE window functions can compute
SELECT
 first_name,
 spend,
 RANK() OVER (ORDER BY spend DESC) AS rk
FROM customers
WHERE RANK() OVER (ORDER BY spend DESC) <= 5; -- ERROR

-- Wrap in CTE or subquery
WITH ranked AS (
 SELECT
 first_name, spend,
 RANK() OVER (ORDER BY spend DESC) AS rk
 FROM customers
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rk <= 5;
-- Equivalently in a subquery
★ EXECUTION ORDER REMINDER

Window functions run AFTER WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING — but BEFORE ORDER BY and LIMIT.

So you can ORDER BY a window function result, but to FILTER by one you need a subquery/CTE.

Worked example — customer cohort analysis

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "For each customer's order history, show: the order amount, the days since their previous order, and their running lifetime spend up to that point. Then keep only orders where they're in the top 3 within their state by lifetime spend at that moment."

WITH order_history AS (
 SELECT
 c.id AS customer_id,
 c.state,
 c.first_name,
 o.order_date,
 o.total,
 LAG(o.order_date) OVER (
 PARTITION BY c.id ORDER BY o.order_date
 ) AS prev_order_date,
 SUM(o.total) OVER (
 PARTITION BY c.id ORDER BY o.order_date
 ) AS running_ltv
 FROM customers c
 INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
 WHERE o.status = 'completed'
),
ranked AS (
 SELECT
 *,
 order_date - prev_order_date AS days_since_prev,
 RANK() OVER (
 PARTITION BY state, order_date
 ORDER BY running_ltv DESC
 ) AS state_rank_at_date
 FROM order_history
)
SELECT
 first_name, state, order_date, total,
 days_since_prev, running_ltv, state_rank_at_date
FROM ranked
WHERE state_rank_at_date <= 3
ORDER BY state, order_date;

-- Uses: LAG (previous order date), running SUM, RANK with multiple partition keys.
-- A non-window-function version would need self-joins for every metric — 5x longer.

Common window function bugs

⚠ TYPICAL MISTAKES
  1. Using a window function in WHERE → error. Wrap in CTE/subquery and filter outside.
  2. Forgetting ORDER BY in OVER for ranking/cumulative — produces nondeterministic or wrong results
  3. LAST_VALUE returns current row instead of last in partition — default frame trap. Specify ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
  4. Confusing RANK vs DENSE_RANK — RANK skips after ties, DENSE_RANK doesn't
  5. Using ROW_NUMBER for "rank" when ties matter — ROW_NUMBER breaks ties arbitrarily
  6. Forgetting PARTITION BY — function applies to the entire result set instead of per-group
  7. Wrong frame for moving averages — ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for trailing, BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND N FOLLOWING for centered
★ ON THE EXAM

"Window function syntax?" → AGG_FN(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...).

"Top N per group?" → ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC), filter rn ≤ N.

"ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK?" → ROW_NUMBER always unique; RANK skips after ties; DENSE_RANK doesn't skip.

"Previous row's value?" → LAG(col) OVER (ORDER BY ...).

"Running total?" → SUM(col) OVER (ORDER BY date).

"Filter on window function?" → Wrap in subquery/CTE — windows can't go in WHERE.

"% of total?" → col / SUM(col) OVER () or with PARTITION BY for per-group.

"7-day moving avg?" → AVG(col) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).

"Per-state ranking?" → Add PARTITION BY state to OVER.

"NTILE(4)?" → splits ordered rows into 4 equal buckets (quartiles).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Window functions compute aggregates per row WITHOUT collapsing rows
  • Syntax: AGG() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ROWS BETWEEN ...)
  • PARTITION BY = group for the window (no collapsing); ORDER BY = sort within partition
  • ROW_NUMBER: unique per partition; RANK: skips after ties; DENSE_RANK: no skip
  • Top-N per group: ROW_NUMBER OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...), filter ≤ N in a CTE
  • LAG / LEAD: access previous/next row — perfect for time-series comparisons
  • Running totals: SUM(col) OVER (ORDER BY date) with default frame
  • Moving averages: AVG(col) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT)
  • LAST_VALUE has a frame gotcha — specify ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  • Window functions can't be used in WHERE — wrap in CTE/subquery and filter there
  • NTILE(N) buckets ordered rows into N equal groups
  • Window functions usually replace self-joins and correlated subqueries — faster and clearer

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Set operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT) combine the RESULTS of multiple queries — stacking rows, finding overlaps, finding differences. They're how you compare two queries instead of two tables, useful for data reconciliation, multi-source reports, and "what's in A but not in B" questions. DataCamp tests UNION especially — UNION vs UNION ALL is a classic exam trap.

The three set operations

OperationReturnsSet theory analog
UNIONRows from EITHER query (deduplicated)A ∪ B
UNION ALLRows from EITHER query (keep duplicates)A ⊎ B (multiset)
INTERSECTRows in BOTH queriesA ∩ B
EXCEPT (Postgres) / MINUS (Oracle)Rows in FIRST but not SECONDA − B

UNION — stacking results

UNION RULES
Both queries must have the SAME NUMBER of columns.
Corresponding columns must have COMPATIBLE TYPES.
Column names come from the FIRST query.
UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them. 
-- "All people in the database — employees AND customers"
SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM employees
UNION
SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM customers;
-- One combined list. If someone is in both tables with same name+email, appears ONCE.

-- UNION ALL — keep duplicates (faster, no dedup work)
SELECT first_name, last_name FROM employees
UNION ALL
SELECT first_name, last_name FROM customers;
-- Same person in both tables → appears twice

-- ⚠ Column count mismatch → error
SELECT first_name, last_name FROM employees
UNION
SELECT first_name FROM customers;
-- ERROR: each query must have the same number of columns

-- Type mismatch → may error or coerce
SELECT id, name FROM products -- (int, text)
UNION
SELECT name, id FROM categories; -- (text, int) — column order matters!
-- Most engines: error. Some auto-cast. Always match column order intentionally.

UNION vs UNION ALL — the exam trap

⚠ UNION DEFAULTS TO DISTINCT

UNION implicitly de-duplicates the combined result — expensive on large queries.

UNION ALL keeps all rows including duplicates — much faster.

Use UNION ALL when:

  • You KNOW there are no duplicates (e.g., disjoint date ranges)
  • Duplicates are meaningful and should be counted
  • Performance matters

Use UNION only when you specifically need deduplication.

Default to UNION ALL — the "safer" choice for big data, unless you actually need dedup.

-- Real use case: combining log tables that are sharded by month
SELECT * FROM events_2024_q1
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM events_2024_q2
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM events_2024_q3
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM events_2024_q4
ORDER BY event_time;
-- Each table is disjoint by time — no duplicates possible — UNION ALL is correct.
-- UNION here would just waste time deduping rows that can't be dupes.

UNION with column aliasing

-- Column names come from the FIRST query
SELECT id AS user_id, name AS full_name FROM employees
UNION ALL
SELECT id, first_name || ' ' || last_name FROM customers;
-- Final columns: user_id, full_name (from first query)

-- Add a "source" column to know which side each row came from
SELECT 'employee' AS source, id, name FROM employees
UNION ALL
SELECT 'customer' AS source, id, first_name || ' ' || last_name FROM customers;
-- Result has a source column distinguishing rows from each table

ORDER BY and LIMIT with UNION

-- ORDER BY applies to the WHOLE union result (not the individual parts)
SELECT name FROM employees
UNION ALL
SELECT name FROM customers
ORDER BY name;
-- Sorts the COMBINED result

-- To order each side independently, wrap in subqueries
(SELECT name FROM employees ORDER BY name LIMIT 5)
UNION ALL
(SELECT name FROM customers ORDER BY name LIMIT 5)
ORDER BY name;
-- Takes the top-5 of each, then merges and orders the result of 10 rows

-- Some dialects (MySQL) require the parentheses; Postgres allows either

INTERSECT — rows in both queries

-- "People who are BOTH employees AND customers (e.g., they bought their own product)"
SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM employees
INTERSECT
SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM customers;
-- Only rows present in both query results (matching on ALL selected columns)

-- INTERSECT also deduplicates by default
-- INTERSECT ALL (Postgres, SQL Server) keeps duplicates — rare use case

-- Same rules as UNION:
-- - Same column count
-- - Compatible types
-- - Column names from first query
⚠ NOT SUPPORTED IN OLD MYSQL

INTERSECT and EXCEPT are NOT in MySQL until version 8.0.31. For older MySQL, use the JOIN equivalent:

-- Instead of INTERSECT:
SELECT DISTINCT a.first_name, a.last_name, a.email
FROM employees a
INNER JOIN customers b
 ON a.first_name = b.first_name
 AND a.last_name = b.last_name
 AND a.email = b.email;

EXCEPT — rows in first but not second

-- "Employees who are NOT customers"
SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM employees
EXCEPT
SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM customers;
-- Order MATTERS — A EXCEPT B is different from B EXCEPT A

-- EXCEPT vs MINUS — same operation:
-- Postgres, SQL Server, SQLite: EXCEPT
-- Oracle: MINUS

-- EXCEPT also deduplicates by default
-- EXCEPT ALL keeps duplicate counts

EXCEPT vs LEFT JOIN + IS NULL vs NOT EXISTS

-- Three ways to express "in A but not in B"

-- Using EXCEPT — cleanest when you're comparing the SAME columns
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2023
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2024;
-- Customers who ordered in 2023 but not 2024

-- Using LEFT JOIN + IS NULL — flexible when you need extra columns
SELECT DISTINCT o23.customer_id
FROM orders_2023 o23
LEFT JOIN orders_2024 o24 ON o24.customer_id = o23.customer_id
WHERE o24.customer_id IS NULL;

-- Using NOT EXISTS — most flexible
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders_2023 o23
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM orders_2024 o24
 WHERE o24.customer_id = o23.customer_id
);

-- EXCEPT shines when comparing identical row shapes.
-- NOT EXISTS shines when you need joins or extra logic.

Chaining set operations

-- Multiple set operations in one query
SELECT id FROM table_a
UNION
SELECT id FROM table_b
EXCEPT
SELECT id FROM table_c;

-- ⚠ Precedence varies by engine. Use parentheses for clarity.
(SELECT id FROM table_a UNION SELECT id FROM table_b)
EXCEPT
SELECT id FROM table_c;
-- "Things in A or B, minus things in C"

Set operations vs OR / AND / NOT IN

-- Many set ops can be rewritten with conditions on a single query

-- UNION — same table, different filters
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE state = 'CA'
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE state = 'NY';
-- Same as:
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE state IN ('CA', 'NY');

-- UNION makes sense when you're combining DIFFERENT TABLES
-- For one table with multiple conditions, use OR / IN
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE state = 'CA' OR signup_date > '2024-01-01';
-- NOT:
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE state = 'CA'
UNION
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE signup_date > '2024-01-01';
-- (works but slower because of dedup; unclear intent)

Combining queries with different shapes via NULL padding

-- Pad columns with NULL to make queries union-compatible
SELECT
 'order' AS event_type,
 order_date AS event_date,
 customer_id,
 total,
 NULL AS product_id -- NULL for column that doesn't apply
FROM orders

UNION ALL

SELECT
 'view' AS event_type,
 viewed_at AS event_date,
 customer_id,
 NULL AS total, -- NULL for amount
 product_id
FROM product_views

ORDER BY event_date;
-- Unified "customer activity feed" combining different event types
-- Each event has only the columns relevant to it; others are NULL

Worked example — source reconciliation

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "We have two customer email lists: marketing_emails and crm_emails. Find:

  1. The combined unique list (all emails across both)
  2. Emails in BOTH (true overlap)
  3. Emails in marketing but NOT in CRM (need to add to CRM)
  4. Emails in CRM but NOT in marketing (need to add to marketing)
-- 1. Combined unique list
SELECT email FROM marketing_emails
UNION
SELECT email FROM crm_emails;

-- 2. Emails in both
SELECT email FROM marketing_emails
INTERSECT
SELECT email FROM crm_emails;

-- 3. In marketing only
SELECT email FROM marketing_emails
EXCEPT
SELECT email FROM crm_emails;

-- 4. In CRM only
SELECT email FROM crm_emails
EXCEPT
SELECT email FROM marketing_emails;

-- Bonus: combine all four into a single report with a category label
WITH all_emails AS (
 SELECT email, 'marketing' AS source FROM marketing_emails
 UNION ALL
 SELECT email, 'crm' FROM crm_emails
)
SELECT
 email,
 COUNT(*) AS source_count,
 STRING_AGG(source, ', ' ORDER BY source) AS sources,
 CASE
 WHEN COUNT(*) = 2 THEN 'both'
 WHEN MAX(source) = 'marketing' THEN 'marketing only'
 ELSE 'crm only'
 END AS category
FROM all_emails
GROUP BY email;

Common set operation bugs

⚠ TYPICAL MISTAKES
  1. Column count or type mismatch — sets must have IDENTICAL shape
  2. Wrong column order — UNION matches by position, not by name. SELECT a, b ... UNION SELECT b, a mixes up the data
  3. Using UNION when you meant UNION ALL — wastes time on unnecessary dedup
  4. Using EXCEPT in wrong order — A EXCEPT B ≠ B EXCEPT A
  5. ORDER BY in middle queries — only the FINAL query can have a top-level ORDER BY (or wrap individual parts in subqueries)
  6. INTERSECT/EXCEPT in old MySQL — not supported pre-8.0.31; use JOIN equivalents
  7. NULL handling — INTERSECT and EXCEPT treat NULL = NULL as TRUE (unlike comparison operators!)
★ A NULL QUIRK YOU SHOULD KNOW

In WHERE clauses, NULL = NULL is NULL (false in filters). But for set operations:

SELECT NULL UNION SELECT NULL;
-- Returns: 1 row of NULL — set operations TREAT NULLs as equal
-- This is the "distinct" semantics inherited from how set theory handles equality
★ ON THE EXAM

"Combine results, no duplicates?" → UNION.

"Combine results, keep duplicates?" → UNION ALL (faster).

"Rows in both queries?" → INTERSECT.

"Rows in first but not second?" → EXCEPT (or MINUS in Oracle).

"UNION rules?" → Same column count, compatible types, column names from first.

"ORDER BY a UNION?" → Goes at the end and sorts the combined result.

"UNION vs OR?" → For multiple conditions on same table, use OR. UNION is for combining different queries/tables.

"UNION ALL faster than UNION?" → Yes — skips deduplication.

"NULL in INTERSECT?" → Treated as equal (different from WHERE clause behavior).

"INTERSECT not working?" → Old MySQL doesn't support it; use INNER JOIN equivalent.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • UNION combines rows from two queries; deduplicates by default
  • UNION ALL is the same but keeps duplicates — faster, prefer when no dedup needed
  • INTERSECT returns rows in BOTH queries
  • EXCEPT (Postgres/SQL Server) / MINUS (Oracle) returns rows in FIRST but not SECOND
  • All set ops require: same column count, compatible types, column-by-position matching
  • Column names come from the FIRST query
  • ORDER BY belongs at the end; applies to the combined result (or wrap individual queries)
  • Use NULL padding to combine queries with different shapes (event timelines, etc.)
  • Set ops treat NULL = NULL as TRUE (unlike WHERE filters)
  • For "in A not in B": EXCEPT, NOT EXISTS, or LEFT JOIN + IS NULL all work — EXCEPT is cleanest when row shapes match
  • For single-table multi-condition queries, OR / IN is clearer than UNION
  • Old MySQL lacks INTERSECT/EXCEPT — use JOIN equivalents (INNER JOIN for intersect, LEFT JOIN+IS NULL for except)

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Most analytics work is reading data, but you'll inevitably need to modify it — fixing a value, loading new records, removing test rows. These three commands (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) are also called DML (Data Manipulation Language). They're tested on the DataCamp exam and they're where mistakes can permanently destroy data — getting them right matters even more than SELECTs.

INSERT — adding new rows

INSERT BASIC SYNTAX
INSERT INTO table (col1, col2, ...)
VALUES (val1, val2, ...);
Always list columns explicitly — protects against schema changes.
Number of values must match number of listed columns. 
-- Insert one row
INSERT INTO customers (first_name, last_name, email, state)
VALUES ('Alice', 'Smith', 'alice@x.com', 'CA');

-- Insert multiple rows (most dialects)
INSERT INTO customers (first_name, last_name, email, state)
VALUES
 ('Alice', 'Smith', 'alice@x.com', 'CA'),
 ('Bob', 'Jones', 'bob@y.com', 'NY'),
 ('Carol', 'Davis', 'carol@z.com', 'CA');

-- Omitting columns: ones not listed get their default (often NULL, sometimes a default value, sometimes an error if NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers (first_name, last_name)
VALUES ('Dan', 'Eaton');
-- email, state default to NULL or column default

-- Without specifying columns (DANGEROUS — depends on column order)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (NULL, 'Eve', 'Foster', 'eve@x.com', 'TX');
-- Must provide ALL columns in their physical order
-- Breaks silently when the schema changes — avoid in production

INSERT from another query (INSERT SELECT)

-- Copy rows from one table to another
INSERT INTO customers_archive (first_name, last_name, email, signup_date)
SELECT first_name, last_name, email, signup_date
FROM customers
WHERE signup_date < '2023-01-01';
-- Bulk-archive old customers

-- Columns must match in number and compatible types
-- The SELECT can have any WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY clauses you need

-- Insert computed/derived values
INSERT INTO email_audit (email, customer_id, audited_at)
SELECT email, id, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
FROM customers
WHERE email NOT LIKE '%@%';
-- Flag malformed emails into audit table

RETURNING — get back what you inserted (Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle)

-- Postgres / SQLite / Oracle / SQL Server (OUTPUT)
INSERT INTO customers (first_name, last_name, email)
VALUES ('Alice', 'Smith', 'alice@x.com')
RETURNING id, created_at;
-- Returns the auto-generated id and timestamp — no second SELECT needed

-- SQL Server uses OUTPUT
INSERT INTO customers (first_name, last_name)
OUTPUT INSERTED.id, INSERTED.created_at
VALUES ('Alice', 'Smith');

-- MySQL: use LAST_INSERT_ID() after the insert
INSERT INTO customers (first_name, last_name) VALUES ('Alice', 'Smith');
SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();

UPSERT — INSERT or UPDATE if exists

-- Postgres: ON CONFLICT
INSERT INTO customers (email, first_name, last_name)
VALUES ('alice@x.com', 'Alice', 'Smith')
ON CONFLICT (email)
DO UPDATE SET first_name = EXCLUDED.first_name, last_name = EXCLUDED.last_name;
-- Inserts if email is new; updates name if email already exists

-- MySQL: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
INSERT INTO customers (email, first_name, last_name)
VALUES ('alice@x.com', 'Alice', 'Smith')
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
 first_name = VALUES(first_name),
 last_name = VALUES(last_name);

-- SQL Server: MERGE (more complex but standard SQL)
MERGE customers AS target
USING (VALUES ('alice@x.com', 'Alice', 'Smith')) AS src(email, fn, ln)
ON target.email = src.email
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET first_name = src.fn, last_name = src.ln
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (email, first_name, last_name) VALUES (src.email, src.fn, src.ln);

-- ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING — skip if already exists (Postgres)
INSERT INTO customers (email, ...) VALUES (...)
ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;

UPDATE — modifying existing rows

UPDATE SYNTAX
UPDATE table
SET col1 = value1,
 col2 = value2
WHERE condition;
WHERE IS CRITICAL. Without WHERE, you update EVERY ROW.
Always test with SELECT first to see what rows you'll affect. 
-- Single row
UPDATE customers
SET email = 'alice.smith@new.com'
WHERE id = 42;

-- Multiple columns
UPDATE customers
SET
 first_name = 'Alice',
 last_name = 'Smith',
 updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE id = 42;

-- Update many rows with same value
UPDATE products
SET price = price * 1.10
WHERE category = 'electronics';
-- Increase electronics prices by 10%

-- Update using an expression involving other columns
UPDATE orders
SET total = subtotal + tax + shipping
WHERE total IS NULL;

-- ⚠⚠⚠ WITHOUT WHERE: updates EVERYTHING
UPDATE customers SET email = 'oops@example.com';
-- Every customer now has the same email. Hope you have backups.
⚠ THE SAFETY HABIT

Before running ANY UPDATE or DELETE:

  1. Run a SELECT first with the EXACT same WHERE clause
  2. Count the rows you're about to affect
  3. Sanity-check — does this number match what you expect?
  4. THEN run the UPDATE/DELETE
-- ALWAYS DO THIS FIRST
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE state = 'CA' AND tier = 'free';
-- "1247 rows" — yes, that matches my expectation

-- ONLY THEN run the update
UPDATE customers SET tier = 'standard' WHERE state = 'CA' AND tier = 'free';

UPDATE with JOIN — using related tables

-- Postgres / SQL Server / SQLite — UPDATE ... FROM
UPDATE customers c
SET tier = 'premium'
FROM orders o
WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
 AND o.total > 1000;
-- Promote customers who have any $1000+ order

-- MySQL syntax
UPDATE customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
SET c.tier = 'premium'
WHERE o.total > 1000;

-- Subquery alternative (universal)
UPDATE customers
SET tier = 'premium'
WHERE id IN (
 SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 1000
);

UPDATE with CASE — conditional updates per row

-- Different new value depending on conditions
UPDATE products
SET price = CASE
 WHEN category = 'premium' THEN price * 1.20
 WHEN category = 'sale' THEN price * 0.80
 ELSE price
END;
-- One UPDATE statement, three different effects based on category
-- Much faster than 3 separate UPDATE statements with WHERE category=...

DELETE — removing rows

DELETE SYNTAX
DELETE FROM table
WHERE condition;
WHERE IS CRITICAL. Without WHERE, deletes EVERY ROW.
No way to undo without backups or a transaction. 
-- Delete one row
DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 42;

-- Delete many
DELETE FROM customers WHERE state = 'XX';

-- Delete with JOIN-like logic (subquery)
DELETE FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (
 SELECT id FROM customers WHERE status = 'banned'
);

-- ⚠⚠⚠ DELETE WITHOUT WHERE = DELETE EVERY ROW
DELETE FROM customers;
-- Empty table. Hope you have backups.

-- TRUNCATE — faster way to empty a table (but no WHERE)
TRUNCATE TABLE customers;
-- Removes all rows. Usually faster than DELETE (drops + recreates).
-- Resets auto-increment counters in some dialects. Can't be selectively rolled back.

DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP

CommandWhat it removesWHERE supported?
DELETESelected rows (or all if no WHERE)Yes
TRUNCATEALL rows; structure staysNo
DROPThe entire table — structure AND dataNo

Soft delete pattern — keep data, mark as removed

-- Many production tables use a deleted_at column instead of actual DELETE
UPDATE customers
SET deleted_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE id = 42;

-- Queries then filter out deleted rows
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- Pros: undoable, preserves history, FK constraints don't break
-- Cons: queries get cluttered with WHERE deleted_at IS NULL; storage grows

Foreign key constraints affect DELETE / UPDATE

-- If orders.customer_id references customers.id with FK:
DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 42;
-- May fail with FK violation if customer 42 has orders
-- Options when setting up the FK:
-- ON DELETE RESTRICT (default) — prevents deletion
-- ON DELETE CASCADE — deletes orphaned orders too
-- ON DELETE SET NULL — sets orders.customer_id to NULL
-- Same options apply for UPDATE

Worked example — bulk data cleanup

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Clean up the customer database: (1) mark test accounts as deleted (don't actually remove), (2) update inactive accounts to 'archived' status, (3) move soft-deleted records older than 1 year to the archive table, then delete from main."

-- ALWAYS verify counts first
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE email LIKE '%@test.com';
-- Returns: 47

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE last_login < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '2 years';
-- Returns: 1834

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE deleted_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year';
-- Returns: 312

-- Step 1: soft-delete test accounts
UPDATE customers
SET deleted_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, deletion_reason = 'test account cleanup'
WHERE email LIKE '%@test.com'
 AND deleted_at IS NULL;

-- Step 2: archive inactive accounts
UPDATE customers
SET status = 'archived'
WHERE last_login < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '2 years'
 AND status = 'active';

-- Step 3a: copy old soft-deleted records to archive
INSERT INTO customers_archive (id, first_name, last_name, email, deleted_at, archived_at)
SELECT id, first_name, last_name, email, deleted_at, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
FROM customers
WHERE deleted_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year';

-- Step 3b: hard-delete those records from main
DELETE FROM customers
WHERE deleted_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year';

-- For real production: wrap everything in a TRANSACTION (next section)
-- so you can ROLLBACK if anything looks wrong.

Common bugs with INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE

⚠ TOP MISTAKES
  1. Forgetting WHERE on UPDATE/DELETE → modifies/deletes EVERY row
  2. INSERT without column names → silently breaks when schema changes
  3. Wrong WHERE clause → updates more or fewer rows than intended
  4. UPDATE with JOIN syntax differs by dialect — copy from the right cheatsheet
  5. NULL constraints violated → INSERT fails for missing required columns
  6. FK violations on DELETE when dependent rows exist
  7. Type mismatches in INSERT — 'abc' for int column
  8. Auto-increment confusion — including or excluding the id column inconsistently
  9. Running on production when you meant the test database
★ ON THE EXAM

"Add a row?" → INSERT INTO table (cols) VALUES (...).

"Multiple rows?" → comma-separated VALUES lists.

"Copy from query?" → INSERT INTO ... SELECT ....

"INSERT or update if exists?" → ON CONFLICT (Postgres), ON DUPLICATE KEY (MySQL), MERGE (SQL Server).

"Change rows?" → UPDATE table SET col = ... WHERE ....

"UPDATE without WHERE?" → Updates ALL rows. Always include WHERE.

"Multi-column UPDATE?" → comma-separate the SET assignments.

"UPDATE based on join?" → Postgres: UPDATE t SET ... FROM other WHERE ...; MySQL: UPDATE t INNER JOIN other ON ... SET ....

"Remove rows?" → DELETE FROM table WHERE ....

"Empty a table fast?" → TRUNCATE TABLE name (no WHERE supported).

"Get back the new row?" → Postgres: RETURNING; SQL Server: OUTPUT; MySQL: LAST_INSERT_ID().

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • INSERT adds new rows; always list columns explicitly
  • UPDATE modifies existing rows; SET assigns values
  • DELETE removes rows; same WHERE semantics as SELECT
  • WHERE clauses are mandatory in practice for UPDATE/DELETE — without them, you affect every row
  • Always SELECT first with the same WHERE to count affected rows before UPDATE/DELETE
  • INSERT can take multiple rows: VALUES (...), (...), (...)
  • INSERT SELECT copies from another query — used for archiving and bulk loads
  • UPSERT: Postgres ON CONFLICT, MySQL ON DUPLICATE KEY, SQL Server MERGE
  • UPDATE with JOIN syntax varies by dialect — Postgres uses FROM, MySQL puts JOIN first
  • UPDATE with CASE: different new values per row in one statement
  • TRUNCATE empties a table (faster than DELETE but no WHERE); DROP removes the table itself
  • Foreign key constraints (RESTRICT/CASCADE/SET NULL) shape DELETE behavior
  • Soft delete (setting deleted_at) is preferable to DELETE in production
  • RETURNING / OUTPUT lets you fetch newly inserted IDs in a single round-trip

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A transaction groups multiple SQL statements into one atomic unit — all succeed or all are undone. They're the safety net that lets you run risky UPDATEs and DELETEs without permanent damage, and they're how databases stay consistent when many users are working at once. ACID — the fundamental contract of databases — is built on transactions. Tested on every database certification.

Transaction basics

TRANSACTION STRUCTURE
BEGIN; -- start transaction
 UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
 UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT; -- save all changes permanently
-- OR
ROLLBACK; -- discard all changes since BEGIN
All statements between BEGIN and COMMIT are one atomic unit.
Either ALL of them commit, or NONE of them do. 
-- Classic bank-transfer example
BEGIN;
 UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
 UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
-- Both updates succeed together. If the database crashes between them,
-- the transaction is rolled back automatically — no half-transfers.

-- If something looks wrong before COMMIT, undo everything
BEGIN;
 DELETE FROM customers WHERE state = 'XX';
 -- ⚠ Wait, that deleted 50,000 rows, not 50. Abort!
ROLLBACK;
-- Database state is exactly as it was before BEGIN. No data lost.

BEGIN / START — dialect variations

-- Postgres / SQLite
BEGIN;
BEGIN TRANSACTION; -- equivalent

-- MySQL
START TRANSACTION;
BEGIN; -- also works

-- SQL Server
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
BEGIN TRAN; -- short form

-- All dialects use COMMIT and ROLLBACK the same way

ACID — the four guarantees

ACID PROPERTIES
A — Atomicity — all-or-nothing: a transaction either fully commits or fully rolls back
C — Consistency — transactions move the DB from one valid state to another (FK constraints, NOT NULL, etc. enforced)
I — Isolation — concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate states
D — Durability — once COMMIT returns, the change survives crashes

What each one prevents

PropertyPrevents
AtomicityHalf-completed transactions on crash (the "$100 vanished mid-transfer" bug)
ConsistencyInvalid data states (negative balances, dangling foreign keys, etc.)
IsolationReads that include another transaction's uncommitted changes
DurabilityCommitted data being lost on power failure

Savepoints — partial rollback inside a transaction

BEGIN;
 UPDATE customers SET tier = 'premium' WHERE id = 1;

 SAVEPOINT before_bulk_update; -- create a checkpoint
 UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.5; -- accidentally on ALL products!

 ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_bulk_update; -- undo bulk update only
 -- The first UPDATE to customer 1 is still pending

 UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.5 WHERE category = 'premium';
 -- now the correct update

COMMIT;
-- Two changes committed: customer 1 tier + premium product prices
-- The bad bulk update never happened from the DB's perspective

Isolation levels

LevelReads see uncommitted?Phantom reads possible?
READ UNCOMMITTEDYes ("dirty reads")Yes
READ COMMITTED (default in Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server)NoYes
REPEATABLE READ (default in MySQL)NoPossible
SERIALIZABLENoNo (strongest)
 
-- Set isolation level for the current transaction
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
 -- queries here run under the chosen level
COMMIT;

-- Higher isolation = more correctness, less concurrency, more locking
-- Default (READ COMMITTED) is fine for 95% of analytics work

Concurrency anomalies

★ THE FOUR CLASSIC PROBLEMS
  • Dirty read: T1 reads a row T2 has modified but not committed. T2 rolls back; T1 has stale data.
  • Non-repeatable read: T1 reads a row, T2 updates and commits, T1 reads the same row again and sees different data within ONE transaction.
  • Phantom read: T1 runs a query, T2 inserts new rows matching the query, T1 runs the same query and sees additional rows.
  • Lost update: T1 reads value, T2 reads same value, T1 writes update, T2 writes update — T1's change is lost.

Locking and concurrency

-- SELECT FOR UPDATE — explicit row lock
BEGIN;
 SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
 -- This row is now locked for write until COMMIT
 -- Other transactions wanting to UPDATE row 1 must wait
 UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;
-- Used for "read, decide, then update" patterns to prevent race conditions

-- SELECT FOR SHARE (Postgres) — read lock (others can read, not write)
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR SHARE;

-- LOCK TABLE — explicit table-level lock (rarely needed)
LOCK TABLE accounts IN EXCLUSIVE MODE;

Deadlocks

-- Two transactions can deadlock if they lock resources in different order:

-- Transaction A: Transaction B:
BEGIN; BEGIN;
UPDATE x WHERE id=1; UPDATE x WHERE id=2;
-- holds lock on row 1 -- holds lock on row 2
UPDATE x WHERE id=2; UPDATE x WHERE id=1;
-- WAITS for B to release -- WAITS for A to release
-- ... waits forever ... -- ... waits forever ...

-- Solution: the database detects this and kills one transaction
-- The losing transaction's app code must retry
-- ALSO: always lock resources in the same ORDER across transactions

Auto-commit mode

-- By default, MOST clients run in auto-commit mode:
-- Each statement is its own implicit transaction that commits immediately.

UPDATE customers SET tier = 'premium' WHERE id = 42;
-- Auto-committed. Cannot ROLLBACK.

-- To group statements, explicitly BEGIN:
BEGIN;
 UPDATE customers SET tier = 'premium' WHERE id = 42;
 UPDATE customers SET tier = 'premium' WHERE id = 43;
COMMIT;

-- Or turn off auto-commit (varies by client):
-- psql: \set AUTOCOMMIT off
-- MySQL: SET autocommit = 0;
-- SQL Server: SET IMPLICIT_TRANSACTIONS ON;

Transactions for safety on destructive operations

-- The pattern every DBA uses for risky changes:
BEGIN;
 DELETE FROM customers WHERE state = 'XX';
 SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE state = 'XX'; -- verify it's 0
 SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers; -- verify total looks right
-- If both numbers look correct:
COMMIT;
-- If something's off:
ROLLBACK;

-- This is the SAFETY NET for production data work.
-- Even a wrong DELETE is recoverable while you're in the transaction.

Worked example — atomic order processing

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Process an order: deduct from inventory, charge the customer's account, insert the order row. All three must succeed or none should happen."

BEGIN;

 -- Lock the inventory row to prevent concurrent overselling
 SELECT quantity FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 42 FOR UPDATE;
 -- ... in app code: check quantity >= requested

 -- Deduct inventory
 UPDATE inventory
 SET quantity = quantity - 3
 WHERE product_id = 42 AND quantity >= 3;

 -- Check the update succeeded (1 row, not 0)
 -- If 0 rows: not enough stock → ROLLBACK in app

 -- Charge customer
 UPDATE accounts
 SET balance = balance - 89.99
 WHERE id = 1001 AND balance >= 89.99;
 -- If 0 rows: insufficient funds → ROLLBACK in app

 -- Record order
 INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product_id, quantity, total)
 VALUES (1001, 42, 3, 89.99);

COMMIT;
-- All three operations succeed together as one indivisible unit
-- If any step fails or the app detects an issue, ROLLBACK reverses everything
-- The database is never left in a state with charged-but-no-order or order-but-no-inventory-deduction

Transactions in scripts vs interactive sessions

-- Interactive (psql, MySQL shell, DBeaver, etc.)
BEGIN;
 DELETE FROM ...;
 SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ...; -- verify in same transaction
 -- ROLLBACK; or COMMIT; based on results

-- In application code (Python example)
conn.autocommit = False
try:
 cursor.execute("UPDATE ...")
 cursor.execute("INSERT ...")
 conn.commit()
except Exception:
 conn.rollback()
 raise
-- Same pattern in any language: BEGIN, try statements, COMMIT or ROLLBACK

Common transaction bugs

⚠ TOP MISTAKES
  1. Forgetting COMMIT — your changes hold locks indefinitely; other queries block
  2. Forgetting to ROLLBACK after an error — same problem
  3. Long-running transactions — hold locks for too long, hurt concurrency
  4. Mixing DDL (CREATE TABLE) with DML — some DDL auto-commits in some dialects, breaking the atomicity guarantee
  5. Lock ordering inconsistency across code paths → deadlocks
  6. Catching exceptions but not rolling back — transaction stays open and broken
  7. Assuming SELECT inside a transaction is safe — depends on isolation level for what other transactions see
★ ON THE EXAM

"Group statements as one unit?" → BEGIN; ... COMMIT; (or ROLLBACK to undo).

"ACID stands for?" → Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

"Atomicity?" → all-or-nothing.

"Consistency?" → DB always in a valid state (constraints upheld).

"Isolation?" → concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate state.

"Durability?" → committed changes survive crashes.

"Undo a transaction?" → ROLLBACK (before COMMIT — after COMMIT it's permanent).

"Partial undo?" → SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT.

"Row-level read with intent to update?" → SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (locks the row).

"Default isolation in Postgres/Oracle?" → READ COMMITTED.

"Default isolation in MySQL?" → REPEATABLE READ.

"Strongest isolation?" → SERIALIZABLE.

"Auto-commit?" → each statement is its own transaction unless you BEGIN explicitly.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Transactions group multiple statements into one all-or-nothing unit
  • Syntax: BEGIN; ... ; COMMIT; (or ROLLBACK to undo)
  • ACID = Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (always valid state), Isolation (no dirty reads), Durability (survives crashes)
  • SAVEPOINT allows partial rollback inside a transaction
  • Isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED (loose) → READ COMMITTED → REPEATABLE READ → SERIALIZABLE (strictest)
  • Postgres/Oracle default = READ COMMITTED; MySQL default = REPEATABLE READ
  • Higher isolation = more correctness, less concurrency
  • Concurrency anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update
  • SELECT FOR UPDATE locks rows for the duration of the transaction — used for "read-decide-write" patterns
  • Deadlocks happen when two transactions hold and need each other's locks — solved by consistent lock ordering
  • Auto-commit mode (default in many clients) makes each statement its own transaction
  • Always wrap destructive operations (DELETE, mass UPDATE) in a transaction so you can verify and ROLLBACK if wrong

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Constraints enforce data quality at the database level — so bad data can't be saved in the first place. Indexes are how databases find rows fast. As an analyst, you mostly read these rather than create them, but understanding them tells you why some queries are blazing fast and others take minutes. DataCamp tests recognizing PK/FK/UNIQUE constraints, reading EXPLAIN plans, and knowing when an index helps.

The five main constraints

ConstraintEnforces
PRIMARY KEYUnique + NOT NULL combined — identifies each row
FOREIGN KEYReferences a PK in another table — preserves referential integrity
UNIQUEValues must be distinct (NULLs usually allowed)
NOT NULLColumn must have a value
CHECKValue satisfies a boolean expression

Defining constraints when creating tables

CREATE TABLE customers (
 id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, -- PK auto-increment
 email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE, -- inline NOT NULL + UNIQUE
 age INT CHECK (age >= 0 AND age < 150), -- CHECK constraint
 state CHAR(2) DEFAULT 'US', -- DEFAULT value
 created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
 id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
 customer_id INT NOT NULL,
 total NUMERIC(10,2) CHECK (total >= 0),
 status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'pending',
 CONSTRAINT fk_customer
 FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)
 ON DELETE RESTRICT
 ON UPDATE CASCADE
);

-- Composite primary key (multiple columns together)
CREATE TABLE order_items (
 order_id INT,
 line_number INT,
 product_id INT NOT NULL,
 quantity INT NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
 PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_number), -- composite PK
 FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id)
);

FK behavior on delete/update

OptionWhen parent is deleted
RESTRICT (default)Block delete if any child rows exist
CASCADEDelete child rows too
SET NULLSet child FK column to NULL
SET DEFAULTSet child FK column to its default value

Adding constraints to existing tables

-- Add a constraint after the fact
ALTER TABLE customers
ADD CONSTRAINT unique_phone UNIQUE (phone);

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id);

ALTER TABLE products
ADD CONSTRAINT positive_price CHECK (price >= 0);

-- Drop a constraint
ALTER TABLE customers DROP CONSTRAINT unique_phone;

-- Rename a constraint (Postgres)
ALTER TABLE customers
RENAME CONSTRAINT unique_phone TO uniq_phone_number;

Indexes — how the database finds rows fast

WHAT AN INDEX IS
A separate data structure (usually a B-tree) that maps column values to row locations.

Think of it as the table's index at the back of a book — instead of scanning every page (full table scan), the database looks up the value and jumps directly to the right row.

PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints automatically create indexes. Other columns you index manually. 
-- Create an index on a single column
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_email ON customers(email);

-- Multi-column (composite) index
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_date ON orders(customer_id, order_date);
-- Used most efficiently when queries filter by customer_id first

-- UNIQUE index
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
-- Same effect as UNIQUE constraint

-- Partial index (Postgres) — only indexes rows that match
CREATE INDEX idx_active_users ON users(email) WHERE is_active = TRUE;
-- Smaller, faster index — but only helps queries with the same WHERE

-- Functional / expression index
CREATE INDEX idx_lower_email ON customers(LOWER(email));
-- Enables LOWER(email) lookups to use the index

-- Drop an index
DROP INDEX idx_customers_email;

What indexes speed up — and don't

Query patternIndex helps?
WHERE email = 'x'✓ Yes — exact match
WHERE email LIKE 'a%'✓ Yes — prefix match
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com'✗ No — leading wildcard kills it
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x'✗ No — unless functional index on LOWER(email)
WHERE age > 30✓ Yes — range scans use B-tree
JOIN ON a.id = b.a_id✓ Yes — index on b.a_id helps the join
ORDER BY created_at✓ Yes — sorted index avoids extra sort
Aggregates (COUNT(*))Sometimes — depends on the engine
Tiny table (< few thousand rows)Often unnecessary — full scan is fast enough

The composite index column-order rule

-- Suppose: CREATE INDEX idx ON orders(customer_id, order_date);

-- USES the index efficiently:
WHERE customer_id = 42 -- ✓ leftmost column
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND order_date > '2024-01-01' -- ✓ both columns
WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY order_date -- ✓ leftmost + sort

-- DOESN'T use the index well:
WHERE order_date > '2024-01-01' -- ✗ skips leftmost column
ORDER BY order_date -- ✗ same

-- Rule: a composite index helps when the query uses a LEFT-TO-RIGHT
-- prefix of the indexed columns. Skipping leftmost columns wastes the index.

Indexes cost something — they slow down writes

⚠ INDEX TRADE-OFFS

Every index must be updated on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE that touches the indexed column.

  • Read-heavy tables: more indexes = faster reads — usually worth it
  • Write-heavy tables: too many indexes = slow writes
  • Storage: indexes take disk space (sometimes 30%+ of table size)
  • Unused indexes: pure overhead — pg_stat_user_indexes / sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats helps find them

Rule of thumb: index columns used in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY on big tables. Don't index speculatively.

EXPLAIN — see what the optimizer plans to do

-- Show the estimated query plan (Postgres)
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = 'alice@x.com';
-- Output (simplified):
-- Index Scan using idx_customers_email on customers
-- Index Cond: (email = 'alice@x.com'::text)
-- Estimated cost: 0.29..8.30 rows=1

-- "Index Scan" = good. "Seq Scan" on big tables = bad.

-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually RUNS the query and shows real timing
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM customers WHERE state = 'CA';
-- Includes:
-- actual rows returned
-- actual time per step
-- total execution time
-- buffer hits/misses

-- Other engines:
-- MySQL: EXPLAIN
-- SQL Server: SET SHOWPLAN_ALL ON; ... or graphical "Display Estimated Execution Plan"
-- Oracle: EXPLAIN PLAN FOR ...; SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY);

Reading a query plan — key terms

Plan nodeMeans
Seq ScanReads every row in the table — fine for small tables, slow on big
Index ScanLooks up rows via index — usually what you want for selective queries
Index Only ScanAll needed data is in the index — no table read needed (fastest)
Bitmap Index ScanCombines multiple indexes for AND/OR filters
Nested Loop JoinGood for small result sets; bad for big tables without indexes
Hash JoinBuilds an in-memory hash of one side, scans the other — fast for big joins
Merge JoinUsed when both sides are pre-sorted by the join key
SortExplicit sort step — sometimes avoidable with a sorted index

Optimizing a slow query — checklist

-- Step 1: EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see what's actually happening
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...;

-- Step 2: Look for problems
-- • Seq Scan on big tables in WHERE → missing index
-- • High "actual rows" vs "estimated rows" → stats out of date (ANALYZE table)
-- • Nested Loop with millions of inner rows → missing index on join key
-- • Sort step in the plan → consider an index that matches the ORDER BY

-- Step 3: Common fixes
-- • CREATE INDEX on the WHERE / JOIN column
-- • Rewrite the query (avoid function calls on indexed columns)
-- • ANALYZE the table to refresh statistics
-- • Increase work_mem (Postgres) if you see "external sort" / "external merge"

-- Step 4: Re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm improvement

Functions on indexed columns kill index use

-- SLOW (index can't be used because of LOWER):
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'alice@x.com';

-- FAST: rewrite if your data is consistent
WHERE email = 'alice@x.com';

-- Or create a functional index:
CREATE INDEX idx_email_lower ON customers(LOWER(email));
-- Now LOWER(email) lookups CAN use the index

-- Same pattern: avoid CAST, SUBSTRING, etc. on indexed columns in WHERE

VIEWS — saved queries you can query against

-- A VIEW is a saved query, queryable like a table
CREATE VIEW active_customers AS
SELECT id, first_name, last_name, email
FROM customers
WHERE deleted_at IS NULL AND status = 'active';

-- Then use it like a table
SELECT * FROM active_customers WHERE state = 'CA';

-- Pros:
-- Hides complex query logic behind a simple name
-- Enables permission control (grant SELECT on the VIEW, not the underlying tables)
-- Encapsulates business rules

-- Cons:
-- Standard views are NOT cached — query runs every time
-- Materialized views ARE cached but must be refreshed

-- Materialized view (Postgres / Oracle / SQL Server) — pre-computed
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue AS
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month, SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY 1;

-- Refresh when underlying data changes
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue;

Worked example — debugging a slow report

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Scenario: "This report takes 45 seconds. Make it faster."

-- The slow query
SELECT
 c.first_name,
 SUM(o.total) AS revenue
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE LOWER(c.email) LIKE '%@gmail.com'
 AND o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.id, c.first_name;

-- Step 1: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows:
-- Seq Scan on customers (cost=0 rows=2M actual time=12000ms)
-- Filter: LOWER(email) LIKE '%@gmail.com'
-- Nested Loop -> Seq Scan on orders (cost=high)

-- Diagnosis:
-- 1. LOWER(email) + leading wildcard prevents any email index from being used
-- 2. orders.customer_id has no index → nested loop has to scan orders per customer
-- 3. orders.status has no index → can't pre-filter

-- Fixes:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_status ON orders(customer_id, status);
-- Helps the JOIN + the status filter

CREATE INDEX idx_customers_email_lower ON customers(LOWER(email));
-- Helps LOWER(email) lookups (still slow with leading wildcard but at least works)

-- Better: store an "email_domain" column and index that
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN email_domain VARCHAR(100);
UPDATE customers SET email_domain = SUBSTRING(email FROM POSITION('@' IN email) + 1);
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_email_domain ON customers(email_domain);

-- Then rewrite:
WHERE c.email_domain = 'gmail.com' -- exact match, uses index

-- Result: 45s → 80ms

Common bugs / misconceptions

⚠ TYPICAL MISTAKES
  1. Indexing every column — slows writes, wastes space, often doesn't help
  2. Composite index in wrong order — must match query column order
  3. Functions on indexed columns in WHERE — silently disables the index
  4. Forgetting that UNIQUE allows NULLs in most dialects (each NULL counts as distinct)
  5. FK to non-PK — works but unusual; usually you want FK → PK
  6. Deleting parent when CASCADE not set → FK violation
  7. EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production — it ACTUALLY runs the query, including DML
  8. Not running ANALYZE/UPDATE STATISTICS after big data changes — optimizer makes bad choices with stale stats
  9. Materialized view never refreshed → stale data presented as fresh
★ ON THE EXAM

"Primary key = ?" → UNIQUE + NOT NULL, identifies each row.

"Foreign key = ?" → references PK in another table, preserves referential integrity.

"NOT NULL = ?" → column must have a value.

"UNIQUE = ?" → values must be distinct (NULLs usually allowed).

"CHECK = ?" → row-level boolean validation.

"What does an index do?" → maps column values to row locations for fast lookup.

"When does an index NOT help?" → leading wildcard LIKE, functions on the column, very small tables.

"Composite index column order?" → use leftmost-prefix; query must filter on left columns to benefit.

"How do you see the query plan?" → EXPLAIN (estimated) or EXPLAIN ANALYZE (actual).

"Seq Scan vs Index Scan?" → Seq Scan reads every row; Index Scan jumps to matches.

"VIEW = ?" → saved query, queryable like a table; standard views recompute each time.

"Materialized view?" → pre-computed VIEW that caches results; must REFRESH.

"ON DELETE CASCADE?" → deleting parent row deletes child rows automatically.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Constraints enforce data quality: PRIMARY KEY (unique + not null), FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK
  • Composite primary keys use multiple columns together: PRIMARY KEY (a, b)
  • FOREIGN KEY behavior: RESTRICT (default), CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT
  • Indexes are separate data structures that speed up lookups — usually B-trees
  • PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE auto-create indexes; create others manually with CREATE INDEX
  • Composite indexes work when queries use a LEFT-TO-RIGHT PREFIX of indexed columns
  • Functions on indexed columns (LOWER, SUBSTRING) prevent index use — use functional indexes if needed
  • Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes — trade-off matters for write-heavy tables
  • EXPLAIN shows the query plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs and shows real timing
  • Look for "Seq Scan" on big tables in EXPLAIN — sign of a missing index
  • Run ANALYZE / UPDATE STATISTICS after big data changes for accurate optimizer choices
  • VIEW = saved query reusable as a table; MATERIALIZED VIEW = cached and must be refreshed
  • Optimize by: EXPLAIN ANALYZE → find Seq Scan or expensive node → add index or rewrite

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Most real analytics is time-series — "show me revenue per month", "compare this week to last week", "what's our 7-day moving average". Date and time functions are everywhere on the DataCamp SQL Associate exam, and they vary by dialect more than any other area of SQL. Knowing the core date functions and the half-open range pattern handles 90% of business reporting.

Date and time types

TypeStores
DATECalendar date: 2025-01-15
TIMETime of day: 14:30:00
TIMESTAMPDate + time: 2025-01-15 14:30:00
TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (TIMESTAMPTZ)Date + time + timezone info
INTERVAL (Postgres)Length of time: '3 days', '2 hours'

Date literals

-- ISO format 'YYYY-MM-DD' works in every dialect
WHERE order_date = '2025-01-15';
WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01 00:00:00';

-- Explicit casting (Postgres)
WHERE order_date = DATE '2025-01-15';
WHERE created_at = TIMESTAMP '2025-01-15 14:30:00';

-- "Current" values — these vary by dialect:
CURRENT_DATE -- today's date (standard SQL)
CURRENT_TIME -- current time
CURRENT_TIMESTAMP -- now (standard SQL)
NOW() -- same as CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (Postgres, MySQL)
GETDATE() -- SQL Server
SYSDATE -- Oracle

Extracting date parts

-- Standard SQL: EXTRACT (works in Postgres, MySQL, Oracle)
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) -- 2025
EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) -- 1
EXTRACT(DAY FROM order_date) -- 15
EXTRACT(HOUR FROM order_date) -- 14
EXTRACT(MINUTE FROM order_date) -- 30
EXTRACT(DOW FROM order_date) -- day of week (0=Sunday in Postgres)
EXTRACT(DOY FROM order_date) -- day of year (1-366)
EXTRACT(WEEK FROM order_date) -- week number
EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM order_date) -- 1-4

-- Postgres shortcut: DATE_PART (same as EXTRACT but takes a string)
DATE_PART('year', order_date)

-- SQL Server: DATEPART
DATEPART(year, order_date)
DATEPART(month, order_date)
DATEPART(weekday, order_date)

-- MySQL: YEAR, MONTH, DAY functions
YEAR(order_date)
MONTH(order_date)
DAYOFWEEK(order_date)
DAYOFYEAR(order_date)
WEEK(order_date)

Truncating dates — DATE_TRUNC

DATE_TRUNC — THE MOST USED ANALYTICS FUNCTION
Rounds a timestamp DOWN to the start of a period.

DATE_TRUNC('month', '2025-01-15 14:30:00') → 2025-01-01 00:00:00
DATE_TRUNC('day', '2025-01-15 14:30:00') → 2025-01-15 00:00:00
DATE_TRUNC('hour', '2025-01-15 14:30:00') → 2025-01-15 14:00:00

Essential for grouping rows by week/month/year for reports. 
-- Postgres / Snowflake / BigQuery: DATE_TRUNC
SELECT
 DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
 SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
-- Granularity options: microsecond, millisecond, second, minute, hour, day, week, month, quarter, year

-- SQL Server: DATEFROMPARTS or FORMAT
SELECT
 DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date), 1) AS month,
 SUM(total)
FROM orders GROUP BY ...;

-- MySQL: DATE_FORMAT or constructing a date
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m-01') AS month, SUM(total)
FROM orders GROUP BY 1;

Date arithmetic — adding and subtracting

-- Postgres: INTERVAL
order_date + INTERVAL '7 days'
order_date - INTERVAL '1 month'
CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year'
NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'

-- MySQL: DATE_ADD / DATE_SUB
DATE_ADD(order_date, INTERVAL 7 DAY)
DATE_SUB(order_date, INTERVAL 1 MONTH)

-- SQL Server: DATEADD
DATEADD(day, 7, order_date)
DATEADD(month, -1, order_date)

-- Difference between two dates
-- Postgres: subtraction gives INTERVAL
order_date - signup_date -- returns an interval

-- DATEDIFF — most dialects
DATEDIFF('day', start_date, end_date) -- SQL Server: DATEDIFF(day, start, end)
DATEDIFF(end_date, start_date) -- MySQL: returns days
TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, start, end) -- MySQL: in any unit

-- Postgres: AGE() returns interval
AGE(end_date, start_date) -- "3 mons 14 days"
EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end - start))/86400 -- days as float

The half-open date range pattern (revisited)

⚠ THE CLASSIC TIMESTAMP BUG

For TIMESTAMP columns, BETWEEN excludes the late part of the end date:

-- BAD — misses orders later in the day on Dec 31
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-12-01' AND '2024-12-31';
-- Translates to BETWEEN '2024-12-01 00:00:00' AND '2024-12-31 00:00:00'
-- An order at '2024-12-31 14:00:00' is EXCLUDED

-- GOOD — half-open interval
WHERE order_date >= '2024-12-01'
 AND order_date < '2025-01-01';
-- Catches everything in December correctly

The pattern: >= start AND < start_of_next_period. Works for any granularity (hour, day, week, month, year).

Common time-series query patterns

1. Per-period totals

-- Daily, weekly, monthly revenue
SELECT
 DATE_TRUNC('day', order_date) AS day,
 SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01'
 AND status = 'completed'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

2. Period-over-period comparison

-- Month-over-month using LAG window function (ch4/s3)
WITH monthly AS (
 SELECT
 DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
 SUM(total) AS revenue
 FROM orders
 WHERE status = 'completed'
 GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
 month,
 revenue,
 LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month,
 revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS abs_change,
 100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
 / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0) AS pct_change
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

3. Rolling / moving averages

-- 7-day moving average of daily orders
WITH daily AS (
 SELECT
 DATE_TRUNC('day', order_date) AS day,
 COUNT(*) AS num_orders
 FROM orders
 GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
 day,
 num_orders,
 AVG(num_orders) OVER (
 ORDER BY day
 ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
 ) AS ma_7day
FROM daily;

4. Year-to-date (YTD)

SELECT SUM(total) AS ytd_revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE_TRUNC('year', CURRENT_DATE)
 AND order_date <= CURRENT_DATE
 AND status = 'completed';

-- Same-period-last-year (for comparison)
SELECT SUM(total) AS prior_ytd
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE_TRUNC('year', CURRENT_DATE) - INTERVAL '1 year'
 AND order_date <= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year'
 AND status = 'completed';

5. Generating a date series — filling gaps

-- Postgres: generate_series
SELECT generate_series(
 '2024-01-01'::date,
 '2024-12-31'::date,
 '1 day'::interval
) AS day;
-- Returns one row per day

-- Use it to build a "calendar scaffold" so empty days appear in reports
WITH calendar AS (
 SELECT generate_series(
 DATE '2024-01-01',
 DATE '2024-12-31',
 INTERVAL '1 day'
 )::date AS day
)
SELECT
 c.day,
 COALESCE(COUNT(o.id), 0) AS num_orders
FROM calendar c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON DATE(o.order_date) = c.day
GROUP BY c.day
ORDER BY c.day;
-- Every day appears, including zero-order days

-- MySQL doesn't have generate_series — use a numbers table or recursive CTE
WITH RECURSIVE days AS (
 SELECT DATE '2024-01-01' AS day
 UNION ALL
 SELECT day + INTERVAL 1 DAY FROM days WHERE day < DATE '2024-12-31'
)
SELECT day FROM days;

6. Cohort analysis — group customers by signup period

-- "For each signup month, how many customers placed at least one order
-- in their 1st, 2nd, 3rd month after signup?"
WITH cohorts AS (
 SELECT
 id AS customer_id,
 DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date) AS cohort_month
 FROM customers
),
order_months AS (
 SELECT
 c.cohort_month,
 c.customer_id,
 DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS order_month,
 EXTRACT(MONTH FROM AGE(o.order_date, c.cohort_month)) AS month_offset
 FROM cohorts c
 INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
SELECT
 cohort_month,
 month_offset,
 COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS active_customers
FROM order_months
GROUP BY cohort_month, month_offset
ORDER BY cohort_month, month_offset;

Worked example — full sales dashboard

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: "Build a monthly report covering all of 2024: monthly revenue, prior month, % change, year-to-date cumulative."

WITH months AS (
 SELECT generate_series(
 DATE '2024-01-01',
 DATE '2024-12-01',
 INTERVAL '1 month'
 )::date AS month
),
monthly AS (
 SELECT
 m.month,
 COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS revenue
 FROM months m
 LEFT JOIN orders o
 ON DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) = m.month
 AND o.status = 'completed'
 GROUP BY m.month
)
SELECT
 month,
 revenue,
 LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month_revenue,
 ROUND(
 100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
 / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0),
 2
 ) AS pct_change,
 SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS ytd_cumulative
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

-- Outputs all 12 months even if some had no sales (calendar scaffold),
-- with month-over-month change and running YTD totals.

Common time-series bugs

⚠ TOP MISTAKES
  1. BETWEEN with timestamps excludes late-day data on the end date — use >= AND <
  2. String comparisons with date columns — works by accident if format is ISO; fails for other formats
  3. Time zone confusion — TIMESTAMP without zone vs WITH zone (TIMESTAMPTZ) behave differently across servers
  4. Missing dates in reports — need a calendar scaffold (generate_series or recursive CTE)
  5. Day-of-week semantics vary by engine — 0=Sunday in some, 1=Monday in others
  6. Mixing DATE_TRUNC level and aggregate level — grouping by day but charting per month
  7. Using YEAR(date) etc. on indexed columns — function call disables the index
★ ON THE EXAM

"Today's date?" → CURRENT_DATE.

"Now timestamp?" → CURRENT_TIMESTAMP or NOW().

"Year of a date?" → EXTRACT(YEAR FROM col) (standard) or YEAR(col) (MySQL/SQL Server).

"Truncate to month?" → DATE_TRUNC('month', col) (Postgres).

"All orders in 2024?" → WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01'.

"Add 30 days?" → col + INTERVAL '30 days' (Postgres) / DATE_ADD(col, INTERVAL 30 DAY) (MySQL).

"Difference in days?" → DATEDIFF(end, start) or subtraction in Postgres.

"Fill gaps in time series?" → calendar scaffold with generate_series or recursive CTE.

"Month-over-month change?" → LAG(metric) OVER (ORDER BY month) window function.

"Cumulative total?" → SUM(metric) OVER (ORDER BY date).

"7-day moving average?" → AVG(metric) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Date types: DATE (day only), TIME (time only), TIMESTAMP (both), TIMESTAMPTZ (with timezone)
  • ISO format 'YYYY-MM-DD' is universal — always safe to write as a literal
  • EXTRACT(unit FROM date) is the standard date-part function (Postgres, MySQL, Oracle)
  • DATE_TRUNC('month', col) is the workhorse for monthly/weekly aggregation in Postgres
  • Dialect-specific shortcuts: YEAR(), MONTH() (MySQL/SQL Server); DATEPART (SQL Server)
  • Date arithmetic: INTERVAL (Postgres), DATE_ADD/DATE_SUB (MySQL), DATEADD (SQL Server)
  • Always use half-open ranges >= start AND < next_period_start for timestamp filtering
  • BETWEEN with timestamps misses late-day data on the end date
  • generate_series (Postgres) or recursive CTE creates date scaffolds for filling gaps in reports
  • Time-series window patterns: LAG for previous period; SUM OVER ORDER BY for running totals; AVG OVER frame for moving averages
  • Day-of-week numbering varies by engine — verify before using DOW
  • Functions on indexed date columns prevent index use — keep WHERE clauses index-friendly
